papers.Title: User Embeddings are Superpositions of Interpretable Behavioral Modes
papers.Abstract: User embeddings are central components of modern recommendation, personalization, and behavioral modeling systems. Though these embeddings can compactly encode rich behavioral information, they are inherently dense and opaque, limiting interpretability. To address this gap, we argue that user embeddings can be understood as sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes. This structure is directly predicted by generative models of user behavior for linear embeddings and extends approximately to deep-learning representations by the superposition hypothesis. Superimposed modes can naturally be recovered by sparse dictionary learning methods, such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and recovered modes can be automatically named and queried in natural language. We validate mode recovery against known ground truth on synthetic data, where SAEs recover modes better than classical sparse baselines, including on transformer-encoded embeddings. We then apply the method to classical and transformer-based user embeddings from two real-world datasets. We also show how the corresponding natural-language labels enable zero-shot audience retrieval and characterization over embeddings never trained on text. The framework is post-hoc and model-agnostic, requiring no modification to the upstream embedding system.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper introduces a sparse superposition framework for user embeddings, where sparse autoencoders recover interpretable behavioral modes automatically labeled via natural language prompts, extending the superposition hypothesis to deep learning representations.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Recommendation Systems, Digital Advertising, E-Commerce, Streaming Media
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate sparse autoencoder mode decomposition into recommendation pipelines within 6 months. Retire black-box embedding architectures that resist sparse decomposability by Q3 2027.
papers.Tags: User Embeddings, Sparse Autoencoders, Behavioral Modes, Interpretability, Recommendation Systems
papers.Hook: Sparse autoencoders decompose user embeddings into named behavioral modes.

papers.Title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
papers.Abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.
papers.Core_Innovation: Agents operate entirely in latent space, avoiding text decoding overhead. A novelty filter selects distinct ideas using hidden-vector distances, while a summarizer aggregates combined KV caches for crossover.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Scientific Computing, Pharmaceutical Research, Financial Modeling
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Legacy LLM Prompting, Traditional Optimization Consulting
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate prototype funding for latent-swarm integration in scientific computing teams within 6 months to measure optimization gains. Reallocate legacy LLM chain-of-thought licensing budgets toward latent-space infrastructure development.
papers.Tags: Latent Space, Evolutionary Optimization, Agent Swarms, KV Caching, Novelty Filtering
papers.Hook: Latent-agent swarms optimize problems without textual chain-of-thought per round.

papers.Title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists
papers.Abstract: AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (+158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists' own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.
papers.Core_Innovation: An autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's research question and reproduces its method as a runnable baseline environment, enabling AI scientist evaluation against human performance.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Scientific Research, Drug Discovery
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Scientific Publishing, Manual Research Methods
papers.Decision_Perspective: Launch a pilot program within 6 months to convert top-cited papers into runnable AI scientist environments for internal R&D acceleration. Invest in teams capable of building and maintaining reproducible research environments.
papers.Tags: AI scientists, research environments, reproducible science, autonomous pipelines, scientific R&D
papers.Hook: Research papers become runnable AI scientist environments instantly.

papers.Title: XStack: A Benchmark for ML Repo Migration
papers.Abstract: ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware. This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2) a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories, and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduce XStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our grading criteria, based on the source repository's published result, authenticated and calibrated by us. Migration by agents remains unreliable: Claude Opus 5 passes 75%, GPT-5.6-sol 45%, and every other agent at most 40%. XStack is a step toward freeing ML code from its ecosystem. We release XStack to make progress toward reliable migration across frameworks and hardware measurable.
papers.Core_Innovation: XStack enforces output grading against authenticated source results and quantifies cross-framework migration reliability
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Cloud Computing, GPU Hardware
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate engineering resources to integrate XStack-style migration pipelines into existing ML workflows within the next quarter. Discontinue framework-exclusive research contracts that cannot demonstrate cross-platform reproducibility.
papers.Tags: ML Migration, Framework Interoperability, Agent Evaluation, Cross-Hardware
papers.Hook: Agents migrate PyTorch repos to JAX on TPUs, benchmarking cross-framework feasibility

papers.Title: Same Behavior, Different Mechanism: What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information
papers.Abstract: Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system's causal transition law that describe how it computes, not what it outputs. Experiments see that law only through finite, partial and noisy interventions. We ask when such a quantity is identifiable from an experiment's access, continuous in the mechanism and certifiable from finite data, and answer exactly for a deliberately demanding case - the integrated information $\varphi$ of integrated information theory - in stochastic networks of four and five units with known ground truth. Behavior can be silent: a recurrent and a feed-forward network with identical input-output laws at their response delay carry 0.28 and 0 bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4-53 trials. Partial access can be just as blind: in our examples, units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of 0.30-1.02 bits that no sample size lowers, and in all-but-self parity networks, recordings of any length see several hidden units only through the product of their fidelities - a symmetry that one intervention broke in exact checks. The measure has sharp edges: because $\varphi$ selects a partition, and the cause and effect it specifies, by one criterion and reports another, infinitesimal changes of mechanism that cross an edge change it by 25-100% at 99% of the edges we found in random networks, and about 1% of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport it by more than 20%. One-sided claims survive: the same data certify a lower bound on both sides of an edge, and we prove $\varphi>1.004$ bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it from about $10^7$ controlled transitions with false-certificate probability at most $α$. Measurability is thus a design question with computable answers.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper establishes exact identifiability conditions for mechanism-level functionals like φ from finite, partial, and noisy interventions, proving that partial access imposes irreducible precision floors regardless of sample size.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Neuroscience, AI Auditing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget for finite-experiment φ audits on black-box AI systems within the next 6 months to certify internal mechanism integrity. Discontinue output-only validation pipelines for high-stakes neural networks once φ precision floors are quantified.
papers.Tags: Integrated Information, Finite Experiments, Mechanism Identifiability, Partial Observability
papers.Hook: Finite experiments certify integrated mechanism from stochastic networks, even with identical input-output laws.

papers.Title: Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion
papers.Abstract: To interpret a direction in a language model's residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.
papers.Core_Innovation: MAEMs are language models trained via a label-free reinforcement learning objective to maximize cosine similarity between residual stream directions and generated text activations, enabling inversion of held-out directions without corpus constraints.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Interpretability
papers.Decision_Perspective: Direct funding to MAEM research teams within the next two quarters to integrate activation inversion into LLM interpretability pipelines. Replace corpus-search-based activation analysis with MAEM-generated exemplars for all new model releases.
papers.Tags: MAEM, Activation Inversion, Residual Stream, SAE
papers.Hook: MAEMs generate text exemplars from residual stream directions at scale, bypassing corpus limits.

papers.Title: Adversarial Training with Large Step Sizes: Implicit Bias, Optimization, and Sharpness
papers.Abstract: Adversarial Training (AT) is an important method for improving model robustness. We study the dynamics of deterministic Gradient Descent (GD) in AT. Most existing works in this direction focus on the small or vanishing step sizes regime, where GD resembles a continuous-time flow. However, such step sizes can make training inefficient and are rarely used in practice. In this paper, we study the AT dynamics of GD with large constant step sizes. We first study GD in adversarial linear logistic regression, focusing on two aspects: where the model parameters converge (implicit bias) and how quickly the losses decrease (optimization). We then turn to neural networks training and study how the sharpness of losses evolve during AT. Our results advance the understanding of the behaviors of GD with large step sizes in AT and highlight three key differences from its behavior in Standard Training (ST): (i) the implicit bias gap between AT and ST, previously established only for small step sizes, persists for arbitrarily large constant step sizes, (ii) different from ST, there is no uniform rate of convergence for the optimization error in AT, and (iii) sharpness can exhibit two-stage dynamics that differ from the Edge-of-Stability behavior observed in ST.
papers.Core_Innovation: This work analyzes GD with large constant step sizes in adversarial training, establishing implicit bias, optimization dynamics, and loss sharpness across linear logistic regression and neural networks, then quantifying three key divergences from standard training behavior
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, Cloud Computing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate capital to large-step-size adversarial training frameworks within 6 months to capture optimization and sharpness advantages. Immediately deprioritize small-step-size AT pipelines as implicit bias gaps emerge in production models.
papers.Tags: Adversarial Training, Optimization, Implicit Bias, Step Size, Sharpness
papers.Hook: Large step sizes enable efficient adversarial training while reshaping implicit bias and loss sharpness

papers.Title: Unpacking the Compute Efficiency of Strong-to-Weak OPD against GRPO
papers.Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning? We systematically compare vanilla reverse-KL OPD with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain, and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs. With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP at matched settings, even when the teacher is further trained with GRPO, and often suffers response-length inflation. Yet a different teacher changes the picture: when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy on math with $50\times$ fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs to reach the same accuracy. Following the same teacher setting, we consistently observe this high efficiency with a larger student, on code, and in a second model family. On a single domain, however, the GRPO checkpoint is already the desired model, so distilling it adds to total compute. Across domains, separate GRPO checkpoints hold different capabilities, and no single checkpoint serves every domain. Multi-teacher OPD (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) consolidates per-domain GRPO experts into a single student that matches each expert's accuracy, with the distillation stage costing only 5.2% (on 2 domains) and 8.0% (on 4 domains) of the specialist training FLOPs. Counting specialist training and distillation together, this pipeline reaches joint GRPO's performance on the 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.
papers.Core_Innovation: When the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD matches its accuracy on math using 50× fewer distillation FLOPs.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Education Technology
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Reinforcement Learning, External Teacher AI
papers.Decision_Perspective: Product teams should immediately prototype OPD pipelines using self-GRPO teachers to validate 50x FLOP savings. Compute-heavy LLM training projects should deprioritize external-teacher GRPO in favor of this distillation pathway.
papers.Tags: OPD, GRPO, Distillation, Compute Efficiency, Math Reasoning
papers.Hook: OPD matches GRPO math accuracy with 50x fewer FLOPs when teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint.

papers.Title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts
papers.Abstract: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.
papers.Core_Innovation: The core innovation pairs a four-component artifact taxonomy with an agent-driven construction workflow and an execution auditor to produce verifiable, reproducible ML experiment runs.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Finance
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget to integrate ReproBridge artifact standards into internal ML pipelines within 12 months. Trigger the integration when model reproduction requests exceed five per quarter.
papers.Tags: ML reproducibility, artifact standardization, agent workflow
papers.Hook: ReproBridge enables agents to reproducibly reconstruct ML experiments from standardized artifacts.

papers.Title: A Hidden Markov Preference Model for Online Prediction of Adversary Actions
papers.Abstract: A defender anticipating an attacker needs a probability distribution over the attacker's next action from information available before that action occurs. Two structures complicate this: the attacker's behavioral regime persists and can switch within an episode, and each action combines an operation with state-dependent arguments whose feasible values change over time. We capture both with a hidden Markov model whose latent state is the active regime and whose regime-conditioned action law is defined on a feasibility-masked tree of executable actions. The same likelihood forms the next-action distribution and updates the regime belief once the action is seen, and a partially observed prefix contributes its resolved local factors. Estimation separates into convex logistic fits that Baum-Welch reuses when regimes are unlabeled. We derive a reach-weighted nodewise KL expression for regime information, a sequence-wise log-loss bound for switching regime paths, and a uniform fallback guarantee. On the CAGE 2 cyber defense benchmark the filtered latent state is worth 0.8 nats per step, and after a controller switch the loss begins to fall in three steps against ten for a recurrent baseline.
papers.Core_Innovation: The model defines regime-conditioned action probabilities on a feasibility-masked executable tree, with a unified likelihood that simultaneously predicts next actions and updates regime beliefs.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Cybersecurity, Defense
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to prototype feasibility-masked hidden Markov models for adversary action forecasting within six months. Phase out static rule-based threat models that cannot adapt to switching behavioral regimes.
papers.Tags: HiddenMarkovModel, AdversaryAction, FeasibilityMaskedTree, RegimeSwitching
papers.Hook: Online adversary action prediction with switching regimes and feasibility-masked trees.

papers.Title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
papers.Abstract: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies, produced by three separate processes and checked for overlap with the training data, with five candidates per question and, for eight of them, also with eighteen. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (English-derived jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release is more accurate in every setting, by up to 0.24. Eleven of these fourteen gains survive a Holm correction (slang with eighteen candidates and descriptive sentences with five do not), and for jargon on all labels the label-level interval excludes zero in both settings. On abbreviations and opaque codes it gives no usable gain: on abbreviations it is not better, and worse on the clean slice, and on opaque codes both releases stay at or below chance once labels related to training options are removed. In most cells where accuracy rises, the risk-coverage area falls, but with eighteen candidates confident errors rise on jargon and slang. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.
papers.Core_Innovation: The augmentation generates multiple surface-form variants of each routing label during inference. This decouples accuracy from developer-controlled fixed wordings.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Technology, Finance
papers.Decision_Perspective: Deploy surface-form label augmentation in typed-decision systems within six months. Replace static label wordings with augmented variants in all production classifiers.
papers.Tags: Label Augmentation, Typed-Decision, Multilingual NLP, Cross-Encoder
papers.Hook: Surface-form label augmentation improves typed-decision accuracy on unfamiliar words at request time

papers.Title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety
papers.Abstract: Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. Yet we continue to build increasingly powerful systems without fully understanding how they work, how they will behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to reliably control them. Mechanistic interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling behaviour. We survey mechanistic interpretability for AI safety in order to answer the question: Does understanding how models work actually make them safer? We place mechanistic interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare its mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation. We introduce the foundations of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and survey methods for feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery and causal verification, explaining intermediate representations in natural language, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Finally, we examine how mechanistic understanding can support AI safety, including knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring, and assess its limitations, failure modes, open problems, and relationship to behavioural safety measures. We also release a repository of code notebooks with worked examples that reproduce key findings from surveyed methods, allowing readers to build intuition through hands-on experimentation.
papers.Core_Innovation: Survey mapping mechanistic interpretability methods to AI internal representation analysis for safety evaluation and control.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Technology, Finance, Healthcare, Cybersecurity
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Opaque AI Providers, Unregulated AI Deployers
papers.Decision_Perspective: Mandate mechanistic interpretability audits for all in-house AI systems within 24 months to satisfy anticipated AI safety regulations. Divest capital from black-box AI deployment projects that cannot demonstrate internal traceability.
papers.Tags: Mechanistic Interpretability, AI Safety, Neural Networks, Model Interpretability, AI Risk
papers.Hook: Mechanistic interpretability enables predictive control and evaluation of AI internal computations.

papers.Title: MedGraph: Maintaining Patient State with Graph Memory for Long-Term Medical Dialogue
papers.Abstract: LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the errors of five memory systems on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph memory built for these three cases. Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. Retrieval ranks the patient's chains as units, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and adds the original dialogue text; a patient profile lists every recorded safety fact with every question. On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph has the highest overall accuracy with both a GPT and a Qwen backbone, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines, with efficient memory construction and answering in the GPT setting.
papers.Core_Innovation: Session-dated facts are extracted and attributed to individual patients, then linked into medication-diagnosis-measurement chains. Retrieval reads chains time-locked to the query, injects original dialogue excerpts, and surfaces a patient-profile safety list.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Healthcare NLP, Clinical Decision Support, Telemedicine
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Medical Transcription, Static EHR Workflows, Generic LLM Assistants
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate MedGraph's graph-memory pipeline into flagship EHR platforms within Q3 2026, triggering mandatory safety-fact profiling for all patient-facing LLMs. Deprecate static-schema medical assistants that cannot attribute facts to individual patients across visits.
papers.Tags: Graph Memory, Longitudinal Dialogue, Medical AI, Patient Safety, Time-Aware Retrieval
papers.Hook: Graph-memory tracks patient state across longitudinal medical dialogues with dated, attributed chains.

papers.Title: Cross-Border Ownership and Input Access: Evidence from the Lithium Supply Chain
papers.Abstract: How does cross-border ownership shape the lithium supply chain? Using global data on mines and refineries, I estimate a model in which ownership can lower refiners' effective ore costs, encourage mines to restrict spot sales, and soften competition. To study these effects, I examine policies motivated by national security concerns about reliable access to critical mineral inputs: divestiture of Chinese stakes in overseas producers and a ban on ore exports to China. Divestiture increases spot ore supply but leaves lithium output nearly unchanged, while continued trade preserves Chinese access to ore. The export ban reduces global lithium supply because refining capacity elsewhere cannot fully replace lost Chinese production. Ownership transfers do not reserve ore for domestic production; restricting Chinese access imposes a substantial supply cost at existing capacities.
papers.Core_Innovation: Structural modeling estimates how cross-border ownership lowers refiners' effective ore costs while inducing mines to restrict spot sales, then quantifies counterfactual supply impacts of divestiture and export bans.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Refining, Spot Trading
papers.Decision_Perspective: Accelerate non-Chinese refinery spot-ore procurement contracts within six months to offset export-ban supply risks. Divest Chinese equity stakes in overseas lithium assets to secure domestic supply chain resilience.
papers.Tags: Cross-Border Ownership, Lithium Refining, Trade Policy, Spot Markets
papers.Hook: Divestiture liberates spot ore without reducing total lithium output.

papers.Title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI
papers.Abstract: Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. Yet the model sees the current dialogue but not the workspace around it. We explore meta access---giving the assistant a structured, permissioned view of the interface itself and propose a ladder of levels: feature tutoring; metadata, settings, and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages, confirmed mutation, and full orchestration. Meta access can turn a chat client from many screens into one entry point for finding, navigating, organising, and operating it, while raising risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. General-purpose agentic harnesses are runtimes; because they can change their own settings, meta access becomes reflexive and needs a separate control-plane boundary. We ground this in the Meta Chat prototype of the Chat AI client. It builds bounded context from, e.g., summaries, settings, and relevant messages; links references to conversations, topics, and personas; supports confirmed, reversible changes; offers a browsable tutorial library; and recommends personas as user-started conversations. By exposing application state in structured form, meta access can extend screen readers from widget descriptions to semantic workspace operations. Meta access thus turns chat from a window onto one conversation into a control layer for the whole workspace, extending chat toward agentic capability without surrendering user control. As assistants become embedded in IDEs, dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels through a debugger-like interface.
papers.Core_Innovation: Meta access introduces a permissioned interface view layer, letting LLMs perceive and interact with workspace elements beyond chat content. A defined ladder governs retrieval, mutation, and orchestration capabilities.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Software, AI, SaaS, Productivity
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund immediate integration of meta access layers into flagship chat AI products within 12 months to secure UX differentiation. Mandate control-plane separation for agentic harnesses to prevent prompt injection exploits.
papers.Tags: Meta Access, LLM Interfaces, Agentic Orchestration, Control-Plane, Prompt Injection
papers.Hook: Meta access grants LLMs structured workspace awareness, unifying chat navigation and orchestration.

papers.Title: Failure Prediction and Classification in Vision-Language-Action Models Via Calibrated Latent Probing
papers.Abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable general-purpose embodied intelligence, but their performance is brittle under distribution shift, where unanticipated failures can damage equipment or endanger people. Deploying VLAs in real-world systems therefore requires a runtime monitor that is timely, calibrated, and informative while being efficient enough to run on the edge. Existing methods fail to fulfill these requirements. We present VLA-Tug, a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a VLA backbone that improves early failure detection and bounds the missed-detection and false-alarm rates, with minimal inference overhead. We show that supervising on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory increases early failure detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline. Under shift to unseen tasks, the bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates remain valid in up to 86% of runs, versus at most 21% for baselines. Unlike existing methods, VLA-Tug predicts the failure mode to enable corrective actions, raising top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44% over a majority baseline. VLA-Tug enables real-time monitoring where the well-timed and informative probe supports lightweight steering that improves task success. We release a dataset of 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes to support future work on latent failure detection in VLAs at https://vla-tug.github.io.
papers.Core_Innovation: VLA-Tug adds a latent-layer probe trained on pre-failure segments to generate calibrated failure-detection bounds with sub-5% inference overhead.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Manufacturing, Autonomous Vehicles
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund VLA-Tug prototype integration into edge robotics platforms within 6 months. Phase out legacy VLA monitoring stacks that lack calibrated shift-bounds.
papers.Tags: Vision-Language-Action, Failure Detection, Edge Computing, Calibrated Probing, Distribution Shift
papers.Hook: Latent probes enable calibrated, real-time failure detection in VLAs at the edge.

papers.Title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents
papers.Abstract: Researchers use large language models as agents in social simulations, where agents are prompted with observations and background information intended to shape their actions. Yet LLM agents have been shown to substantially change their behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, creating a validation problem for social simulation. One plausible hypothesis is that this brittleness reflects a lack of grounding and can be reduced by enriching the context provided to the agents. Whether richer context improves robustness remains unclear, in part because context richness and robustness are rarely defined in ways that support controlled comparisons. We address the first need with controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that systematically enriches distinct types of context: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding. We address the second by introducing selective robustness as a validation criterion: insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt variation combined with a directional response to decision-relevant changes in the social world. We demonstrate the framework in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, showing how it can be used to identify which forms of context enrichment produce more desirable and robust agent behavior. We find that these forms of enrichment produce distinct behavioral patterns that vary between the two models tested.
papers.Core_Innovation: Systematic prompt substitution rules generate four distinct context enrichment types, enabling isolation of grounding effects from nominal prompt variations.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Social Media, Virtual Assistants, Gaming, Customer Service
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate resources to integrate controlled context enrichment into LLM agent pipelines within the next quarter. Deprecate uncalibrated prompt-variation testing suites that cannot validate selective robustness.
papers.Tags: LLM Agents, Context Enrichment, Selective Robustness, Social Simulation, Prompt Substitution
papers.Hook: LLM agents gain systematic context enrichment with provable behavioral stability under prompt variations.

papers.Title: FlowReconBench: Accuracy, calibration and cost of learned and classical flow reconstruction from sparse sensors
papers.Abstract: Reconstructing full flow fields from sparse sensors requires prior assumptions about unmeasured regions and physical variables. Yet it remains unclear when learned models outperform classical estimators and which aspects of their predictions can be trusted. FlowReconBench evaluates ten learned and five classical methods on three regimes: a laminar cylinder wake across Reynolds numbers, two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence and a large-scale three-dimensional (3D) isotropic turbulence. Methods share leakage-controlled splits and sensor draws and are scored on per-channel error, ensemble spread, calibration, spectra and cost. The leading method changes for each regime. Classical methods perform strongly in low-order and dense-sensing regimes. On the cylinder wake, linear stochastic estimation and gappy proper orthogonal decomposition lead, including for unobserved pressure. In 3D, inverse-distance weighting matches the best learned methods on observed channels. Data-driven methods become superior at decreasing sensor density or poor sensor observability. On Kolmogorov flow, continuous ranked probability score and error yield different method rankings: generative models offer broader but underdispersed ensembles, while deterministic models prioritize pointwise error. Generative models balance this tradeoff through their sampler budget, with a larger budget improving ensemble quality at higher computational cost. In 3D, scaling tests demonstrate that queryable methods are flat in memory, while full-grid construction methods run out of memory. Observing only 2 of 4 fields leaves the problem kinematically underconstrained, yet a latent model can reproduce structural similarities to the ground truth.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces a controlled benchmark with shared leakage splits and five metrics to head-to-head evaluate learned and classical flow reconstruction across turbulence regimes.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Aerospace, Automotive, Environmental Monitoring
papers.Decision_Perspective: Mandate classical flow reconstruction benchmarks for all learned model claims within the next six months. Immediately deprioritize any method that underperforms classical estimators on per-channel error across target turbulence regimes.
papers.Tags: flow reconstruction, sparse sensors, turbulence benchmark, learned models, classical methods
papers.Hook: Enables regime-specific flow reconstruction benchmarking against classical and learned baselines.

papers.Title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories
papers.Abstract: Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces a 1,000-sample 11-task-type benchmark with fine-grained annotations for affordance grounding trajectory planning and operation reasoning specifically designed to evaluate MLLM execution capabilities in self-driving chemical labs.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Pharmaceuticals, Chemical Manufacturing, Laboratory Automation
papers.Decision_Perspective: Require MLLM agent development aligned to BEAKER tasks within 12 months to gain first-mover advantage in autonomous chemical execution. Redirect R&D funds from generic multimodal models to teams achieving top BEAKER benchmark scores.
papers.Tags: Embodied AI, Chemical Automation, Benchmark, MLLM, Affordance Grounding
papers.Hook: First benchmark enables execution-oriented evaluation of embodied AI for chemical laboratory automation.

papers.Title: FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research
papers.Abstract: AI agents are playing an increasingly important role in physics research. However, existing physics benchmarks only evaluate fixed questions, isolated sub-tasks, or paper reproduction with given solutions, and rarely check research quality alongside correctness. We introduce FrontierPhysics, an end-to-end benchmark with 56 tasks made by 42 physicists based on their own research, covering nine domains across theoretical, computational, and experimental physics. Each task requires agents to review the literature, develop a research plan, conduct research and experiments, and produce structured outputs and scientific manuscripts. Combining deterministic verifiers with expert-authored rubrics, FrontierPhysics evaluates whether agents' research is correct and publishable. Across 22 models in 26 configurations, no configuration passes more than 46 of its 168 rollouts. Manual review of agent trajectories shows that frontier agents' main weaknesses are insufficiently rigorous reasoning and limited expert intuition, rather than gaps in physics knowledge or execution errors.
papers.Core_Innovation: FrontierPhysics constructs 56 end-to-end research tasks from actual physicist workflows, requiring literature review, planning, execution, and manuscript generation, then evaluates agent outputs using deterministic verifiers paired with expert-authored rubrics.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Pharmaceuticals, Energy, Materials Science, Semiconductors
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Simulation Software, Manual Research Services
papers.Decision_Perspective: Invest in benchmark-driven agent development to achieve publishable physics research within eighteen months. Prioritize funding teams integrating deterministic verifiers with expert rubrics for immediate deployment.
papers.Tags: AI Agents, Physics Research, End-to-End Benchmark, Deterministic Verifiers, Scientific Manuscript
papers.Hook: AI agents now autonomously conduct end-to-end physics research and generate publishable manuscripts.

papers.Title: Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation
papers.Abstract: Humanoid robots have the potential to automate a wide range of physical tasks. Progress toward generalist humanoid autonomy, however, remains constrained by a data bottleneck: mapping pixels and free-form language to low-level joint commands requires paired supervision, and no corpus of such data exists at sufficiently large scale. Some approaches rely on human teleoperation and wearable capture devices, which require at least an hour of human time to produce an hour of data. We present HALO, a humanoid autonomy system powered by a pipeline that synthesizes vision-language-motion data across a thousand procedurally generated homes. The corpus scales with compute rather than human labor. HALO acquires a repertoire of physical skills, including sitting on chairs, navigating to named objects, stepping sideways through half-open doors, crouching and crawling beneath tables, and pushing boxes. It orchestrates these skills to solve composite, long-horizon tasks. Without ever seeing a real home during training, HALO transfers zero-shot to the physical world, achieving a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-halo/ for code and videos.
papers.Core_Innovation: The system couples procedural home generation with vision-language-motion modeling to synthesize humanoid skill repertoires at compute scale, bypassing human teleoperation
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Home Service Robotics, Manufacturing, Logistics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate capital to large-scale simulation pipelines within 12 months to capture synthetic data advantages before real-world collection costs spiral. Phase out human teleoperation data labeling contracts once composite task success rates exceed 80% in validated benchmarks.
papers.Tags: Humanoid Motion, Simulation, Vision-Language, Procedural Generation
papers.Hook: Procedural home simulation generates generalist humanoid skills at scale without human teleoperation

papers.Title: Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement
papers.Abstract: The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings - where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task - which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment - targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously - and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models.
papers.Core_Innovation: Develops a multi-task RL framework enabling simultaneous generalist policy improvement across diverse robot manipulation and navigation tasks, replacing single-task adaptation pipelines.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Manufacturing, Logistics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Mandate internal robotics teams to integrate multi-task RL adaptation layers within 9 months, triggering immediate evaluation of single-task vendor performance. Phase out single-task robotics contracts upon demonstrated multi-task improvement, redirecting budgets to generalist policy development.
papers.Tags: Reinforcement Learning, Generalist Policies, Multi-Task Robotics
papers.Hook: Generalist robot policies now improve across diverse tasks via RL adaptation.

papers.Title: Occlusion for Free: Detecting Occlusion from the Disagreement Between Two Monocular Distance Cues
papers.Abstract: Knowing that a pedestrian is occluded is useful to a robot even when the detector cannot recover the hidden pixels, but occlusion estimators are normally trained on occlusion annotations that deployment settings rarely have. We show that occlusion can be read off two distance estimates a camera-only pipeline already computes. Apparent height is largely unchanged by occlusion, because the detected box still spans the whole person; monocular metric depth is pulled toward the occluder, because the nearest surface inside the box is what a depth map reports. Only their ordering matters, so no focal length, stature, or depth scale is needed, provided the depth model's error is close to a pure gain, a condition that can be checked without labels. The score detects heavy occlusion on KITTI with AUC 0.909 (0.888 over all annotated pedestrians, including those the detector misses), requires no training and no occlusion labels, and is not a proxy for range: within fixed distance bands it holds AUC 0.894-0.925 while true distance alone sits near chance. On synthetic CARLA scenes with measured visibility it reaches 0.819, against 0.644 for distance alone. We arrived here after measuring three standard architectural responses to occlusion, depth fusion, occlusion-simulating augmentation, and attention, none of which improved detection outside its training distribution in the configurations we tested, and after finding that a detector trained on German roads loses half its accuracy on self-annotated street scenes in Lagos, Nigeria. Signals that need no local annotation are worth more in settings that benchmarks do not represent.
papers.Core_Innovation: The method exploits the divergent occlusion sensitivity of monocular apparent height and metric depth cues within existing camera pipelines. It requires no training data, no occlusion annotations, and only assumes depth estimation error approximates a pure gain.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Autonomous Vehicles, Robotics, Surveillance
papers.Decision_Perspective: Product teams should integrate this occlusion-detection heuristic into current monocular depth models within the next quarter to immediately improve pedestrian safety metrics. Competitors relying on annotated occlusion datasets should transition to this label-free approach or risk obsolescence.
papers.Tags: monocular, occlusion detection, depth cues, robotics
papers.Hook: Monocular systems detect occlusion via depth-height disagreement without training or labels.

papers.Title: Dull, Dirty, Dangerous? Working Conditions and the Limits of Occupational AI Exposure
papers.Abstract: Automation is often justified as relief from dull, dirty, and dangerous work. I examine how these conditions relate to occupational AI exposure using 21 O*NET items across 754 US occupations. Higher exposure is associated with lower condition scores under a large language model (LLM) measure and AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE), with equal occupation weights and employment weights. Adjustment for physical demands, required education, training and experience, and wages reduces the composite association. The adjusted confidence intervals include zero for LLM exposure and remain below zero for AIOE. Separating repetition from restricted discretion also changes what the combined Dull score conveys. These comparisons show how item groupings and occupational characteristics shape the interpretation of exposure estimates. Occupational profiles offer a starting point for selecting contrasting research settings. Establishing desired automation or realized relief requires evidence about workers' preferences and specific interventions.
papers.Core_Innovation: The study maps 21 O*NET working-condition items across 754 occupations to show that AI exposure estimates systematically decline with dull/dirty/dangerous scores. Only AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) maintains significance after adjusting for physical demands, education, training, experience, and wages, while repetition-versus-discretion decomposition drives divergent interpretations of the combined Dull score.
papers.Decision_Perspective: Require condition-adjusted AI exposure audits for all occupations classified as dull, dirty, or dangerous within the next 18 months to prevent misallocated automation investments. Fund only those pilot projects that demonstrate net worker condition improvement under AIOE-negative adjustment thresholds.
papers.Tags: AI exposure, working conditions, O*NET, adjustment bias
papers.Hook: Exposes how occupational condition categories systematically bias AI exposure estimates across 754 US jobs

papers.Title: Adaptive Multi Mode: Budget-Aware Routing of Optimizers By Online Landscape Probes
papers.Abstract: The best classical optimizer for a continuous black-box problem depends on its budget and landscape. Existing routers decide from the dimension and budget, past improvement or features fitted to one benchmark, and few test an optimizer's implicit assumptions online. AMM (Adaptive Multi Mode) routes a known budget among quasi-Newton, trust-region, coordinate, multistart and evolution-strategy optimization engines with online probes of curvature, plateaus, separability, kinks, basins and fractal structure. Each probe has a default, a dimension-by-budget validity range and a cost charged to the budget. In its pre-registered development loop on bbob, 32 of 36 predictions held over the last 16 confirmations. AMM was then tested once on held-out bbob instances 101-110 (D=2-40, 10*D-1000*D) against up to seven competitors. It has the highest target share in 382 of 600 function-dimension-budget cells (236 outright, 146 tied) and, by a descriptive posterior rule, is credibly behind in 35, mostly at 10*D and 30*D. At every budget it also leads the controls built from its own engines (the best engine alone, the best engine per dimension and budget, and a greedy schedule), narrowly at 10*D and 30*D, and nevergrad's NgIohTuned. In pre-registered runs its lead over IPOP-CMA-ES holds under affine and box transformations, on box-constrained bbob and, pooled, on rotated f2-f4, but rotating the separable f3 and f4 removes most of the lead there. On held-out MA-BBOB its final share at 2000*D is level with IPOP-CMA-ES's and its anytime area lower. We published AMM as an open-source Python package (pip install amm-optimizer; https://github.com/BjBodner/amm-optimizer).
papers.Core_Innovation: AMM employs dimension-budget-validated online landscape probes to dynamically allocate budget across optimizer modes, with each probe incurring a cost calibrated to problem structure.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Computational Finance, Engineering Design
papers.Decision_Perspective: Engineering teams should prototype AMM integration into black-box optimization pipelines within the next two quarters, testing against their specific landscape profiles. Investment committees should fast-track funding for AMM-driven optimization tools that achieve >30% target-share improvement on held-out benchmark suites.
papers.Tags: Adaptive Routing, Landscape Probes, Budget Allocation, Optimizer Selection, Black-Box Optimization
papers.Hook: AMM dynamically routes optimizers via online landscape probes, adapting to budget and problem structure in real time.

papers.Title: Learning to Decode Linear Codes with Generalized Belief Propagation Network
papers.Abstract: Error correcting codes are a fundamental component of communication systems, enabling reliable data transmission over noisy channels. Recently, neural decoders have demonstrated notable performance gains over classical iterative algorithms. In this paper, we propose a Generalized Belief Propagation Network (GBPNet) that preserves message-passing symmetry while enhancing the decoder's learning capability. The architecture uses cascaded variable-node updates and learned element-wise message scaling while retaining the Tanner graph structure. We also introduce two training strategies, progressive training and high-SNR training, that improve decoding accuracy. Experimental results on several linear codes show that GBPNet achieves lower bit error rates than conventional belief propagation and the evaluated state-of-the-art neural decoders.
papers.Core_Innovation: Employs cascaded variable-node updates with learned element-wise message scaling within a symmetry-preserving generalized belief propagation framework, augmented by progressive and high-SNR training strategies.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Telecommunications, Data Communications, Networking
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate GBPNet into next-generation 5G baseband ASICs within 12 months. Phase out legacy belief propagation decoders in satellite uplink systems once GBPNet achieves validated SNR gains.
papers.Tags: Generalized Belief Propagation, Neural Decoding, Error Correcting Codes, Message Passing, Linear Codes
papers.Hook: Neural decoder preserves code symmetry while achieving state-of-the-art error correction gains.

papers.Title: On Turn-Level Best-of-N Sampling for Scaling LLM Agents
papers.Abstract: In this work, we evaluate a simple inference-time scaling approach based on \textit{turn-level best-of-N sampling} (\method) for large language model (LLM) agents on complex, long-horizon tasks. We instantiate this using a \textit{generator-selector} framework with two LLMs; at each turn, a \emph{generator} model generates $N$ candidate actions and a \emph{selector} model selects one of them, which is then executed in the environment. This paper is closely related to the work of \cite{zainullina2025guided} who used critic models for guided search at inference time. Different from their work, we evaluate if off-the-shelf, open-weight LLMs can be effective at comparing different candidate actions directly. Experiments on long-horizon terminal tasks show that \method can lead to significant performance improvements, both in terms of accuracy (5--10\%) and consistency across repeated attempts. Analysis of agent trajectories reveal a shift in agent behaviour towards desirable patterns such as reduction in number of attempts to solve the task, improved task instruction following, debugging and testing.
papers.Core_Innovation: A generator proposes N action candidates per turn; a selector model directly compares and chooses without reward-model fine-tuning.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Software Development, Customer Service, Enterprise Workflow
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget to integrate turn-level best-of-N sampling into existing LLM agent stacks within Q3 2026. Phase out static-prompt agent workflows that lack inference-time action selection.
papers.Tags: LLM agents, inference scaling, best-of-n sampling
papers.Hook: Off-the-shelf LLMs select optimal actions per turn via best-of-N sampling.

papers.Title: CounterFactual Retrieval for Evidence-Aware Individual Animal Identification
papers.Abstract: Automated identification of individual animals is moving from small curated studies toward shared benchmarks and reusable foundation models. This progress is useful, but current evaluation leaves the evidence behind a match unresolved, i.e., high retrieval accuracy does not show whether a model used animal features or identity-correlated shortcuts. We address this with Counterfactual Foreground Retrieval (CFR), an evidence-aware evaluation protocol. CFR evaluates the same query-gallery task under different views: full image, foreground-only, and shortcut-only. The full-image measures standard retrieval performance; the foreground-only measures foreground-supported retrieval; and shortcut-only view measure how much identity signal is recoverable from background, or silhouette. This turns a retrieval score into an evidence profile: how well the model performs on the original images, how much of that performance remains when only the animal is visible, and how much identity signal remains recoverable when the animal is removed. We release around 0.5M masks for 34 datasets and code for mask generation and CFR evaluation.
papers.Core_Innovation: It introduces a counterfactual retrieval protocol that isolates foreground animal features from background shortcuts, then measures performance under each view to produce an evidence profile.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Wildlife Conservation, Veterinary Science, Biometrics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate CFR protocols into animal ID model pipelines within the next quarter. Require shortcut-only retrieval reporting as a condition for foundation model grants.
papers.Tags: counterfactual retrieval, evidence-aware evaluation, animal identification, model shortcuts
papers.Hook: Models can now be evaluated on whether they use animal features or background shortcuts for identification.

papers.Title: Balancing hierarchical representation and quantization: A performance trade-off in text embeddings
papers.Abstract: Hierarchical text embedding models offer variable-length representations, while quantization reduces numerical precision; both aim to improve computational efficiency. This work is an empirical benchmark study of how these two orthogonal, already-established techniques interact. We evaluate 38 tasks from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) using four transformer-based embedding models, covering 1D and 2D hierarchical representations combined with 32-bit, 8-bit, and binary quantization, for 168 configurations per task. We report each efficiency dimension separately: theoretical per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time. Under a Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis, int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall, whereas binary quantization is significantly worse across every task category. Halving the embedding dimension once is not statistically detectable above $m=16$; two successive halvings always are. Combining an 8x dimensionality reduction with int8 yields a 32x reduction in per-vector storage at 94.4% of baseline effectiveness. Because evaluation times were measured once, we treat them as indicative: we find no evidence that quantization speeds up evaluation, whereas sampling from intermediate layers shortens it substantially. Retrieval degrades far faster than every other category, so we report findings per task category.
papers.Core_Innovation: int8 quantization incurs at most 1.5 percentage points overall accuracy loss versus float32 on pair-classification and re-ranking, making it viable for efficiency-critical pipelines. Binary quantization degrades performance across every MTEB task category, rendering it unsuitable for accuracy-sensitive applications.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Enterprise Search, LLM Serving, Cloud AI Platforms, Semantic Retrieval
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund int8-quantized embedding pipelines for production re-ranking systems within 3 months due to the negligible accuracy penalty versus float32. Immediately retire binary-quantized models across all deployment tiers due to consistent MTEB performance degradation.
papers.Tags: text embeddings, int8 quantization, MTEB, efficiency
papers.Hook: int8 quantization matches float32 accuracy on re-ranking while reducing storage costs by 75%

papers.Title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?
papers.Abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires AI systems to improve the models and infrastructure used by subsequent systems. LLM compression offers a concrete efficiency objective: retain a pretrained model's behavior within a smaller model storage budget. We study whether coding agents can carry out this step autonomously. We formulate compression as a terminal task in which an agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, inference environment, and time budget, then constructs compressed weights and executable inference code. The agent controls its algorithm and experiments; perplexity feedback guides search, and independent verification checks the final model. Across six agents and six model--size settings, 29 of 36 submissions pass verification. Selecting the lowest-perplexity agent design per task yields an average 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16 and 77.33% downstream accuracy, compared with 79.56% for BF16. Recorded experiments reveal how agents achieve these outcomes and where improvement breaks down. Agents lower PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage; complete-model feedback reverses 17 of 79 prior local rankings; and generation and inference tests expose failures that likelihood alone misses. The results identify representation design, experimental judgment, and capability validation as central to agent-driven model compression, a measurable component of efficiency-oriented self-improvement.
papers.Core_Innovation: Shifts model compression from human-engineered heuristics to an autonomous agent-led loop of algorithm design, experimentation, and perplexity-based optimization.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Edge Computing, Mobile Hardware, Cloud Infrastructure
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund autonomous ML-Ops pipelines that replace manual quantization teams within 12 months. Buy hardware optimized for smaller, agent-compressed weights to reduce inference CAPEX.
papers.Tags: LLM Compression, Autonomous Agents, ML-Ops, Model Efficiency
papers.Hook: Coding agents can now autonomously compress LLMs while maintaining near-original performance and verification.

papers.Title: Visual Token Routing: Learning to keep tokens that matter
papers.Abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) have recently achieved superhuman performance on several long-horizon benchmarks. However, their computational cost limits their use in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains such as video games. A key bottleneck is representing each screenshot as thousands of visual tokens, which accumulate into long contexts as agents reason over extended interaction histories. We observe that most of these visual tokens are either semantically irrelevant to the agent's next action or temporally redundant across screenshots. Building on this observation, we introduce Visual Token Routing (VTR), a joint training framework for learning sparse visual representations that preserve the information needed for action prediction. In VTR, we train the vision-language model together with a lightweight spatio-temporal router that examines each image region in the current and previous screenshots and decides whether its visual token enters the language model. We optimize the router using an adaptive loss to keep the number of visual tokens as small as possible while minimizing performance degradation. With just 2,000 training steps, VTR matches the performance of the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video game action prediction, while using 2.5-5.8x fewer visual tokens. These savings reduce inference cost by up to 3.3x and speed up prefill by up to 2.9x. VTR also outperforms lowering the image resolution and other baselines for dropping tokens, by up to 12.8 points on OSWorld. Overall, VTR enables computer-use agents to process only the visual tokens they need, allowing them to be used in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains at a fraction of the computational cost. Code and models are available at https://pranjal2041.github.io/vtr
papers.Core_Innovation: The vision-language model and a lightweight spatio-temporal router are jointly trained to dynamically prune visually redundant or irrelevant tokens across sequential screenshots
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Video Game Development, Autonomous Systems, Robotics
papers.Decision_Perspective: AI research teams should integrate spatio-temporal token routers into existing VLMs within 6 months to validate cost-performance tradeoffs. Venture funds should prioritize startups deploying dynamic visual pruning over raw-parameter scaling for real-time CUA products.
papers.Tags: VisualTokenRouting, SparseRepresentation, SpatioTemporalRouter, ComputerUseAgents
papers.Hook: Sparse visual tokens routed in real-time enable action-predictive agents without full-context overhead

papers.Title: Navigating Disagreement Among Criteria for Evaluating Explanation Faithfulness
papers.Abstract: Faithfulness requires that algorithmic explanations accurately reflect the model's behavior. Yet existing operationalizations of faithfulness can disagree about whether the same explanation is faithful, leaving developers and auditors to choose among conflicting evaluations. In this paper, we investigate disagreement among evaluation criteria and offer a practical path forward for evaluating explanation faithfulness. We first identify how operationalizations of faithfulness differ. We introduce a faithfulness functional that locates their disagreements in what an explanation claims about the model, which comparisons bear on that claim, and how agreement across those comparisons should be aggregated, and we reconstruct existing evaluation criteria within it. We argue these reconstructions support understanding faithfulness as a common though incompletely specified relation between the model and explanation, so the differences reflect choices left open by the general requirement. Justifying an operationalization then comes down to justifying these choices, which, on our view, draws on explanatory, institutional, and normative considerations. We support this argument with a case study of adverse action notices, reconstructing the evaluation implicit in an industry-proposed procedure and identifying which of its choices the setting justifies and which remain open. Our work gives auditors and practitioners a way to navigate disagreeing evaluations of faithfulness. It also explains why the literature should expect multiple operationalizations, while showing how concrete settings can narrow the choice among them. More broadly, our analysis shows how a shared requirement of faithfulness can support contextually justified evaluations despite disagreement among existing metrics.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper introduces a faithfulness functional that decomposes evaluation into explanation claims, comparison pairs, and aggregation rules, reconstructing existing criteria as special cases.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Explainable AI
papers.Decision_Perspective: Mandate adoption of the faithfulness functional in internal model audits within 90 days. Fund open-source tooling to implement the aggregation protocol immediately.
papers.Tags: Explanation Faithfulness, Evaluation Criteria, Functional Framework, Disagreement Aggregation, Model Interpretability
papers.Hook: A unified functional maps where explanation fidelity criteria disagree, enabling systematic reconciliation.

papers.Title: DreamX: Video Diffusion Model is a Universal Latent Action Learner
papers.Abstract: Learning a universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. Existing latent action models infer actions from visual transitions, but their representations often entangle the underlying action with irrelevant visual variations, limiting transfer across embodiments. We introduce DreamX, which repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a universal latent action learner. Our approach extracts compact latent actions from the video model's rich spatiotemporal features, compressing each latent video frame by $\boldsymbol{300\times}$ ($\boldsymbol{1{,}200 \rightarrow 4}$ tokens). In addition, by leveraging the video model's generative prior, these latent actions capture action-relevant dynamics disentangled from visual appearance. The resulting latent space serves as a shared action interface across embodiments (human and robot), environments, and action parameterizations. On LARY-Bench, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models. Moreover, actions encoded in one setting remain effective in another: the latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and zero-shot action transfer across diverse embodiments and environments. Furthermore, this shared interface also enables policy learning in a compact latent action space, reducing the computational cost of video-diffusion-based policies.
papers.Core_Innovation: DreamX extracts 4-token latent actions from pretrained video diffusion spatiotemporal features, achieving 300x compression while disentangling action dynamics from visual appearance via the model's generative prior
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Animation, Virtual Reality
papers.Decision_Perspective: Prototype DreamX-integrated robot policy pipelines within 6 months. Divest legacy motion-capture licensing assets rendered obsolete by diffusion-based action alternatives.
papers.Tags: video diffusion, latent actions, robotics, animation
papers.Hook: Video diffusion models now extract universal embodiment-agnostic action latent spaces from raw footage

papers.Title: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence
papers.Abstract: For a decade, progress in artificial intelligence has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Large foundation models now write code and run multistep tasks, and personal agents act on a person's behalf. Yet people still forget what they once knew, miss what they are not looking at, fail to find the right words, and face hard choices without the benefit of their own history, because the machine that could help stands outside the situation. As AI moves into the physical world, attention has settled on one kind of intelligent individual, the embodied robot; we argue that the era of Physical AI holds a second kind of equal importance, the person augmented by AI. Alongside artificial general intelligence, which asks how intelligent a machine can be, stands AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), which asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. Realizing it calls for a new kind of system, a cognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive companion that senses what the person senses through external devices, keeps their context across years, models their situation and their mind, takes part in their thinking at the right moment, carries out everyday tasks with their context, and keeps learning the person as both change. We give the paradigm a conceptual core, the cognitive gap between what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold in working memory, and organize its design space as a symbiosis loop of sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by a personal runtime and by trust. Because a symbiont changes what a person can do in front of others, it also raises risks of a new kind, from covert assistance in examinations to pressure on everyone to adopt it, and we treat their governance as part of the paradigm.
papers.Core_Innovation: Transitions AI architecture from external task-execution agents to lifelong, embedded systems integrated into human cognitive workflows.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Wearable Technology, Neural Interfaces, Healthcare, Education
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Software As A Service, Standalone AI Chatbots
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund hardware startups developing low-latency, embedded AI sensors for real-time cognitive augmentation. Pivot software portfolios away from standalone LLM interfaces toward integrated OS-level symbionts by 2027.
papers.Tags: Cognitive Symbiosis, AHI, Embedded AI, Human Augmentation
papers.Hook: AI shifts from autonomous agents to embedded cognitive symbionts augmenting real-time human intelligence.

papers.Title: Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization
papers.Abstract: Direct Nash Optimization (DNO) aligns a language model to a general preference function by approximating the Nash equilibrium of a two-player preference game. Its practical variant, DNO-Prct, iterates on-policy sampling, LLM-based rating of the samples together with a teacher's gold response, large-margin preference-pair selection and a DPO-style contrastive update. We re-implement DNO-Prct independently and study it on two open-weight instruct models, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1, with GPT-4o or a larger open-weight model of the same family as the annotator.
