On AlpacaEval 2.0 with GPT-4o as judge, three iterations raise the length-controlled (LC) win rate against GPT-4o from 31.7% to 45.3% for Llama and from 6.8% to 18.4% for Mistral, and the tuned 8B model scores above Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on every reported win rate. With same-family open-weight annotators, the runs retain 62% (Llama) and 82% (Mistral) of the LC gain achieved with GPT-4o as annotator, so the rating step does not require a proprietary model. In a separate ablation configuration, variants that remove the gold responses, remove the data look-back, or accept only teacher-preferred pairs score 6 to 10 LC points below the full procedure, whereas varying the number of on-policy samples per prompt (1 to 7) moves the LC win rate by at most 2.1 points, and a margin sweep (1 to 5) run in its own pipeline by at most 2.4 points. We also report the cost of the pipeline and where the practical algorithm departs from the theory it approximates. All results are single runs, and GPT-4o is both the teacher and the evaluation judge; we discuss what this implies for the reported gains.
papers.Core_Innovation: DNO-Prct introduces large-margin preference-pair selection as a core component within an on-policy DPO-style contrastive update loop, directly steering LLM optimization toward a Nash equilibrium of the preference game
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Generative AI, LLM Alignment, Conversational Platforms
papers.Decision_Perspective: Engineering teams should prototype DNO-Prct alignment on 8B instruct models within two training iterations to validate cost-performance parity with 70B baselines. Product groups must integrate these aligned 8B models into production chat flows by Q3 2026, replacing larger model endpoints.
papers.Tags: direct nash optimization, preference alignment, large-margin selection, on-policy sampling
papers.Hook: DNO-Prct aligns 8B instruct models to surpass 70B baselines via preference-game Nash optimization

papers.Title: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning
papers.Abstract: Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments. Precise IK remains laborious: redundancy and singularities complicate the inverse mapping, execution depends on hand-tuned controllers, and training data on physical robots are costly to collect. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision IK. It updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain resolve millimeter residuals while preserving large motions. Progress and dwell rewards teach it to both reach the tolerance and stay within it. In simulation, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps the mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2° on 93.5% of held-out tasks, and a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%. When trained directly on a physical arm with an off-policy RL learner, PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, PolicyIK executes the end-effector commands of the $π_{0.5}$ VLA policy with 95.7% success. These results show that reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/PolicyIK.
papers.Core_Innovation: The policy maintains a joint-position reference accumulated against measured joint feedback, using an error-dependent gain across two temporal scales to suppress sub-millimeter residuals while preserving large motions.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Manufacturing, Logistics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Prioritize PolicyIK integration into VLA pipelines within 18 months to replace hand-tuned IK stacks. Allocate funding for a pilot program targeting 6-DOF robotic arms in high-precision assembly by Q3 2026.
papers.Tags: Reinforcement Learning, Inverse Kinematics, Robotics, Precision Control
papers.Hook: RL-driven IK achieves millimeter precision without hand-tuned controllers.

papers.Title: GUILD: Guided Iterative Data Collection for Imitation Learning
papers.Abstract: Imitation learning policies in robotics are trained on datasets collected through costly real-world teleoperation. Often, the data-collection process is unguided, relying on the teleoperator's intuition, resulting in data that contributes little to overall policy performance. Recent work has shown that curating such unguided datasets can substantially improve policy performance, but these approaches operate by filtering existing datasets after collection and therefore do not prevent the acquisition of uninformative data. In this work, we propose GUILD, a novel Guided Data Collection (GDC) method that actively reasons about which data should be collected to maximize downstream policy performance. We introduce an iterative framework that alternates between 1) task proposal and data collection and 2) data evaluation to close the loop. For task proposal, we leverage semantic priors from vision-language models to identify relevant environments, object configurations, and goals for data collection. However, since semantic relevance does not imply policy improvement, we perform data evaluation. By leveraging predictive data attribution we approximate how the collected trajectories influence policy performance on a target deployment setting. This signal is then used as feedback to guide subsequent data collection, closing the data collection loop. We evaluate our approach in simulation and real robot settings, demonstrating that guided data collection substantially improves sample efficiency and deployment performance compared to passive data collection strategies, multiple baselines and experienced roboticists. More information at https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/guild2026/
papers.Core_Innovation: GUILD replaces post-collection data filtering with an interleaved loop of vision-language-model task proposal and real-time evaluation during teleoperation.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Autonomous Systems, Manufacturing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate GUILD into robot fleet teleoperation pipelines within nine months to replace unguided data collection. Allocate funding for VLM-guided data collection systems to active robotics R&D teams by Q3 2026.
papers.Tags: Imitation Learning, Guided Data Collection, Vision-Language Models, Robotics
papers.Hook: GUILD uses vision-language priors to guide robot teleoperation toward informative data.

papers.Title: Suppressing Misaligned Behaviors in Language Models, Durably
papers.Abstract: Undesired model behaviors can emerge or re-emerge at any stage of training. Once observed, how effectively can we suppress them? To study this question, we first construct two model organisms--language models deliberately trained to exhibit a specific misalignment--that differ in what triggers the behavior. The narrow-trigger organism misbehaves only when the prompt contains a specific cue: it cheats on multiple-choice questions by following a planted hint that points to a wrong answer, and behaves normally otherwise. The broad-trigger organism has no such cue: after fine-tuning on insecure code, it gives harmful responses across a wide range of open-ended prompts. We then formalize post-hoc behavioral suppression and evaluate methods along three criteria: immediate suppression of the target behavior, durability under further training, and preservation of general capability. We compare standard methods--SFT, GRPO, and gradient-ascent unlearning--along these dimensions. Building on prior work on alignment shallowness, we hypothesize that more durable suppression requires the ability to recover from a wider range of misalignment states. We introduce Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (PEARL), a GRPO variant that augments rollouts with continuations from intermediate states sampled along cached organism trajectories. Across both organism settings and two model families (Qwen3-4B, GPT-OSS-20B), PEARL achieves strong immediate suppression while preserving task accuracy, and remains durable under further fine-tuning on either the organism's data or unrelated data. It obtains the greatest benefit when the undesirable behavior is broad and cannot be addressed through targeted SFT. Together, our framework and method offer a step toward more durable post-hoc removal of undesired behaviors.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces a tri-criteria framework optimizing immediate behavior correction, durability under further training, and general capability preservation
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Cloud Computing, Enterprise AI
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund integration of tri-criteria suppression frameworks into production LLMs within 90 days. Halt deployment of models lacking verified durable alignment safeguards.
papers.Tags: LLM Safety, Behavioral Suppression, Alignment Unlearning
papers.Hook: Enabling durable post-hoc behavior suppression in LLMs while preserving general capability

papers.Title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
papers.Abstract: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every step is a Born measurement - attention $|\langle q|k\rangle|^4$ normalised over each row, a measured product in place of the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout. With its denominators held at their values for the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share, to $10^{-11}$ or better. On e-SNLI natural language inference, with about 98k parameters outside the embedding, the model reaches $76.98 \pm 0.17$% test accuracy, level with a softmax transformer of the same size ($76.62 \pm 0.36$%). Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 45% of test pairs, out of the 53% any single deletion can change, against 32% for the softmax model explained the same way and 40% by its attention x gradient. Attention can look more like the words annotators highlighted, yet accounts for the answer less well: deleting the word it ranks first changes the Born Transformer's answer in 32% of pairs. The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronic optics and to qubits, and a coherent attention layer becomes one circuit equal to the model (852 CNOTs on 23 qubits). On IBM's ibm_kingston, reading only the attention overlaps by Hadamard tests, the device gave the model's answers on two short test pairs and kept or changed them under deletion as the model does; the evidence itself did not yet survive the device, and we work out the shots and calibration that measuring it on hardware would need.
papers.Core_Innovation: Each transformer layer replaces attention and feed-forward operations with Born measurements, making class probabilities exact polynomials of word amplitudes and enabling quadrature-free integrated-gradient attribution.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Natural Language Processing, Explainable AI, AI Chipsets
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate Born-measured attribution into production model auditing pipelines within two quarters to enable exact word-level accountability. Phase out approximate gradient methods for explainability-critical deployments.
papers.Tags: Born measurements, Integrated Gradients, Transformer Attribution
papers.Hook: Exact word evidence via Born measurements eliminates quadrature error in transformers

papers.Title: Agnostic Learning by Imitating
papers.Abstract: Given a class of machine learning models and sample access to a data distribution with binary labels, which computational task is harder: training a discriminative model that distinguishes positive and negative labels as well as the best member of the class, or training a generative model whose outputs are indistinguishable from real data by all members of the class? We prove that these two fundamental tasks in computational learning theory are not just closely related, but actually equivalent to each other in complexity. One direction of this equivalence was previously known. Indeed, the powerful regularity lemma in complexity theory gives an efficient oracle reduction from the indistinguishability task (a.k.a. multiaccuracy) to the distinguishing task (a.k.a. agnostic learning) in the style of boosting algorithms. Our main contribution is an efficient oracle reduction in the other direction. Taking this idea further, we show that a multiaccuracy oracle is a remarkably powerful primitive, achieving not just agnostic learning but also a wide range of seemingly more demanding learning objectives via similarly efficient and direct constructions. Our results crucially use the power of making adaptive queries to the oracle, and stand in stark contrast to prior work, which showed that post-processing a single multiaccurate predictor is insufficient for even weak forms of learning. On a technical level, we draw a connection between our (offline) problem and a version of no-regret learning in the online setting, which allows us to use follow-the-leader type algorithms to modify the label distribution and aggregate the predictions of the multiaccuracy oracle.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper delivers the first efficient oracle reduction from agnostic learning to generative indistinguishability, reversing the known boosting-style direction and establishing multiaccuracy as a fundamental primitive.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Statistics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate capital to startups developing multiaccuracy oracles within 18 months. Acquire teams building hybrid discriminative-generative model frameworks to capture efficiency gains.
papers.Tags: Agnostic Learning, Generative Imitation, Computational Equivalence, Oracle Reduction, Machine Learning
papers.Hook: Agnostic learning and generative imitation are proven computationally equivalent.

papers.Title: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents
papers.Abstract: Speculative decoding has been treated purely as a systems optimization that speeds up large language model decoding without changing the model behavior. Under this view, the growing effort to train better draft models has been focused solely on acceptance rate. We argue that this view does not hold true for long-horizon agent reasoning. Measuring frontier open-weight models on complex agentic tasks with different speculative decoding approaches, we found that numerical noise grows within verification windows, and the draft acceptance results of the thinking process can change the output distribution of the model after 30 steps, thus noticeably influencing the reasoning accuracy of long-horizon agents in random directions. In this work, we improve the reasoning capability of target models by controlling such noise. While we cannot change the overall token distribution verified by the target model, we can encode critical reasoning with highest precision by training the draft model to be rejected. We identify these points in agent traces and train the draft model to favor adversarial preference. At inference the trained draft and the target part ways precisely at these decision points, verification restarts, so that critical thinking tokens are sampled from the target model and encoded under its least noisy conditions. This approach makes critical reasoning better indexed and more durable over a long horizon. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, our approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution. Our results recast the speculative decoding mechanism from a pure accelerator into an active allocator for context precision that improves the accuracy of long-horizon agents by training 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.
papers.Core_Innovation: Draft models are trained to prioritize precision-critical reasoning tokens, actively suppressing verification-window noise that would otherwise distort long-horizon output distributions.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Finance, Healthcare, Software
papers.Decision_Perspective: Accelerate draft-model training for reasoning precision to deploy robust long-horizon agents within two quarters. Kill legacy speculative decoding pipelines that ignore verification-window noise.
papers.Tags: Speculative Decoding, Long-Horizon Agents, Reasoning Noise Control
papers.Hook: Precise noise control in draft models enables reliable long-horizon agent reasoning.

papers.Title: A Circuit for In-Context Learning
papers.Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets a pretrained language model perform a task specified by demonstrations in its prompt, with no parameter updates. With arbitrary labels the model must acquire a mapping it cannot have memorized, so the learning happens within a single forward pass. Prior work found candidate parts but not how they compose. We give the composition for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B-parameter transformers. The model implements a key-value memory over label-token positions: each label token's residual stream encodes the label's identity, and middle-layer attention heads write into it the class of the preceding demonstration as its key. At the query, upper-layer heads match the query's class against the stored keys and copy out the matching labels. An early-layer signal encoding whether any label has repeated gates this readout; in its absence the readers attend to the start of the prompt and no label is favored. A separate set of heads suppresses the most recently seen label. Each step is established causally by activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the model's own signals. A softmax model of the readout with two constants per head, fit on one prompt distribution, predicts another. The computation is conserved across the three models, the named heads alone reproduce the behaviour, and a transformer trained from scratch grows the same parts. The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and to labels with meaning, and the same parts, with a causal gate, appear from 0.6B to 8B in one family and survive instruction tuning. ICL in this setting is a gated associative lookup built from a few identifiable component types, traced causally from demonstrations to prediction.
papers.Core_Innovation: Middle-layer heads write demonstration classes into label-token residual streams as keys, while upper-layer heads match query classes against these stored keys to copy matching labels.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Natural Language Processing, Software Engineering
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget to audit label-routing circuits in 3-4B transformers within Q2 to validate ICL reliability for production workloads. Suspend fine-tuning pipeline upgrades until circuit behavior is benchmarked against task-specific fine-tuned models.
papers.Tags: In-Context Learning, Transformer Circuits, Few-Shot Classification
papers.Hook: Transformers compose a key-value memory circuit for in-context label routing.

papers.Title: Left-Digit Bias: Theory and Empirical Evidence from a Tax Salience Experiment
papers.Abstract: Demand often drops sharply at whole-dollar prices. To explain this phenomenon, known as left-digit bias, we develop a random utility model in which consumers consider a good only if its price is below a heterogeneous attention threshold. Masses of consumers with integer attention thresholds generate demand discontinuities. When a tax is introduced, the model predicts a weaker demand response compared to rational choice for left-digit biased consumers. Using data from a tax experiment, we find that the model matches behavioral moments and partially identify the distribution of willingness to pay relative to thresholds. A weak demand response need not imply a low excess burden of taxation and understanding the specific mechanism is important for welfare analysis.
papers.Core_Innovation: Proposes a random utility model where heterogeneous integer attention thresholds generate demand discontinuities at whole-dollar prices, and tax salience weakens demand response for biased consumers versus rational choice.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Retail, Tax Administration
papers.Decision_Perspective: Implement whole-price threshold analytics in retail pricing engines within the next quarter. Acquire behavioral data firms specializing in tax salience experiments.
papers.Tags: Left-Digit Bias, Tax Salience, Random Utility, Demand Discontinuities, Willingness-to-Pay
papers.Hook: Tax salience experiments now partially identify WTP distributions under left-digit bias.

papers.Title: Weight-space programming for auditing clinical decision networks
papers.Abstract: Machine learning models in radiotherapy are commissioned by testing them on cases with known answers, which may not reveal a shortcut that the test cases share with the training data. Frontier language models have recently been reported to read and write the raw weights of small neural networks, an ability called weight-space programming. The purpose of this study was to determine whether such a model, given only a clinical protocol and a network's weights, can audit and repair the network. Networks with 433 to 4,801 parameters were trained to screen head-and-neck planning requests against four rules. Flaws were planted through the training data: confounds that hid each rule, a 3 Gy shift in the cord threshold, and a hidden trigger. Claude Opus 5.5 audited each network blind, without tools, data or code execution, and every claim and repair was tested on about 420,000 requests. The language model named the broken rule in 16 of 18 flawed networks (95% CI 67% to 97%), including all 15 with a confound or a threshold shift. It repaired each of the 16 by changing a median of 3 parameters. Fine-tuning on protocol-labeled requests also repaired every network, but changed nearly every parameter. Each confound and shift it found was visible in single units, and a simple statistic chosen for each flaw type found the same flaws. It cleared 2 of 5 healthy networks without being forced and found 1 of 3 triggers. Testing against the protocol detected every flaw, and black-box testing found the confounds and the shift faster. The results indicate that, in small networks, weight-space programming can locate and repair flaws that silence an input or shift a threshold, but cannot yet certify that a network is correct.
papers.Core_Innovation: Frontier models audit and repair neural networks by directly manipulating raw weights guided solely by clinical protocol text, without data, tools, or code execution.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Healthcare AI, Radiotherapy, Clinical Decision Support
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Opaque Clinical AI, Unverified Radiation Tools
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate funding for weight-space auditing toolkits across clinical AI networks within 12 months to pre-empt rule violations. Require blind protocol-based auditing of all radiotherapy decision models before patient deployment.
papers.Tags: weight-space programming, clinical auditing, neural network repair
papers.Hook: Frontier models audit and repair neural networks via weight-space programming from clinical protocols.

papers.Title: MedPhysBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Language Models on Medical Physics Calculations and Error Detection
papers.Abstract: Medical physicists turn a prescription into a delivered dose and check one another's calculations, because one error in a beam calibration or a monitor-unit (MU) calculation can affect every patient treated with it. MedPhysBench has ten seeded generators of calculation items in radiation therapy, diagnostic imaging, nuclear medicine and radiation protection, up to clinical tasks such as a TG-51 calibration worksheet. Reference answers come from code implementing the governing protocols, and a grader converts units and applies tolerance bands. From the same inputs, separate checking items test error detection, showing a colleague's worksheet or only the colleague's result, half correct and half with one planted error. On a held-out test split of 1,200 items (half for two models), 12 models scored 33.3 to 100.0% on calculation. Of the nine answers graded incorrect for the four best (99.3-100.0%), five contained model errors and four followed NCRP Report 151 on points our items misstate or leave open. Below them, most models did worst on level-3 clinical tasks, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 omitted the inverse-square correction in 19 of 20 isocentric MU items. Five models detected at least 96.7% of mostly large planted errors with at most 4% false alarms; for four of the other seven, checking only the result raised false alarms significantly. In an exploratory targeted test with 20 public cases of an omitted inverse-square correction, the three best models tested caught it in every worksheet, and three weaker models accepted 16 to 18 of 20 planted worksheets, one of them while applying the correction in most of its own calculations. Claude Opus 5.5 accepted 6 of 20 wrong results, although it applied the correction in all 20 of its own. We report the effect of two problems in our shielding items, found after the runs, and release the code, per-item outcomes and targeted-test responses.
papers.Core_Innovation: 10-domain seeded generators produce paired calculation and error-detection prompts from protocol-implemented reference code, enabling simultaneous LLM evaluation of arithmetic accuracy and error identification.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Medical Physics, Diagnostic Imaging, Nuclear Medicine
papers.Decision_Perspective: Radiology departments must adopt MedPhysBench-validated LLM auditing within 3 months to catch calculation errors before patient treatment. Vendor selection committees should reject clinical calculation assistants lacking MedPhysBench compliance.
papers.Tags: Medical Physics, Language Models, Error Detection
papers.Hook: New benchmark evaluates LLM medical physics calculations and error detection for patient safety.

papers.Title: A simple adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization in $p$-norm geometry
papers.Abstract: Efficient preconditioning plays an important role in large-scale first-order optimization. In this paper, we propose an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging ($\text{A}^2$ODA) method for unconstrained convex optimization that adopts low-cost preconditioning based on $p$-norm geometry for $p\in[2,\infty]$. The method is line-search-free and employs a new stepsize selection technique based on an aggregated affine lower model. Its update structure is simple and unified across $p\in[2,\infty]$, with the case $p>2$ requiring no more elaborate updates than the Euclidean case $p=2$. Under a generalized local smoothness condition, we derive a convergence bound that separates the effects of constant and gap-dependent curvature, with the latter potentially yielding faster-decaying terms. In the special case of local smoothness, this bound recovers a nearly optimal convergence rate.
papers.Core_Innovation: The key innovation is a unified dual averaging update that achieves p-norm preconditioning at Euclidean computational cost, coupled with a convergence bound separating constant and gap-dependent curvature.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Machine Learning,Quantitative Finance,Operations Research
papers.Decision_Perspective: Begin pilot deployment of p-norm adaptive optimizers in ML training pipelines within 6 months to quantify compute savings. Phase out static first-order optimizers across high-dimensional convex problems after pilot results confirm efficiency gains.
papers.Tags: p-norm preconditioning,accelerated optimization,dual averaging
papers.Hook: Enables unified adaptive p-norm preconditioning for convex optimization without line searches.

papers.Title: CATF: A Manager-Worker Framework for Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting
papers.Abstract: We study context-aware time-series forecasting, in which a single target variable is predicted from its own history and a set of contextual variables, such as weather and calendar information. As the context becomes more diverse, a single model struggles to capture all of its regimes, while ensemble learning and Mixture-of-Experts approaches rely on manual data partitioning or soft routing, which increases the inference cost and hinders interpretability. We propose CATF, a Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting framework built on a Manager-Worker architecture: a Transformer-based Manager routes each input to a single Worker based on the context, using hard routing during both training and inference. The Workers thus specialize without manual data partitioning, and any single-model forecaster can serve as a Worker. On five context-rich datasets, four horizons, and two normalization schemes, CATF improves over its standalone counterpart in 162 of 200 comparisons, the best CATF-enhanced model outperforms the best standalone baseline in 19 of 20 settings, and it outperforms the zero-shot Time-MoE foundation model in 15 of 20 settings. A case study on bike-sharing data shows that the Manager routes inputs by the calendar and that each Worker specializes in a different weekly pattern.
papers.Core_Innovation: A Transformer Manager uses deterministic hard-routing to assign each context-instance to a single Worker, enabling specialization without manual partitioning and compatibility with any base forecaster.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Energy,Finance,Retail
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to prototype hard-routing Manager-Worker frameworks for energy demand forecasting within the next two quarters. Phase out legacy soft-routing ensemble models that lack deterministic context assignment.
papers.Tags: context-aware, manager-worker, hard-routing, time-series, ensembles
papers.Hook: Transformer Manager hard-routes inputs to specialized Workers, enabling context-aware forecasting without ensemble overhead.

papers.Title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data
papers.Abstract: Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator's job. In our DataFarm, the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views together consistently. The output is real-ready data: synchronized camera views labelled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep 87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is fully automatic and costs \$21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus \$5 for a render contract; every further episode costs \$0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and review, with no robot or operator. One hour of three-view data for a task costs \$107 on average, these costs included, slightly below a quote of \$117 for teleoperation in China and below \$290 in labour alone in North America.
papers.Core_Innovation: The innovation is an LLM-driven pipeline that reconstructs task geometry, expert dynamics, and success criteria from one calibration episode, then renders synchronized photorealistic video data with action labels for direct policy training.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Manufacturing, Autonomous Vehicles
papers.Decision_Perspective: Acquire or partner with teams deploying LLM-driven simulation pipelines within 6 months to secure cost-efficient robot data pipelines. Teams not adopting LLM-driven data generation will be outpaced in robot policy training efficiency.
papers.Tags: LLM Agents, Simulation, Real-Ready Data, Policy Training, Teleoperation
papers.Hook: LLM agents synthesize real-ready robot data from single calibration episodes, matching teleoperation yields.

papers.Title: Pixel: A Co-Designed Full-Stack Robot System for Learning General-Purpose Mobile Manipulation
papers.Abstract: General-purpose mobile manipulation requires a combination of capable robot hardware, scalable demonstration collection, expressive whole-body control, and effective policy learning. Yet these components are often developed independently, creating mismatches that limit the capabilities of the complete system. We present Pixel, a co-designed full-stack system for learning general-purpose mobile manipulation. Pixel combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers, multiple teleoperation and robot-free human data-collection interfaces, a unified whole-body controller, and a common policy learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations. A hierarchical learning stack further enables language-conditioned visuomotor control and long-horizon task execution. We evaluate the system across hardware, data collection, and policy learning, and demonstrate mobile-manipulation behaviors requiring dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body coordination. We hope that Pixel provides an integrated and extensible foundation for studying how robot hardware, data, control, and learning can be designed together for robot learning. More results at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel
papers.Core_Innovation: Pixel integrates a co-designed wheeled humanoid platform with a unified whole-body controller and hierarchical language-conditioned policy learning, enabling end-to-end mobile manipulation from human demonstrations.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Manufacturing, Logistics, Warehousing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate capital to prototype Pixel-inspired mobile manipulators in mixed-case fulfillment centers within 12 months. Divest legacy fixed-automation suppliers lacking adaptive whole-body control capabilities.

papers.Title: Pixel-UMI: Learning Environment-Aware Whole-Body Manipulation from Sensorized Human Demonstrations
papers.Abstract: Sensorized human demonstrations offer scalable data for mobile manipulation, but embodiment differences complicate policy learning. We present Pixel-UMI, a pipeline for learning environment-aware whole-body policies from human data. We first introduce Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR), which combines reconstructed scene geometry with demonstrated head and gripper trajectories to determine robot posture and generate collision-aware joint and base targets. Delay-calibrated action assignment converts these trajectories into actions. However, kinematic differences can leave residual pose errors, creating viewpoint mismatches between human demonstrations and robot observations. We therefore introduce Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking (REAM), which uses these errors during training to reduce reliance on mismatched views at deployment. Finally, because estimated actions cannot fully capture contact-rich interactions, we collect on-policy human corrections through DAgger to improve performance. We evaluate Pixel-UMI on five challenging tasks spanning articulated-object manipulation, deformable-object handling, constrained-space reaching, whole-body collision avoidance, and contact-rich bimanual coordination, achieving 87.0% average task progress. Video results are available at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel-umi
papers.Core_Innovation: Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR) jointly optimizes robot posture and collision-aware joint/base targets from reconstructed scene geometry and demonstrated trajectories. Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking (REAM) trains policies to discount viewpoint mismatches caused by kinematic differences between human and robot embodiments.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Logistics, Manufacturing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to prototype EAR+REAM integration on mobile manipulation platforms within 6 months to enable adaptive fleet operations. Phase out legacy teleoperation workflows that lack environment-aware retargeting capabilities.
papers.Tags: Whole-Body Manipulation, Policy Learning, Environment-Aware Retargeting, DAgger
papers.Hook: Robot whole-body policies now adapt to environment geometry and correct pose errors from human demos.

papers.Title: From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles
papers.Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation has substantially improved the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, including code generation, data analysis, and exam-style question answering. Despite these advances, purely neural LLMs continue to struggle with elementary logical reasoning problems and lack the determinism, soundness, and reliability characteristic of symbolic reasoning systems. Conversely, classical symbolic methods such as SAT solving and exact cover guarantee correctness and completeness, but require problems to be expressed in highly specialized formal encodings, limiting their applicability to natural language inputs. In this work, we present a synergistic neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by combining neural semantic parsing with deterministic exact cover reasoning. Given a Zebra-style logic puzzle in natural language, an LLM translates entities and constraints into structured tool calls that construct an exact cover instance. A symbolic solver then computes the solution and provides feedback to iteratively refine invalid, under- or overconstrained encodings, exploiting the uniqueness property of Zebra puzzles. We conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple parameter scales, post-training paradigms, and LLM families. The results demonstrate that our hybrid approach consistently outperforms strong plain neural baselines, including CoT prompting, as well as recent neuro-symbolic methods.
papers.Core_Innovation: Neural semantic parsing generates structured tool calls that encode puzzle constraints as exact cover problems, enabling deterministic resolution without manual formalization.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Finance, Logistics, Legal
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate venture capital to neuro-symbolic AI startups within 12 months to secure early-mover advantage in automated logical reasoning. Integrate exact-cover-based compliance tools into fintech platforms by Q2 2025.
papers.Tags: neuro-symbolic, exact-cover, logical-reasoning, llm, optimization
papers.Hook: LLMs translate natural language logic puzzles into deterministic exact cover instances.

papers.Title: WebHarbor: Docking Real Websites for Evolving GUI Agent Environments
papers.Abstract: GUI web agents require realistic and interactive environments that remain stable during both evaluation and training. Live website evaluation suffers from changing content, access restrictions, and limited coverage of authenticated workflows, while existing synthetic environments for training often lack functional depth and visual fidelity. We propose WebHarbor, a suite of 153 executable and dockerized website environments that faithfully reconstruct the visual interfaces, content, and functional workflows of real-world web services under deterministic control. We build WebHarbor through task-driven human-agent collaboration, where environments evolve as new tasks expand their functional scope, coding agents implement the required changes, and human contributors audit visual fidelity, functional correctness, and task validity. The resulting suite comprises 3,518 tasks spanning multi-step and post-authentication workflows, where existing works often fail to cover. Beyond reliable evaluation, WebHarbor provides high-fidelity synthetic web environments for cost-efficient reinforcement learning (RL). We demonstrate that a Qwen 4B-level GUI agent trained with RL in WebHarbor generalizes to unseen tasks and performs competitively with leading open-source GUI web agents across four benchmarks. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/aiming-lab/WebHarbor.
papers.Core_Innovation: Replaces live-site volatility with a task-driven, human-agent collaborative pipeline to build executable, version-controlled website replicas.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Software Testing, Cybersecurity
