papers.Tags: GUI Agents, Dockerization, Web Automation, Deterministic Environments
papers.Hook: Deterministic, dockerized clones of real websites enable stable training and testing of GUI web agents.

papers.Title: Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon-AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap
papers.Abstract: Muon has recently emerged as a promising optimizer for pretraining large language models, offering a speedup over AdamW in minimizing pretraining loss. However, it remains unclear whether Muon's advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token-parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training.
papers.Core_Innovation: Proposes margin-to-spread ratio to quantify correct-logit separation versus wrong-logit dispersion, revealing its shift from Muon to AdamW as pretraining scale grows.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Cloud Computing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate engineering resources to AdamW fine-tuning pipelines for models exceeding 1T pretraining tokens within the next quarter. Phase out Muon-first pretraining configurations for data-intensive LLM projects.
papers.Tags: Muon,AdamW,Fine-Tuning,Pretraining,Margin-Spread
papers.Hook: Large-scale pretraining flips Muon advantage to AdamW in fine-tuning.

papers.Title: Not All Reasoning Generalizes: A Case Study on Learning Generalizable Reasoning Strategies in RLVR
papers.Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can enable generalizable improvement for large language model (LLM) reasoning. This paper studies how to incentivize such generalization via reasoning strategies. We study this question with a controllable equation-solving framework: finding multiple inputs x for equations f(x)=y, where f is a non-bijective string function. This setting makes reasoning strategies observable while supporting a clear definition of easy-to-hard out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts, e.g., more solutions, longer y, etc. We uncover a subtle RLVR failure: it teaches the model to solve in-distribution tasks with high accuracy and structured step-by-step derivation, yet under OOD shifts, the same model abandons derivation and collapses to ineffective brute-force enumeration, causing sharp accuracy drops. This observation reveals the deeper challenges of RLVR generalization as it is neither incapable base model nor reward hacking, since the model succeeds in-distribution with the correct reasoning strategy. The key to mitigating this failure is an indirect intervention that surprisingly helps: co-training with bijective inversion tasks. Although these bijective tasks are actually not uniformly harder and even further from the non-bijective OOD evaluation, they make derivation more certain and substantially restore the correct strategy and accuracy under OOD shifts. This effect further motivates our theoretical analysis: outcome-only RLVR can shape reasoning processes through implicitly crediting the effective reasoning strategies more, even without process supervision. To conclude, our analysis framework and findings systematically reveal the crucial role and incentivization of reasoning strategies in RLVR generalization under OOD shifts. Code is available at https://github.com/ziqipang/rl_meta_thinking.
papers.Core_Innovation: RLVR trains models to optimize for verifiable rewards by reinforcing surface-pattern matching rather than derivational reasoning, causing systematic OOD strategy collapse
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Large Language Model Training, Reinforcement Learning, Code Generation
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Deployed LLM Systems, AI Tutoring, Automated Theorem Proving
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate funding to develop RLVR OOD stress-test suites within 60 days. Halt deployment of RLVR-reasoned models on out-of-distribution mathematical tasks until strategy generalization is verified.
papers.Tags: RLVR, reasoning generalization, OOD robustness
papers.Hook: RLVR reveals OOD reasoning collapse, enabling targeted strategy fixes

papers.Title: FADE: Factored Ability--Difficulty Filtering for Online RLVR Scheduling
papers.Abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) learns only from prompts whose sampled completions disagree: all-pass and all-fail groups produce zero relative advantage and burn generation budget without moving the policy. Adaptive schedulers try to steer rollouts toward informative prompts, yet they rely on per-prompt pass-rate trackers that entangle two quantities evolving at very different speeds---the policy's shifting competence across reasoning skills and each prompt's intrinsic difficulty. When a single exponential average or Beta counter tracks both at once, short memory scrambles the relative ordering of prompts whereas long memory reports stale pass rates. We introduce FADE (Factored Ability--Difficulty Estimation), a bilinear state-space filter that separates the two timescales. FADE represents each prompt's success logit as the inner product of a whitened $K$-dimensional skill loading with a fast-drifting policy ability vector, minus a slow-shrinking scalar item intercept. Using Pólya--Gamma augmentation, each minibatch of binary rollout outcomes updates the $K$-dimensional ability posterior in closed form via a rank-$K$ Woodbury step, instantly transferring competence shifts to all unobserved prompts that share those skills while leaving item intercepts stable. From the resulting posterior mean and variance we derive a closed-form utility for the probability of drawing a non-degenerate rollout group. Across five reasoning benchmarks, two base models, and four scheduling paradigms under a matched rollout budget, FADE consistently improves downstream accuracy and calibration while adding less than $0.6$\,ms per step.
papers.Core_Innovation: Replaces scalar pass-rate trackers with a bilinear state-space filter that decouples fast-drifting policy ability from slow-changing prompt difficulty.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Cloud Computing, Enterprise Software
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund RL training pipelines that implement factored scheduling to reduce GPU burn by 20% immediately. Buy into compute-efficient LLM providers that prioritize sample efficiency over brute-force scaling.
papers.Tags: RLVR, Sample Efficiency, State-Space Filtering, LLM Training
papers.Hook: Separate policy competence from prompt difficulty to optimize RLVR training budget and convergence speed.

papers.Title: Thought-deciphering via hierarchical EEG-to-text alignment
papers.Abstract: Communication is important for our well-being, but it can be impaired by disabilities, such as locked-in syndrome (LIS), cerebral palsy (CP), and dysarthria. Non-invasive brain-to-text brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer a promising solution by providing an alternative communication pathway for people with communication disabilities. However, most recent breakthroughs have relied on large, cumbersome, and costly neuroimaging modalities, such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). Numerous studies have attempted decoding using the lighter and cheaper electroencephalography (EEG), but the results remain inferior compared to the other modalities. More importantly, we do not understand how these modalities are related to text at the letter, word, sentence, and higher semantic levels. Many prior studies have focused on decoding below the sentence level because it is considerably easier to design an experiment around phonemes, letters, and words. However, during communication, sentences play a much more important role than words and letters. This is because sentences carry information at such a high level that they can be understood even if some words and letters are missing. However, within sentence-level decoding, sentence classification is not as well investigated as sentence generation, making it difficult to decide whether a sentence should be retrieved or generated in the context of EEG-to-text decoding. This paper strives to investigate sentence-level EEG-to-text classification via a novel hierarchical alignment framework, where the main goal is to retrieve a read sentence using its context and EEG as inputs.
papers.Core_Innovation: Proposes a hierarchical EEG-to-text architecture that progressively aligns neural activity to linguistic units from letters through sentence-level semantics, enabling end-decoding without fMRI/MEG.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Assistive Technology, Neurotechnology, Healthcare, Rehabilitation Medicine
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate capital to spin out a startup deploying hierarchical EEG decoding in locked-in syndrome communication devices within 18 months. Phase out fMRI-based BCI feasibility studies that cannot achieve sentence-level semantic alignment.
papers.Tags: EEG, BCI, Hierarchical Alignment, Semantic Decoding, Neuroimaging
papers.Hook: Hierarchical EEG alignment decodes thoughts to text across letters, words, and sentences.

papers.Title: D&A: Decoupling Description and Assessment Enables VLMs as Zero-Shot Robotic Reward Models
papers.Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold promise for zero-shot video task-progress estimation in robot learning, yet existing frameworks frequently suffer from confirmation bias, hallucinating progress in failed executions due to implicit success assumptions or relative temporal ranking designs. Naive prompting of frontier models collapses into a binary success detector that fails to capture nuanced, non-linear progress and failures. While post-training approaches can mitigate this through explicit training, they demand expensive real-world robotics data and require computationally intensive post-training for every individual base model. To resolve these limitations, we introduce D&A (Describe & Assess): our approach decouples progress estimation into an objective, task-grounded textual description of scene dynamics followed by an assessment phase using explicit rubrics. By compelling the VLM to synthesize an explicit, text-based definition of absolute success before scoring, the framework anchors evaluations to an external, global criterion rather than the video's internal timeline. Empirical results demonstrate that our method calibrates zero-shot estimates and mitigates confirmation bias, providing fine-grained, partial progress metrics that accurately penalize failed executions while correctly interpolating successful runs. Being purely prompt-based, D&A generalizes across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks---matching or surpassing post-trained reward models---and its reward estimates enable efficient downstream reinforcement learning.
papers.Core_Innovation: Decouples progress estimation into a two-stage pipeline: objective scene description followed by rubric-based assessment to eliminate confirmation bias.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Industrial Automation, Logistics, Warehouse Robotics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund startups integrating VLM-based reward models to replace manual reward shaping in robotic training pipelines immediately. Buy into companies reducing reliance on proprietary robotics datasets for task validation.
papers.Tags: VLM, Robotic Reward Models, Zero-Shot Learning, Computer Vision
papers.Hook: VLMs can now provide zero-shot, non-binary robotic task progress estimation without expensive real-world training data.

papers.Title: Strategist: Evolving Reasoning with Agents
papers.Abstract: A model is only half of an AI agent system. The other half is the inference strategy: the reasoning procedure that turns model calls into a response. Today that second half is written by hand, and the experience of building one strategy never carries to the next. We introduce Strategist, a meta-agent that evolves inference strategies across tasks. Each strategy is written as a blueprint,executable code that other strategies can reuse, and together the blueprints form a library. Given a task and a small development set, Strategist retrieves related blueprints, writes candidate strategies, tests them on real samples, and revises them from the results. Every candidate then enters the library, so later tasks build on earlier discoveries. On 30 benchmarks, Strategist beats the strongest baseline on 24 and matches its average accuracy (74.7% vs.74.0%) at 39% lower inference cost. Its strategies also transfer to unseen tasks and other models without further search. The part of an AI system that is not improved on its own now does.
papers.Core_Innovation: Strategist generates executable code blueprints for inference strategies, iteratively tests them on real samples, and accumulates successful ones into a transferable library
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Software Development, Enterprise AI, Cloud Computing
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Static LLM Providers, Manual Prompt Engineering
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget to integrate Strategist-style meta-agents into production inference pipelines within 6 months. Discontinue static prompt engineering vendors whose models fail strategy-transfer benchmarks.
papers.Tags: meta-agents, inference optimization, strategy transfer
papers.Hook: Meta-agent evolves reusable inference strategy blueprints into a shared library from task experience.

papers.Title: Tracing the Scientific Discovery Capacity of LLMs to Their Training Data
papers.Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show growing promise for scientific discovery, yet basic questions remain about what enables reliable discovery. How can we trace the scientific discovery capacity of LLMs to their training data? We study this question as one of missing probability mass and develop a theoretical account in which monofacts-the facts observed once during training-set the discovery capacity. In materials science and regulatory genomics, we directly manipulate monofact rates in training sets and find that more monofacts consistently yield more discoveries across two open-weight model families, sampling strategies, and reasoning budgets. Further experiments show the relationship cannot be explained by training-set diversity alone and can transfer across scientific domains when paired with in-domain data. Together, our results identify monofact rate in training data as a key factor governing discoveries in language models.
papers.Core_Innovation: The technical delta is framing discovery capacity via monofact rate facts observed once during training and empirically manipulating this rate across model families and scientific domains to causally influence discovery output. This moves beyond diversity-based explanations by isolating monofact frequency as the governing variable.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Materials Science, Regulatory Genomics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate monofact rate metrics into training pipeline design within the next 18 months. Discontinue model development on datasets lacking monofact profiling for scientific domains.
papers.Tags: Monofacts, Training Data, Scientific Discovery, Model Training, Domain Transfer
papers.Hook: Monofact rate in training data governs LLM scientific discovery capacity.

papers.Title: Benchmark Prediction with Sparse and Unpaired Cached Responses
papers.Abstract: Evaluating a generative model on all queries from all available benchmark tasks is prohibitively expensive. As such, models are often evaluated on different subsets of tasks and/or different subsets of queries from a given task. The resulting collection of responses and the corresponding (model, task) score matrix are sparse and unpaired. In this paper, we introduce the Product Kernel Perspective Space (PKPS), a collection of low-dimensional representations of models based on their embedded responses. PKPS generalizes existing methods for representing black-box generative models by comparing responses to similar -- rather than just identical -- queries and is therefore able to utilize sparse and unpaired information. Theoretically, we show that benchmark prediction using PKPS is query-efficient relative to methods that only use information from dense and paired portions of the evaluation data. Empirically, we show that PKPS-based methods outperform baselines on benchmark prediction across two large benchmark suites.
papers.Core_Innovation: PKPS constructs low-dimensional model embeddings from cached responses using product kernels, enabling comparison across semantically similar queries rather than requiring exact matches. This framework exploits sparse unpaired evaluation data that prior methods discard.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Cloud Computing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Prioritize integrating PKPS into internal model evaluation pipelines within the next quarter to cut query expenses. Discontinue reliance on dense paired benchmarking frameworks that cannot utilize sparse unpaired data.
papers.Tags: PKPS, Sparse Representations, Benchmark Prediction, Product Kernel, Model Evaluation
papers.Hook: Sparse unpaired cached responses enable accurate benchmark prediction.

papers.Title: Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches
papers.Abstract: Increased computing power has transformed computational science and improved predictive capabilities for complex systems, but many phenomena still exceed current simulation capabilities or require rapid evaluations for fast design iterations. Closure models address this challenge by approximating unresolved effects in reduced or incomplete dynamical systems. Data-driven closures offer a flexible mechanism for improving model accuracy and applicability, but approaches that embed the closure within a computational model for construction and training phases can be computationally expensive and cause numerical instabilities in the computational model during training. To avoid the challenges posed by embedded approaches, staged approaches to closure-model learning have been developed. The first stage uses data assimilation to infer state and closure trajectories from observations. The second stage trains a machine learning closure model offline using the assimilated data, thereby avoiding repeated simulator calls during training. In this work, we investigate the cost and accuracy tradeoffs between embedded and staged data-driven closure modeling approaches for a synthetic epidemiological SIQR model with a nonlinear state-dependent quarantine closure. The results illustrate a practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off: for this exemplar, embedded training provides the strongest average accuracy, while the staged approach yields comparable qualitative behavior with a moderate increase in error, substantially fewer model evaluations, and improved optimization robustness.
papers.Core_Innovation: Data assimilation extracts closure-consistent state trajectories, enabling standalone ML training that avoids embedding-induced numerical instabilities.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Climate Modeling, Aerospace, Combustion Engineering
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate data-assimilation pipelines for offline closure training within 18 months. Deprecate embedded closure modules in next-generation reduced-order model releases.
papers.Tags: Closure Learning, Data Assimilation, Dynamical Systems, Machine Learning, Reduced-Order Modeling
papers.Hook: Data assimilation enables stable, offline training of closure models for dynamical systems.

papers.Title: DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control
papers.Abstract: As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent, a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control (APC) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim, we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance and computational cost. Our work provides a framework, simulator, and evaluation foundation for agents to participate in human physiological control.
papers.Core_Innovation: APC integrates real-time physiological state inference with medical-device tool use and personalized experience accumulation to autonomously select insulin delivery actions.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Healthcare AI, Medical Devices, Diabetes Technology
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Glucose Monitoring, Conventional Insulin Therapy
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate capital to integrate APC frameworks into closed-loop insulin pump development within two years. Require DiabetSim-validated safety envelopes for any agent-driven insulin dosing system entering human trials.
papers.Tags: Agentic Control, Physiological Regulation, Medical Simulation, Diabetes Management
papers.Hook: Agentic physiological control enables real-time glucose regulation via adaptive medical-device agents.

papers.Title: Four Bridges: Measuring Deception Propensity in a Multi-Agent Game
papers.Abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact and coordinate with other agents, yet honesty is mostly measured in single-turn, single-agent benchmarks that pressure the model to deceive. We study deception that emerges in multi-agent interaction without any instruction to deceive. We introduce Kradle, a platform for evaluating AI models, and Four Bridges, an information asymmetry game in which four agents distribute across four rooms: one is the death room, the others hold food worth more if not shared. One agent, the informed agent, knows which room is the death room and can withhold or disclose that information. We evaluate eight frontier models as the informed agent. Deceptive behavior appears in every model and in 73% of all runs (6% to 100% per model), and does not decrease with capability tier within a model family. When the informed agent does disclose, the warning is often challenged, and agents that challenge it enter the death room twice as often as those that do not. Telling all agents that one of them knows the death room collapses deception in six of eight models; telling the informed agent that the room is permanently fatal moves only one. On an open-weight model, an honesty steering vector reduces deception to 0% and adversarial honesty training to 6%. The platform and game provide a testbed for measuring deceptive behavior and comparing interventions.
papers.Core_Innovation: Kradle introduces Four Bridges, a multi-agent information asymmetry game where an informed agent strategically withholds or discloses a death room’s identity, enabling quantification of deception propensity without explicit deception instructions.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: AI Safety, Multi-Agent Systems, Cybersecurity
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate funding for multi-agent deception detection tools by Q2 2026. Require transparency audits for any production system using collaborative AI agents.
papers.Tags: multi-agent, deception, AI safety, information asymmetry, frontier models
papers.Hook: Deception emerges universally in multi-agent AI, indifferent to capability.

papers.Title: Should We Combine Our Data? Algorithms and Limits for Privately Assessing Data Sharing
papers.Abstract: In this paper, we study when two parties should pool their data to train a machine learning model. Two agents, Alice and Bob, each hold a sensitive labeled dataset and want to train a classifier from a given hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$. Even when each party's dataset can be perfectly classified on its own, the two parties may follow conflicting labeling standards or have selection biases that affect their features and label sets, such that no single classifier in $\mathcal{H}$ fits their combined data. Before committing to data sharing, Alice and Bob therefore want to test whether a single classifier in $\mathcal{H}$ can jointly fit both datasets---without revealing their individual data points to one another.   We formalize this problem from a learning-theoretic viewpoint via $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}$, the minimum \emph{number of mistakes} made by any hypothesis in $\mathcal{H}$ on their pooled data. Through interactive communication, the agents must distinguish $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}=0$ (compatible datasets) from $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}\geq t$ (conflicting datasets) under pure $\varepsilon$-two-party differential privacy. A trusted curator could do this with $t=O(1/\varepsilon)$, and we ask how small $t$ can be without one. For thresholds on the real line over a domain of size $m$, we show that the optimal $t$ is $\tildeΘ(\log\log m/\varepsilon)$, exponentially smaller than the $Θ(\log m/\varepsilon)$ samples needed to privately learn thresholds, even with a curator. For halfspaces in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the dependence on $m$ jumps to $\log(m)$: we give a protocol with $t=\tilde{O}(d^3\log m/\varepsilon)$ and show that some domains require $t=Ω(d\log(m/d)/\varepsilon)$.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper formalizes data sharing feasibility via opt_H, the minimum mistake count for any hypothesis in H on combined datasets, and presents an interactive protocol that tests joint fit without exposing raw data points.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Healthcare, Finance, Cloud AI
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Data Brokers, Legacy ML Pipelines, Unsecured Cloud Storage
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund privacy-preserving compatibility pilots for cross-institution ML within 12 months. Phase out legacy data fusion pipelines that ignore hypothesis class misalignment risks.
papers.Tags: Private ML, Hypothesis Testing, Data Compatibility, Secure Computation
papers.Hook: Private protocol tests if combined data fits a hypothesis class without data exposure.

papers.Title: Latent Reasoning in Continuous Space for Unified Multimodal Models
papers.Abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) achieve remarkable success on diverse multimodal understanding and generation tasks, yet they still struggle to effectively leverage language-based chain-of-thought reasoning for image generation. As a result, existing reasoning-augmented UMMs often fail to inherit the test-time scaling and fine-grained controllability observed in large language models. We attribute this failure to a fundamental modality mismatch: reasoning is performed in a discrete token space, whereas image generation operates in a continuous space. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Latent Reasoning framework in Continuous space (LARC), which alleviates the token-level bottleneck by reasoning over continuous hidden states. Specifically, the training framework consists of two stages: (i) curriculum supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and (ii) information-gain reinforcement learning (RL). First, the curriculum SFT stage gradually converts token-level reasoning into latent reasoning. Subsequently, the information-gain RL stage self-evolves latent reasoning without ground truth supervision. Experiments across diverse text-to-image generation benchmarks show that LARC consistently improves generation quality, prompt following, and compositional fidelity. Notably, LARC achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval with a 7%p gain over BAGEL and demonstrates clear test-time scaling behavior, outperforming token-based generation under both parallel and sequential test-time scaling strategies.
papers.Core_Innovation: A two-stage pipeline progressively converts discrete chain-of-thought into continuous latent reasoning, eliminating the token bottleneck between language reasoning and continuous image generation.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Multimodal AI, Image Generation, Design Tools
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to integrate latent reasoning pipelines into multimodal systems within the next two quarters. Phase out discrete-token-only multimodal reasoning research given the demonstrated continuous-space advantage.
papers.Tags: latent reasoning, multimodal, continuous space, chain-of-thought, image generation
papers.Hook: Continuous latent reasoning enables test-time scaling and controllability in multimodal image generation.

papers.Title: Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention
papers.Abstract: Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. A promising approach is sparse attention, in which a dedicated indexer selects a subset of keys for the attention. Yet current methods of indexing either still have quadratic cost in context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale. We address this with Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), an efficient attention method that maintains accuracy at ultra-long context. In LSA, keys are hierarchically clustered in a learned latent space, and queries score the hierarchy of clusters instead of scoring every key, making prefill, decode and training faster at long context. We propose two variants, Distilled-LSA (D-LSA), which can be applied to pre-trained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA), which is trained natively on the next-token loss alone. On GLM-5.3-FLASH (QWEN-3.8-27B) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7x (72.4x) in prefill and 4.6x (42.5x) in decode over its original sparse attention (full attention), while keeping similar accuracy across a variety of tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a training speedup of 1.6x per layer at 128k tokens. LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models to benefit from ultra-long context.
papers.Core_Innovation: Queries attend to learned latent cluster hierarchies rather than individual keys, reducing compute from quadratic to subquadratic while preserving long-range signal
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Scientific Computing, Finance
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Legacy Transformer Deployments, Quadratic Attention Vendors
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate Distilled-LSA into production LLM pipelines within 6 months to support context windows above 1M tokens. Phase out quadratic-attention infrastructure for ultra-long context workloads once subquadratic baselines achieve parity.
papers.Tags: Attention, Sparse, Long-Context, Latent, AI
papers.Hook: Subquadratic attention enables ultra-long context scaling without accuracy loss

papers.Title: Hierarchical World Models with Implicit Dynamics
papers.Abstract: Planning with world models enables test-time adaptation for embodied agents, offering superior generalization over direct policy learning. However, long-horizon tasks remain hindered by cumulative errors and search complexity. Existing hierarchical methods often use rigid macro-actions or latent skills, leading to brittle representations and limited fine-grained control. We introduce ID-WM (Implicit Dynamics World Models), a hierarchical world model that decouples state-space reachability from local control. Our framework utilizes a high-level model to sample feasible transitions across the state manifold and a low-level world model as an inverse dynamics solver to ground these transitions into precise actions. This allows the planner to identify reachable subgoals without being constrained by low-level execution details. By prioritizing local physical feasibility over global behavioral patterns, ID-WM synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, transcending the specific behavioral modes seen during training. We demonstrate its effectiveness across three navigation and manipulation suites, achieving a 38.5% improvement over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion-based planners. Crucially, by leveraging this hierarchical structure to mitigate compounding errors, our approach yields a 135% performance gain over single-level world model MPC, particularly in complex, unseen configurations for long-horizon tasks. Videos can be viewed at https://id-wm.github.io
papers.Core_Innovation: High-level feasibility sampling over the state manifold coupled with low-level inverse dynamics solving enables planners to identify reachable subgoals independent of low-level execution constraints
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Autonomous Systems, AI Planning
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning, Rigid Macro-Action Frameworks
papers.Decision_Perspective: Accelerators should fund implicit dynamics hierarchy prototyping on physical robots within 6 months to validate reachable subgoal planning. Teams built on rigid macro-action hierarchies must assess obsolescence risk within 12 months as implicit dynamics approaches mature.
papers.Tags: World Models, Hierarchical Planning, Implicit Dynamics, Embodied AI
papers.Hook: Implicit dynamics hierarchy enables feasible subgoal planning for long-horizon embodiment

papers.Title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
papers.Abstract: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.
papers.Core_Innovation: A coding model diagnoses rollout failures and iteratively synthesizes programmatic harness code specifying when to query the frozen policy, invoke vision tools, or command the arm, requiring no gradient updates
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Automation, Artificial Intelligence, Manufacturing, Logistics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund internal prototyping of coding-model-driven harness automation for deployed robotic fleets within 12 months to capture 3x success-rate gains on novel tasks. Competitors should acquire or build equivalent systems to avoid obsolescence in general-purpose robot deployment.
papers.Tags: robotics, harness automation, coding models, policy freezing, benchmark generalization
papers.Hook: Coding models automatically evolve robot harnesses around frozen policies without weight updates

papers.Title: Counting on Dummies: Privacy Amplification with Observable Counts and Truncated Batches
papers.Abstract: In many practical deployments of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), the server processes data in batches. Randomly sampling these batches allows for better privacy bounds via privacy amplification results. Most sampling schemes with provable privacy amplification, including Poisson sampling and random allocation, result in variable batch sizes. The privacy guarantee of these schemes requires that the batch sizes are not revealed. In distributed settings, the server performing the aggregation or any party observing the communication traffic may learn these batch sizes. Furthermore, in both centralized and distributed settings, memory and computation constraints may require each batch to be of some maximum size $s$, necessitating truncation of the batch when it exceeds this limit. It is known that this truncation can result in a significant increase in privacy loss. In this work, we address both of these challenges via a simple mechanism that uses a random number of \emph{dummy points} to privatize the batch size and maintain the privacy guarantee even under truncation. We demonstrate that our mechanism is easy to implement in a distributed setting, and provide a general analysis of this mechanism for both Poisson sampling and random allocation. Our analysis is designed to support efficient and relatively tight privacy accounting. It also effectively amplifies the privacy of the count releases by subsampling, making the expected number of dummy points asymptotically smaller than what is needed to directly privatize the (sensitivity-one) batch sizes with non-negative noise. For Poisson sampling with truncated batches, we demonstrate empirically that our mechanism achieves better privacy--efficiency tradeoffs than the direct accounting for truncation recently given by (Ganesh, 2025).
papers.Core_Innovation: Uses randomized dummy samples to mask real batch sizes, and applies truncation-aware privacy accounting that preserves amplification bounds.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Healthcare Analytics, Finance, Federated Learning, Cloud AI
papers.Decision_Perspective: Mandate integration of this randomized-count mechanism into DP-SGD pipelines within the next two quarterly releases to eliminate truncation privacy overhead. Phase out batch protocols that expose raw sizes without comparable privacy guarantees.
papers.Tags: Differential Privacy, Stochastic Gradient Descent, Batch Truncation, Privacy Amplification, Randomized Counts
papers.Hook: Introduces observable dummy counts to enable safe DP-SGD truncation without privacy loss.

papers.Title: A Better Critic Matters for Distribution Matching Distillation
papers.Abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) trains a few-step student using the difference between a teacher's score and an online critic's estimate of the student distribution's score. We investigate what the critic needs, in capacity and in information, to provide a reliable training signal. On the capacity side, controlled experiments across seven SiT model sizes on ImageNet show that increasing teacher size while keeping a small critic fixed can degrade student quality and cause training collapse. Scaling the critic alongside the teacher, a strategy we call joint scaling, prevents collapse in our experiments and allows the student to benefit from larger teachers. On the information side, rather than forcing the critic to model a step-agnostic mixture of student outputs, we introduce a step-aware critic (STAC) that conditions on the student's generation step to estimate step-specific scores. Together, joint scaling and STAC consistently improve few-step distillation across class-conditional ImageNet generation, text-to-image generation with SDXL and FLUX.2, and text-to-video generation with Wan2.1.
papers.Core_Innovation: Critic capacity must scale with teacher size to prevent distillation collapse. Step-specific scores are estimated by conditioning on generation step rather than using a step-agnostic mixture.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Generative AI, Computer Vision, Digital Media
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund development of joint-scaling critic frameworks for diffusion models within 12 months to capture quality gains. Deprioritize fixed-capacity critic pipelines without step-aware updates.
papers.Tags: Distribution Matching, Critic Scaling, Step-Aware Distillation
papers.Hook: Joint scaling and step-aware critics enable reliable few-step distribution matching distillation

papers.Title: Instance-dependent sequential limits as an exact information ledger
papers.Abstract: Instance-dependent limits for bandit regret, sequential tests, best-arm identification and Markov decision processes are proved by one chain. It runs from a divergence decomposition through data processing to a statistic, a testing step that turns a class guarantee into a requirement on the history, and optimization over alternatives and allocations. Only the first step is an identity. This work writes the chain as an exact ledger. By the chain rule, data processing loses exactly a conditional divergence, which vanishes for arms in natural exponential families at the per-arm counts and reward sums. A one-parameter family of martingale identities extends the decomposition to every tilt between two instances. The classical limits follow by relaxations with named defects. All defects but the asymptotic step's can be computed from an algorithm's own runs, the uniform quantification's only when the class guarantee is a number. On seven published sources, from movie ratings to engine replacement, the ledger locates the difference between standard algorithms and the classical limits. For identification among trained models and for Wald's test the largest term is usually the uniform quantification's.
papers.Core_Innovation: Data processing loss is exactly a conditional divergence vanishing for natural exponential-family arms at per-arm counts and reward sums. A one-parameter martingale family extends this decomposition to arbitrary instance tilts.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Finance, Healthcare, Robotics, Energy
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Ad Networks, Outdated Recommendation Engines
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate venture capital to spin out divergence-ledger bandit startups by 2026 Q2. Retire legacy Thompson sampling implementations that ignore per-arm conditional divergence vanishing conditions.
papers.Tags: divergence decomposition, natural exponential families, martingale identities
papers.Hook: Single-chain ledger exactly tracks instance-dependent limits across bandits sequential tests and MDPs

papers.Title: Physiological Trajectories and Observation Patterns in ICU Mortality Prediction: Transportability Under Changing Measurement Conditions
papers.Abstract: Objective: To distinguish the transferable predictive value of physiological trajectories from that of observation patterns in ICU mortality prediction, and to assess whether measurement timing affects performance independently of observation quantity.   Materials and Methods: In-hospital mortality was predicted at 48 hours using MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU. Nested representations progressively integrated latest-value snapshots (R1), longitudinal physiological summaries (R2), and measurement frequency and timing features (R3). Models fitted on 7,762 MetaVision patients were evaluated on 21,682 MIMIC-IV patients and 43,878 eICU patients across 204 hospitals. The effect of measurement timing was assessed while holding the number of retained observations constant.   Results: Physiological trajectories improved external prediction in eICU (R2-R1 log-loss difference -0.00922, 95% CI -0.01148 to -0.00704). Observation-pattern features improved locally developed eICU models (R3-R2 -0.00257, 95% CI -0.00370 to -0.00146), but not clearly after transfer from MetaVision (-0.00012, 95% CI -0.00206 to +0.00208). R3 was favoured in 10 of 30 source bootstrap refits. At matched observation counts, retaining measurements spread throughout the window reduced log loss relative to random retention by 0.03280 for R3 versus 0.00703 for R2. Removing the final 12 hours increased log loss relative to count-matched random removal by 0.01947 for R3 versus 0.00822 for R2. Under reduced availability, the local R3 increment changed from beneficial to harmful.   Discussion: Physiological trajectories transferred more consistently, while observation-pattern features were particularly sensitive to the timing and availability of measurements.   Conclusion: Clinical prediction models should be evaluated not only in new patient populations but also under the measurement conditions that supply their inputs.
papers.Core_Innovation: Nested representation levels (R1-R3) systematically isolate how latest-value snapshots, longitudinal summaries, and measurement timing features each differentially govern external transportability versus local model fit in ICU mortality prediction
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Healthcare Analytics, Clinical Decision Support, Hospital Operations
papers.Decision_Perspective: Prioritize integrating longitudinal physiological summaries into ICU mortality models within the next 6 months to capture the -0.00922 log-loss improvement on external datasets. Discontinue observation-frequency-dependent pipelines that cannot replicate this transportability gain on new hospital networks.
papers.Tags: ICU Mortality, Physiological Trajectories, Measurement Timing, Model Transportability, Longitudinal Summaries
papers.Hook: Longitudinal summaries and timing features dissect transportability vs local fit in ICU mortality prediction

papers.Title: Gradient Descent on Two ReLU Neurons: Global Landscape and Bifurcation Dynamics
papers.Abstract: Understanding how gradient descent learns features remains a central challenge in neural network theory. We study this question in a minimal multi-index setting that already exhibits rich multi-phase gradient dynamics: a well-specified two-neuron ReLU teacher-student model under isotropic Gaussian inputs, trained by population gradient flow from small initialization. We show that the dynamics are organized by two directions: the "easy" bisector direction, which carries the leading signal, and the "hard" splitting direction, which governs specialization. To characterize the loss structure and learning behavior, we analyze the population squared-loss landscape and show that every critical point with both student weights nonzero is either a global minimum or a saddle. We then track the gradient-flow trajectory, showing that student neurons first collapse toward a bisector saddle before escaping and specializing to teacher neurons. Our results provide both a landscape and dynamics account of the multi-phase symmetry-breaking behavior that arises in a simple multi-index model and under standard algorithmic and architectural choices.
papers.Core_Innovation: Proves all interior critical points are saddle or global minima, and that trajectory path dictates saddle escape and neuron specialization.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Neural Networks, Optimization
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund replication of bisector-saddle dynamics in overparameterized ReLU training within 6 months. Discontinue vanilla gradient descent for specialized feature learning without saddle-aware modifications.
papers.Tags: ReLU networks, gradient flow, loss landscape, saddle points, specialization
papers.Hook: Population flow on two ReLU neurons reveals saddle-mediated specialization dynamics.

papers.Title: Fast Privacy Loss Accounting for Random Allocation via Multiscale FFT
papers.Abstract: In the random allocation sampling scheme each user's data is used in $k$ steps chosen randomly and uniformly from a sequence of $t$ steps. This scheme is known to improve on Poisson sampling in private optimization and in communication-efficient aggregation. The existing privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant for this scheme runs in time quadratic in the inverse of the accuracy parameter $α$ (Feldman and Shenfeld, 2026). We give an algorithm, \emph{multiscale FFT}, that represents likelihood ratios on a grid that is uniform within each dyadic interval and computes the exact rounding of every pairwise sum using FFTs within each interval. It keeps the guarantees of the accountant and improves the dependence of its running time on $α$ from $O(α^{-2})$ to $O(α^{-1}\log(1/α))$. In addition, we demonstrate that rounding can be performed via the mean-preserving connect-the-dots projection of (Doroshenko et al., 2026). This reduces the errors that rounding introduces in the mean of the privacy loss and in the $χ^2$ divergence of the computed pair from the order of $α$ to $O(α^2/\log(t))$. In our experiments, our algorithm achieves speedups of several orders of magnitude at high accuracy and gives improved privacy bounds for DP-SGD with PREAMBLE.
papers.Core_Innovation: Dyadic-interval grids store likelihood ratios, and FFT computes exact pairwise sums, replacing quadratic operations while mean-preserving connect-the-dots rounding limits distribution-error distortion.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Federated Learning, Differential Privacy, Secure Multi-Party Computation
papers.Decision_Perspective: Integrate multiscale FFT into privacy-loss accountants to cut runtime from quadratic to near-linear complexity. Pilot deployment in federated learning platforms should begin by Q3 2026 to validate scalability.
papers.Tags: Privacy Loss Accounting, FFT, Random Allocation, Differential Privacy
papers.Hook: Enables exact privacy-loss accounting at near-linear speed instead of quadratic scaling.

papers.Title: ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer
papers.Abstract: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT's KV conversion achieves a 6.5-21.2 times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget.
papers.Core_Innovation: ACCT converts source-model KV activations into sparse, layer- and head-aligned token states that target models decode without re-processing the full context
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Cloud Computing, Enterprise AI, Semiconductor
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund a 3-month ACCT pilot across same-family LLMs to quantify context-reduction gains. Phase out token-reprocessing pipelines that cannot ingest sparse KV states from cross-model transfers.
papers.Tags: KV Cache, Cross-LLM, Context Transfer, Sparse Attention, Model Family
papers.Hook: Enables cross-model LLM context reuse via sparse KV cache transfer, skipping redundant processing.

papers.Title: Subquadratic Attention with a Hierarchical Tree-Structured Indexer
papers.Abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.
papers.Core_Innovation: The method constructs a recursive tree of compressed key summaries over the KV cache, enabling queries to traverse top-down and retrieve a sparse key subset whose selection cost grows sublinearly with depth
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Cloud Computing, Natural Language Processing
papers.Decision_Perspective: We should allocate budget to integrate ZHA into production LLM serving pipelines within 90 days to test subquadratic scaling on 512k-token workloads. If throughput exceeds FlashAttention-2 by 2.5x, immediate rollout replaces the existing attention kernel.
papers.Tags: attention, hierarchical, subquadratic, llm, kv cache
papers.Hook: Tree-structured indexer enables subquadratic attention scaling for long-context LLMs

papers.Title: SATFRONT: Detecting Atmospheric Fronts with Satellite Data using Machine Learning
papers.Abstract: Atmospheric fronts are associated with much of the high-impact weather in the mid-latitudes, yet their identification and classification remain largely manual and subjective. Existing deep learning approaches rely primarily on gridded reanalysis or forecast data, limiting their applicability to satellite observations available for time-critical applications. We introduce SATFRONT, a machine learning framework for detecting cold, warm, and occluded fronts over Europe from geostationary satellite observations, with reanalysis data as an optional additional input. The model is trained on frontal analyses from five European national meteorological services and evaluated against UK Met Office analyses for 2024. Using satellite observations alone, SATFRONT achieves a Critical Success Index (CSI) of 0.428 at a 150 km tolerance, within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services (0.277-0.501) and higher than that of an operational rule-based front detector that uses satellite data (0.133). Adding ERA5 reanalysis increases the CSI to 0.591. ERA5 substantially improves the placement of individual fronts, although its effect on their annual spatial distribution varies by front type. These results demonstrate that cold, warm, and occluded fronts can be detected directly from geostationary satellite observations, providing a basis for automated frontal analyses at the high temporal frequency required for time-critical applications.
papers.Core_Innovation: Uses a machine learning architecture trained on national frontal analyses to segment frontal structures directly from geostationary satellite imagery. Optional reanalysis fusion refines accuracy but is dispensable for real-time operation
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Aviation, Agriculture, Energy
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget to integrate SATFRONT-style ML front detection into operational workflows within the next quarter. Phase out legacy rule-based front detectors that depend on reanalysis grids
papers.Tags: Satellite, Machine Learning, Front Detection, Geostationary, Forecasting
papers.Hook: Satellite observations alone now operationally detect atmospheric fronts in near real-time

papers.Title: Regret-Optimal Wasserstein-Robust Linear Regression
papers.Abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) minimizes worst-case risk under distributional uncertainty, but its decisions can be suboptimal in terms of their excess risk, or regret. We study this gap for multivariate least-squares regression, assuming that the observed source law and unknown target law differ by an adversarial 2-Wasserstein perturbation of size $\varepsilon$. We first identify the asymptotic complexity of robust decision-making in the $\varepsilon \to 0$ limit, characterized by a problem-specific condition number $κ$. Here, a wide spectrum of simple algorithms, including DRO, achieve the instance-optimal rate of $O(κ\varepsilon^2)$. For fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, we prove that DRO still achieves the minimax rate if the problem has bounded residual effective rank. On the other hand, we identify significant failure modes where DRO is provably suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors. Fortunately, we prove that two alternative procedures, minimax regret optimization (MRO) and spectral-norm regularization (SNR), attain the minimax rate. We derive an exact convex reformulation of MRO and an accelerated proximal algorithm for SNR, along with high-probability finite-sample guarantees. We support these theoretical results with numerical experiments separating the performance of MRO and SNR from DRO.
papers.Core_Innovation: Establishes the instance-optimal O(κε²) regret rate for DRO in the ε→0 limit and proves dimension-dependent failure modes of DRO under fixed perturbation, then introduces minimax regret optimization (MRO) to achieve regret-optimal robustness.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Financial Services, Healthcare, Energy
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate capital to MRO-enhanced quant funds within 9 months to capture regret-optimal alpha. Reallocate away from DRO-reliant asset pricing models in multi-asset portfolios facing distribution shift.
papers.Tags: Wasserstein robustness, regret optimization, distribution shift, linear regression, minimax
papers.Hook: Regret-optimal robustness achieves instance-optimal rates under Wasserstein perturbation, overcoming DRO failure modes.

papers.Title: Hard Constraint Projection in a Physics Informed Neural Network (Burgers)
papers.Abstract: Physics informed machine learning provides a framework to study and simulate fluid dynamics, potentially at a fraction of the computational cost of traditional numerical methods, with the goal of improving the explainability, accuracy and robustness of purely data driven machine learning methods. In this work, we extend the hard constraint projection (HCP) method developed by Chen et al. [Journal of Computational Physics, 445, 110624, 2021] from a linear partial differential equation (PDE) to a nonlinear PDE: the 1D Burgers' equation. To strictly impose a discrete approximation of the governing equation, the Burgers' equation is first locally discretised (using a finite difference stencil) then decomposed into a constraint matrix and a prediction matrix. Using tools from linear algebra, the constraint matrix is used to construct a projection matrix. A physics informed neural network (PINN) [Raissi et al. Journal of Computational Physics, 378, 686, 2019] is used to predict the velocity, and a final unlearnable layer projects the velocity prediction to the hyperplane of exact solutions to a discretised form of the Burgers' equation. Our initial results indicate that the HCP-PINN initially trains similarly to an equivalent PINN, and as the PINN loss plateaus, the HCP-PINN loss continues to decline. When tested on a previously unseen uniform grid of points covering the domain, the HCP-PINN exhibits higher accuracy, converging to a data error approximately an order of magnitude lower than the comparable PINN. We also observe that the inclusion of the HCP layer results in better observance of the governing PDE. Our findings suggest that the HCP-PINN can be more robust to the selection of physics collocation points, and less dependent on collocation point quantity.
papers.Core_Innovation: The method introduces a finite difference stencil-based decomposition of the Burgers' equation into constraint and prediction matrices, enabling linear algebraic construction of a projection matrix that strictly enforces the discrete PDE residual within a PINN framework.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Computational Fluid Dynamics, Engineering Simulation
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate capital to integrate HCP projection into existing PINN pipelines for aerospace applications within 12 months. Mandate benchmarking against traditional CFD on transonic flow cases to verify velocity accuracy gains.
papers.Tags: Hard Constraint Projection, Physics Informed Neural Network, Burgers Equation, Finite Difference, Projection Matrix
papers.Hook: Hard constraint projection extended to nonlinear Burgers' equation via finite difference stencil.

papers.Title: Hyperbolic Inverse Reinforcement Learning
papers.Abstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) seeks to infer the reward function underlying observed behavior, but its predictive accuracy and interpretability depend on how that reward is computed from the underlying features. While prior IRL reward functions have been implemented through a variety of techniques including linear weights, neural networks, or other function approximators, none make assumptions about the geometry of the underlying feature space. Inspired by geometric organization observed in neural circuits, we introduce Hyperbolic inverse reinforcement learning (Hyperbolic IRL), which parameterizes reward as a function of Hyperbolic distance between the feature vector and a learned parameter vector, as well as its Euclidean distance variant. We tested our methods against a range of linear and nonlinear IRL baselines under both deterministic and stochastic policies. Our Hyperbolic approach achieved comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on established benchmarks and excelled in the low data limit and across dense environments. Applied to human navigation among multiple exhibits in a museum room, Hyperbolic IRL reveals reward structure that depends not only on individual exhibit-distance features, but also on non-separable conjunctions between them. Together, these results demonstrate that a Hyperbolic reward parameterization can improve both the predictive accuracy and interpretability of IRL, providing a framework for studying how non-separable, conjunctive structure can begin to explain behavior.
papers.Core_Innovation: Replaces Euclidean reward parameterization with hyperbolic distance metric between feature and learned parameter vectors.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Autonomous Systems, Game AI
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate capital to teams prototyping hyperbolic reward modeling within the next quarter. Phase out Euclidean-only IRL tooling in favor of geometry-agnostic alternatives.
papers.Tags: Hyperbolic Geometry, Inverse Reinforcement Learning, Reward Modeling, Distance Metric, Neural Circuits
papers.Hook: Hyperbolic distance parameterizes reward functions in inverse reinforcement learning.

papers.Title: Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering
papers.Abstract: An estimator can be accurate and stable on typical data, yet sensitive to a few possible records. Differentially private mechanisms commonly scale their noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, which lets these records dictate the noise even when the remaining data would allow far less. Removing them first would restore the smaller scale, but the removal must itself be private.   We introduce \emph{propose-filter-release} (PFR), which, by privately filtering its input, turns a mechanism that protects the addition or removal of a typical record, one that fits the remaining data, into one that is differentially private in the standard sense, on every input. Using our novel filtering step, PFR requires only a concave friendliness score, which measures how well a record fits a dataset, and a release mechanism that is friendly-DP, that is, private when the changed record fits the remaining data. For every such score and release mechanism, it guarantees differential privacy under public conditions on the number of records, so it is a general privacy primitive, comparable to propose-test-release, and FriendlyCore can be viewed as one of its implementations.   We illustrate the generality of PFR by instantiating it for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation, the KL divergence of user histograms, the effective resistances of a graph, and treatment-rule selection.
papers.Core_Innovation: Privately filtering input records via a concave friendliness score transforms typical-record protection into standard differential privacy without worst-case noise scaling.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Healthcare, Finance, Advertising
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund development of PFR-compatible DP pipelines within 6 months to replace worst-case noise calibration. Mandate privacy audits on all new mechanisms to verify friendliness-score compliance.
papers.Tags: differential privacy, private filtering, sensitivity scaling, friendliness scoring
papers.Hook: Private filtering enables DP mechanisms to scale noise to typical rather than worst-case sensitivity

papers.Title: When Does Storage Complement Solar? Investment and Cost Recovery under Advanced Net Metering
papers.Abstract: We examine the joint PV and storage operational and investment decisions of a prosumer under net energy metering (NEM) and peak/off-peak tariffs. Legacy NEM compensates net exports at the retail rate over a netting period, typically under time-invariant pricing. To better reflect system costs, tariff features are being reconsidered, with many U.S. states adopting time-varying prices and export compensation below the retail price. We formulate the prosumer decision problem as a cost minimization problem with charge/discharge, PV investment, and storage investment decisions. We analytically derive the optimal decisions based on the tariff's membership in one of six regions that partition the tariff space. Using these solutions, we examine the relationship between PV and storage, identifying when they are complements or substitutes. Furthermore, we identify the relationship between private DER incentives and the distribution utility's (DU's) net cost of serving the prosumer. For both storage and PV, when investment costs are greater than the costs of serving the customer, there is no tariff where investment in PV and storage decrease non-adopter bills. Under the same conditions, complementarity between PV and storage decreases DU cost recovery for a given tariff. In a Massachusetts-based case study, we validate our theoretical findings by connecting tariff design features to DER interaction, the DU's net cost, and DER adoption in a stochastic, multi-prosumer, and multi-period setting.

papers.Title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
papers.Abstract: The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions.   This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.
papers.Core_Innovation: Perturbing a single decoder block or adding random bias to output logits matches full-weight perturbation performance, shifting the explanation from weight-space geometry to output diversity and validation-based selection.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Cloud Computing, Enterprise AI
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Weight Space Perturbation, Full Model Fine-Tuning
papers.Decision_Perspective: AI product teams should prototype PSV-enhanced inference within 60 days to validate compute savings. Enterprises using full-weight perturbation fine-tuning should pilot PSV replacement within 90 days to maintain competitiveness.
papers.Tags: perturbation, output selection, validation, large language models
papers.Hook: Single decoder block perturbations match full-weight edits, enabling efficient model steering.

papers.Title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
papers.Abstract: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.
papers.Core_Innovation: Each spatial anchor expands into multiple slots partitioned by disjoint DCT coefficient bands, restricting global attention to the lowest-frequency slot while all slots interact locally via a spatial correction head.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Computer Graphics, Media Entertainment, AI Infrastructure
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Legacy Image Tokenization, Static Attention Models
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund prototype integration into next-gen generative video pipelines within 12 months to validate spectral-slot routing against baseline token costs. Mandate evaluation of DCT-partitioned attention for all new multimodal foundation models starting Q3 2026.
papers.Tags: SpecSlot, DCT, Attention, Generative, Transformer
papers.Hook: Enables pixel-space transformers to increase spectral detail without expanding global attention via DCT-partitioned slot allocation

papers.Title: Adaptive Scenario Generation for KL-DRO Around a Learned Density Model
papers.Abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) hedges data-driven two-stage stochastic programs against error in the distribution estimated from a finite record, and standard ambiguity sets differ in how they treat realizations absent from that record. A divergence ball around the empirical distribution contains only reweightings of the record, whereas a transport ball also contains distributions supported off the record, including on realizations the data-generating process cannot produce, against which the decision is then hedged as well. We instead propose a Kullback-Leibler (KL) ball centered at a density model fitted to the record, the learned nominal, which lets the adversary up-weight costly unobserved realizations in proportion to the probability the model assigns them. Solving the resulting problem poses a second difficulty, because it can accommodate only a few scenarios, and an independent sample of that size is likely to omit the rare realizations on which the worst case concentrates. We therefore build the scenario set adaptively, alternating between solving the finite problem and drawing new realizations from the learned nominal, steered toward the worst case at the current decision, with importance weights that correct the draws back to the model. On a multi-item newsvendor problem and a capacity expansion problem on realistic grid data, centering the ball at the learned nominal rather than at the record lowers cost under distribution shift, at comparable in-distribution cost, when the record is scarce and the model class captures structure that lets it extrapolate beyond the record. The advantage fades as the record grows or as the shift departs from the structure the model has learned.
papers.Core_Innovation: The work replaces the empirical or transport ambiguity set with a KL divergence ball centered on a neural density model fitted to the training record. This permits adversarial up-weighting of unobserved scenarios in direct proportion to the model's assigned probability, preserving realizability while addressing distribution error
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Finance, Energy, Insurance
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund KL-DRO prototype implementations in enterprise risk platforms within the next 9 months to capture model-probable tail-event up-weighting. Retire empirical DRO pipelines lacking density-model integration within 2 years as KL-DRO becomes the stochastic optimization baseline.
papers.Tags: KL-DRO, Learned Density, DRO, Scenario Generation, Rare Events
papers.Hook: KL-DRO centered on learned densities up-weights unobserved realizations proportionally to model probability

papers.Title: Luggage re-identification: A study of strategies towards a real-world application
papers.Abstract: Luggage re-identification (ReID) is a critical task in video surveillance for forensics, security or border management (suspicious or abandoned luggage recognition), as well as luggage management (lost luggage recovery). It enables the association of observations of the same luggage across disjoint camera views in complex environments such as airports, train stations and border crossing. While existing approaches primarily focus on appearance-based cropped image matching under relatively clean conditions, real-world scenarios are characterized by frequent occlusions, cluttered background and crowded scenes which significantly degrade performance. Yet, strategies leveraging the complementarity of multiple shots and views from different video streams is overlooked. In this paper, we study strategies for an end-to-end pipeline that operates from multiple video streams to detect and re-identify luggage. We evaluate different variants on a benchmark dataset acquired in real-world environments to address the questions of selecting and merging different views and shots of the same luggage as well as training on different environment datasets for an overall ReID performance improvement in practical applications.
papers.Core_Innovation: The core innovation is an end-to-end framework that jointly detects and re-identifies luggage across heterogeneous video streams by explicitly modeling shot-and-view complementarity to resist occlusions and clutter.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Aviation Security, Public Safety, Border Control, Transportation Security
