papers.Tags: Sparse Coding, Dictionary Learning, Model Interpretability
papers.Hook: Enables reproducible concept discovery in foundation models via per-sample sparse coding.

papers.Title: Task-aware Kernel Stein certificates for Rényi differential privacy
papers.Abstract: Rènyi differential privacy, based on Rènyi divergence, has become a notion of choice for privacy guarantees. However, outside the Gaussian setting, Rènyi divergence can be difficult to compute. In particular, Rènyi differential privacy guarantees that exploit task-specific information, as in Rènyi Pufferfish privacy, can be challenging. Here we use kernel Stein discrepancies based on escort distributions to provide certificates for Rènyi differential privacy. By designing the kernel to focus on the relevant privacy directions, we also derive task-aware privacy certificates. We provide exact identities for Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms and bounds for exponential mechanisms, with separate task-aware guarantees. A real data set example illustrates how the protected comparison set and the released subspace jointly determine the resulting certificates.
papers.Core_Innovation: The authors construct kernel Stein discrepancies using escort distributions to approximate Rényi divergence and design kernels that align with privacy‑relevant directions, yielding task‑aware certificates. They provide exact identities for Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms and derive bounds for exponential mechanisms.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Data Privacy, Cybersecurity, Healthcare, Finance
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Anonymization, Generic Differential Privacy Consulting
papers.Decision_Perspective: Enterprises handling sensitive user data should pilot integrating task‑aware kernel Stein certificates into their privacy pipelines within the next six months to replace generic Rényi DP bounds. Vendors of privacy‑preserving ML libraries should allocate Q3 2025 R&D funds to implement and benchmark these certificates for Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms.
papers.Tags: Rényi DP, Kernel Stein, Task-aware Privacy, Certificate Mechanism
papers.Hook: Enables task‑aware Rényi privacy certificates via kernel Stein discrepancies.

papers.Title: FuTransformer: FP8 prefill and INT4 decode for Llama-style inference on Hopper
papers.Abstract: Transformer prefill reuses weights across tokens and is dominated by matrix multiplication and activation data movement; single-token decode has limited reuse and is dominated by weight and KV-cache reads. We present FUTRANSFORMER, a CUDA implementation of a Llama-style Transformer block for NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. It applies CODA's GEMM-plus-epilogue approach to inference, adding direct KV-cache placement, folding the fixed RMSNorm gain into weights, writing FP8 output directly with delayed scaling, and supporting prefill without padding. Decode uses INT4 projection weights and an INT4 KV-cache copy. Weights and keys follow Tensor Core fragment layouts for direct dequantization into MMA operands without full intermediate tiles. A block-diagonal Hadamard transform reduces cache quantization error from outlier channels. On one H100, prefill is up to 1.48x faster than compiled PyTorch FP8 and reaches 1.29 PFLOP/s. For gate/up projection with SwiGLU at the 8B shape, our BF16 path is 1.13x faster than CODA. Our FP8 path is 2.02-2.18x faster than the evaluated BF16 CODA path. Across 8B and 70B shapes at batches 1-32, INT4 decode is 1.3-2.4x faster than the faster of PyTorch's BF16 and INT4 blocks at each point: 2.1-3.3x faster than compiled, CUDA-graphed BF16 and 1.3-6.3x faster than the same block using PyTorch's INT4 projection kernel, which targets a single query row and loses to BF16 at batch 32. It is also 31-51% faster than our FP8 path. Complete Llama-3.1-8B decode takes 2.8 ms per step at batch one, versus 8.1 ms for the compiled transformers implementation. Decoding every WikiText-2 token through the INT4 weight path raises perplexity from 6.24 to 7.23 with round-to-nearest weights or 6.99 with GPTQ in the same format; the rotated INT4 cache adds 0.20. The kernels match a quantized reference computation within 0.001 perplexity.
papers.Core_Innovation: It folds the RMSNorm gain into weights, writes FP8 output directly with delayed scaling, and uses INT4 projection weights and KV-cache copy for decode. It also applies a block-diagonal Hadamard transform to reduce cache quantization error and uses Tensor Core fragment layouts for direct dequantization.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: AI Infrastructure, Cloud Computing, Semiconductor, Enterprise AI
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Legacy CPU Inference, Traditional Deep Learning Frameworks
papers.Decision_Perspective: Deploy FuTransformer-based inference servers on H100 clusters for FP8/INT4 Llama workloads by Q1 2027. Discontinue funding for generic FP16 inference pipelines on Hopper after Q2 2027.
papers.Tags: FP8, INT4, Hopper, LLM Inference, Tensor Core
papers.Hook: Enables FP8 prefill and INT4 decode on Hopper, cutting LLM inference latency by up to 48%.

papers.Title: LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation
papers.Abstract: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. The code, datasets, and demos can be found on the project website: https://libero-perm.github.io/.
papers.Core_Innovation: LIBERO-PeRM introduces a simulation‑based benchmark that decouples task success from preference satisfaction by defining a taxonomy of language‑expressible motion, skill, and user‑profile preferences. It provides standardized protocols for zero‑shot preference following, learning from demonstrations, and measuring generalization across layouts and tasks.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Personal Robotics, Human-Robot Interaction, AI for Embodied Agents, Simulation
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund the development of preference‑aware imitation learning algorithms for household robots within the next six months. Deprioritize investment in pure task-success metrics for consumer robotics after Q4 2025.
papers.Tags: Preference Learning, Robotic Manipulation, Benchmark, Simulation, Human-Robot Interaction
papers.Hook: Robots can now be evaluated on how well they learn and obey user preferences in simulation.

papers.Title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
papers.Abstract: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.
papers.Core_Innovation: The method couples an LLM generator that proposes quantum circuit mutations with a separate evaluator that checks reversibility and scores Toffoli/qubit cost, enabling evolutionary search over circuit space.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Quantum Computing, Pharmaceuticals, Finance, Materials Science, Cryptography
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Classical EDA, Manual Quantum Algorithm Design
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund quantum‑startup teams that integrate LLMs into circuit‑search pipelines within the next six months. Buy or license the LLM‑evolution framework from the authors to accelerate internal quantum‑algorithm development.
papers.Tags: LLM, quantum circuit design, evolutionary search, Toffoli reduction, reversible architecture
papers.Hook: LLM-driven evolution yields quantum circuits with fewer Toffoli gates and qubits across multiple domains.

papers.Title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models
papers.Abstract: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.
papers.Core_Innovation: T2-Z adds a learnable environment latent vector that is optimized at test time to minimize prediction error, while the world model parameters remain fixed. Training alternates between updating the world model with fixed latents and updating latents with a frozen world model, enabling the latent to capture unobserved environmental factors.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Autonomous Vehicles, Manufacturing, Logistics
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Control Engineering, Manual Sensor Calibration
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund startups that embed test-time latent optimization into robotic perception stacks within the next 12 months. Kill investment in static world-model pipelines lacking online latent adaptation within six months.
papers.Tags: robotics, world models, latent optimization, test-time adaptation, environment modeling
papers.Hook: Enables robots to instantly adapt world-model predictions to unseen physical conditions via test-time latent optimization.

papers.Title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies
papers.Abstract: Generative simulation can automate robot environment construction, but physically valid environments are not necessarily useful for training. The challenge is to identify environments that address a policy's failures and supervision that helps it overcome them. We introduce CoDA, a framework in which a simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve through a shared heterogeneous memory of environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress. The memory compiles validated diagnoses from a vision-language critic into generation programs that recreate difficulties and training programs that help the policy overcome them. We further propose Text2potential to convert these diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning, providing dense supervision for policy updates while preserving the task's optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions. Measured learning progress guides further generation and program refinement. Across four manipulation task families, CoDA improves out-of-distribution success from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, exceeding the strongest closed-loop baseline by 9.5 percentage points with the same generation budget. On LIBERO-Pro, 15 rounds of generation and training raise success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations.
papers.Core_Innovation: CoDA introduces a shared heterogeneous memory that stores environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress; a vision-language critic extracts validated diagnoses which are turned into generation programs that recreate difficulties and into staged potentials via Text2potential for dense, shaping‑preserving supervision.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Industrial Automation, Manufacturing, Simulation Software
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Manual Environment Design, Traditional RL Simulation
papers.Decision_Perspective: Build a CoDA‑integrated simulation pipeline for robotic manipulation tasks within the next six months to cut policy‑learning cycles by half. Allocate seed funding to teams developing vision‑language critics that can diagnose policy failures in real‑time for deployment by Q3 2025.
papers.Tags: CoDA, Vision-Language Critic, Heterogeneous Memory, Text2potential, Robot Learning
papers.Hook: Enables policies to autonomously generate challenging training environments that directly target their current failures.

papers.Title: PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting of Multivariate Trajectories
papers.Abstract: Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general-purpose forecasting. However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified. This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it. To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths. We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws. Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model. The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly. PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME. To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics. PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines. Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse. PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications.
papers.Core_Innovation: PathFM uses flow matching to model the joint distribution of future multivariate trajectories, then distills the sampler to one or two steps and shares the history attention cache across draws, allowing many paths to be generated at the cost of a single quantile query.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Energy, Transportation, Finance, Supply Chain, Manufacturing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget to pilot PathFM‑based multi‑path generation in electricity load forecasting pipelines by end of Q2 2026. Purchase the distilled model weights and integrate them into existing quantile‑forecast APIs to enable dependence-aware calibration.
papers.Tags: flow matching, trajectory forecasting, model distillation, calibration loss, multi-path sampling
papers.Hook: Generate many future path samples as fast as one quantile forecast, enabling dependence-aware calibration.

papers.Title: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts
papers.Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling model parameters. Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales.
papers.Core_Innovation: MirrorMoE introduces a token‑adaptive gating mechanism that suppresses experts whose routing probabilities fall below a learned threshold, thereby reducing the effective expert set per token and restoring exploration pressure in fine‑grained MoE architectures. This is combined with a shared‑expert baseline to maintain capacity while improving routing diversity.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Cloud Computing, Natural Language Processing, Autonomous Vehicles
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Dense Model Vendors, Static Routing ASICs
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund startups that integrate token‑adaptive expert suppression into MoE layers within the next six months. Divest from static‑routing MoE designs that lack adaptive gating capabilities.
papers.Tags: Mixture-of-Experts, Routing Exploration, Token‑Adaptive Gating
papers.Hook: Enables full utilization of fine-grained expert segmentation in MoE models via token-adaptive expert suppression.

papers.Title: FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery
papers.Abstract: Existing agent benchmarks typically evaluate agents on well-specified tasks defined by issue reports, specifications, or task tickets. Real-world customer delivery is different: forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must clarify ambiguous requirements, work in live systems, and uncover unstated constraints. We introduce FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects. In simulated customer environments with scripted stakeholders and modifiable customer systems, agents interact with stakeholders and operate on production-like systems to deliver working solutions. FDE-Gym scores a delivery by how much it improves the customer's own success metric, normalized between 0 (unchanged system) and 1 (reference solution), with penalties for stakeholder interactions (messages, trial runs, and waiting time). An online platform lets humans practice FDE skills under the same grading criteria. We evaluate 13 model configurations from seven providers. In the realistic setting, where unstated constraints must be discovered, the best configuration achieves a mean FDE-Gym score of 0.56 and resolves only 14 of the 95 tasks (a score of at least 0.8 with no incident). Discovering unstated constraints is the primary bottleneck: performance drops sharply when models must uncover them without explicit guidance. Yet information discovery alone does not account for the gap: even on the 23 tasks where the best configuration obtains every key fact from stakeholders, it reaches a normalized business uplift of 0.8 or above on only 10. These results reveal a substantial gap between solving well-specified tasks and delivering effective AI systems for real customers.
papers.Core_Innovation: FDE-Gym provides a simulated, interactive environment where agents must negotiate requirements with scripted stakeholders and modify live‑like systems, with performance measured by normalized improvement in the customer’s success metric minus interaction penalties.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Consulting, Information Technology, Healthcare, Finance, Manufacturing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund the integration of FDE-Gym scoring into agent training pipelines by Q3 2026. Purchase or license the FDE-Gym platform for internal AI delivery teams effective immediately.
papers.Tags: AI agents, benchmarking, forward-deployed engineering, stakeholder interaction, simulated environments
papers.Hook: Agents can now be evaluated on real‑world, ambiguous delivery tasks with stakeholder interaction penalties.

papers.Title: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering
papers.Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes. We propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks.
papers.Core_Innovation: We introduce a post‑training supervision selection algorithm that identifies informative sub‑trajectories from lengthy MLE interaction logs and uses them to fine‑tune a 35B Mixture‑of‑Experts agent, enabling the model to learn from intermediate experiment outcomes without exhaustive replay.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning Operations, Automated Machine Learning, Data Science, Software Engineering
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Manual Machine Learning Engineering, Traditional ML Consulting
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund the development of an internal post‑training pipeline for long‑horizon ML agent models within the next six months to cut dependence on third‑party AutoML services. Discontinue or deprioritize spending on legacy human‑in‑the‑loop ML workflow platforms that lack autonomous feedback integration by the end of Q4 2025.
papers.Tags: Agentic ML, Post‑training, Mixture‑of‑Experts, AutoML, Autonomous Experimentation
papers.Hook: Autonomous ML engineering models can now learn from intermediate experiment outcomes over long horizons.

papers.Title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling
papers.Abstract: Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment. Experiments show that GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo, supports geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. Project page: https://hongchang-liu.github.io/GeoState-project-page/
papers.Core_Innovation: GeoState introduces a scene tokenizer that fuses multi‑view GFM features into a single view‑invariant latent, and a geometry decoder that reconstructs geometry from this latent using camera rays, while an autoregressive model evolves the latent independently of camera motion.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Autonomous Vehicles, Robotics, Augmented Reality, Virtual Reality, Simulation
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Structure-From-Motion, Multi-View Stereo, View-Dependent Feature Modeling
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate R&D budget to prototype GeoState-based world models for autonomous vehicle navigation by Q2 2025. Acquire or license geometry foundation model technology to enable multi-view feature aggregation in existing simulation stacks by end of 2025.
papers.Tags: 3D World Modeling, View-Decoupled Representation, Geometry Foundation Models, Autoregressive Prediction, Camera‑Independent Scale
papers.Hook: Predict future 3D scene geometry independent of camera viewpoint, enabling consistent long-horizon world modeling.

papers.Title: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code
papers.Abstract: We introduce 3DCodeVerse, a research ecosystem that enables coding agents to create editable and verifiable 3D content at scale. 3DCodeVerse comprises large-scale, high-quality datasets of executable 3D code, a coding harness for spatial reasoning and automated verification, and practical guidance for 3D coding. First, we construct 3DCodeVerse-2M, a large-scale curated dataset of standalone 3D executable code. We build this corpus by collecting open-source data, converting specialized representations, and generating new programs with coding agents. Each program is packaged with the source files and associated assets required for execution in its declared environment, along with available descriptions and verification records. Second, we develop the 3DCodeVerse Harness, a multi-agent directed acyclic graph framework for generating and refining 3D content. It uses execution checks, spatial measurements, and visual feedback to automatically evaluate and revise generated programs without human feedback during generation. Third, we conduct systematic empirical studies of 3D coding, establishing baselines with fine-tuned open models and deriving practical guidance through component-level analyses of our harness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning on our dataset significantly improves the 3D coding capabilities of open-source models. Notably, our 3DCodeVerse harness achieves a 90% win rate against Claude Design (3D Object) in pairwise human evaluations, when both are utilized by Claude Opus 5.5.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper introduces a curated dataset of standalone executable 3D programs with associated assets and verification records, and a multi-agent DAG harness that iteratively refines generated code using execution checks, spatial metrics, and visual feedback.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Video Game Development, Virtual Reality, Computer-Aided Design, Animation, Simulation
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional 3D Modeling Studios, Manual Asset Creation Services
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund startups that integrate the 3DCodeVerse harness into game engines within six months. Acquire licensing for the 3DCodeVerse-2M dataset to train internal generative AI models by Q2 2027.
papers.Tags: 3D generation, coding agents, procedural content, verification harness, dataset
papers.Hook: Enables AI agents to automatically produce editable, verifiable 3D worlds from code.

papers.Title: Dexterity from Supervised Play
papers.Abstract: How can robots autonomously collect the contact-rich experience needed to learn dexterous manipulation? We present DSP: Dexterity from supervised play, a framework in which a robot learns a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning, then deploys it autonomously to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model. During inference, the same play policy then guides model-predictive control (MPC) by proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model. To accelerate inference, we also introduce a method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. We evaluate this framework on underactuated pushing and any-to-any in-hand pose reorientation with a multifingered hand, in simulation and real world. In real world experiment, our method outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6% in success rate and achieves comparable success to reinforcement learning with 490 times less interaction data. These results demonstrate that supervised play can autonomously collect interaction data, guide model-based planning, and enable policy learning without any task-specific demonstrations or sim-to-real transfer.
papers.Core_Innovation: The framework learns a short‑horizon play policy via behavior cloning from minutes of human demonstration, then deploys that policy to autonomously generate interaction data for learning a predictive world model. At test time, the same policy proposes action sequences for MPC, while a self‑play distillation step yields a fast, goal‑conditioned closed‑loop policy.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Manufacturing, Logistics, Healthcare, Agriculture
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Reinforcement Learning Robotics, Manual Robot Programming
papers.Decision_Perspective: Invest in integrating DSP-derived play policies into warehouse picking robots within the next 12 months to cut training data collection costs. Divert funding from legacy RL‑heavy manipulation projects that demand extensive real‑world trial‑and‑error to support DSP‑based pilot programs.
papers.Tags: Robot Dexterity, Behavior Cloning, World Model Learning, MPC, Self‑Play Distillation
papers.Hook: Robots learn dexterous manipulation from minutes of human play, needing far less data.

papers.Title: Lean Graph Search for Formal Theorem Proving
papers.Abstract: Retrieving relevant lemmas is crucial for formal theorem proving, enabling provers to build machine-checkable proofs from established mathematical results. Recent retrieval systems match library declarations to a target theorem or its intermediate proof steps, but make limited use of multi-hop dependencies among declarations. These dependencies can reveal supporting lemmas that are not necessarily lexically similar to the target theorem but recur in proofs of related problems. To this end, we propose LeanGraphSearch, a graph-based retrieval method for Lean 4 that constructs a graph from Mathlib's forward dependencies and traverses it to uncover supporting lemmas through multi-hop dependency chains. Specifically, LeanGraphSearch links each declaration to the premises it depends on, uses a graph-based ranking algorithm to propagate relevance from semantically matched declarations to their dependencies, and reranks the expanded candidates against the original query. Across two mathematical retrieval benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves recall by up to 12% over the strongest baseline, LeanSearch v2, on MathlibQR and increases coverage of complete annotated proof routes on MathlibMPR, covering up to 3.7% of extra groups. More importantly, we evaluate whether these retrieval gains translate into improved end-to-end theorem proving by integrating LeanGraphSearch into an iterative proving loop guided by Lean feedback. Across three theorem proving benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves pass rate at {8, 16, 32} reflection turns by as much as 40% compared to vanilla prover and at most 10% compared to LeanSearch v2, showing higher accuracy-cost efficiency. These findings highlight the value of dependency graph search for theorem proving and motivate further research on structure-aware search for proof discovery.
papers.Core_Innovation: LeanGraphSearch builds a directed graph of forward declarations from Mathlib and applies a relevance‑propagation algorithm that spreads match scores from query‑matched lemmas to their dependencies, then reranks the expanded set.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Formal Methods, Automated Theorem Proving, Ai For Mathematics, Software Verification
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund integration of LeanGraphSearch into Lean 4 IDE plugins by Q3 2026 to boost lemma suggestion accuracy. Kill reliance on pure lexical matching retrieval in new theorem‑proving projects starting immediately.
papers.Tags: Lean 4, graph search, lemma retrieval, dependency propagation, formal verification
papers.Hook: Enables discovery of non‑lexically similar supporting lemmas via multi‑hop dependency traversal in Lean 4.

papers.Title: Robust Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Treatment Regimes under Model and Measurement Uncertainty
papers.Abstract: We develop a robust reinforcement learning (RL) framework for learning adaptive treatment policies that generalize across patients and remain reliable under errors in the measured biomarker and shifts in the disease dynamics. By modeling the patient as a hidden context, we address generalization and robustness in a unified manner through robust contextual Markov decision processes. Applying our framework to adaptive therapy for metastatic prostate cancer in a simulator calibrated to clinical data, we obtain generalizable and robust policies that substantially outperform the existing adaptive therapy method. In particular, we attain robustness with almost no loss of performance when the biomarker is accurate and the disease evolves as anticipated, and find that the resulting policy Pareto-dominates the existing method across a diverse array of scenarios. Our findings suggest that robust RL holds great promise as a principled methodology for learning reliable adaptive treatment policies.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces a robust contextual MDP where patient-specific hidden contexts capture unobserved heterogeneity, and learns policies by optimizing worst-case reward over ambiguity sets for transition dynamics and observation noise. This yields adaptive treatment policies provably robust to both model misspecification and biomarker measurement errors.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Healthcare, Pharmaceuticals, Medical Devices
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund development of a robust contextual MDP-based adaptive therapy software suite for metastatic prostate cancer, targeting a prototype by Q4 2025. Allocate budget to integrate biomarker uncertainty quantification modules into existing clinical decision support systems, with rollout triggered by successful validation in simulated trials.
papers.Tags: Robust Reinforcement Learning, Adaptive Therapy, Contextual MDP
papers.Hook: Enables adaptive cancer therapy policies that stay effective despite biomarker noise and disease dynamics shifts.

papers.Title: Evaluation Awareness Beyond English: Do LLMs Act Differently When Tested in Indic Languages?
papers.Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can often tell when they are being tested. This ability, known as evaluation awareness, can lead models to act more cautiously during safety evaluations than in real use. Existing work has studied evaluation awareness almost entirely in English, although models serve users in many languages. Indic languages are spoken by over a billion people, yet evaluation awareness remains almost entirely unstudied in them. We test four instruction-tuned models from three families in five Indic languages alongside English. A set of cues varies whether the model is told that it is monitored and whether the monitoring is a safety test. Models refuse harmful requests more often when they are told that they are being tested. This increase appears in all four models and all six languages. In Indic languages, refusal of harmful requests rises by 14.4 percentage points on average. The test cue also brings Indic refusal of harmful requests level with English, but raises refusal of benign Indic requests from 6.9% to 11.3%. We release all 47,880 judged responses to support further work. These results suggest that safety evaluations in Indic languages may not reflect how models treat their everyday users.
papers.Core_Innovation: The study shows that explicit test cues about monitoring and safety testing increase refusal of harmful requests uniformly across six languages, closing the gap between Indic and English refusal rates. This demonstrates that evaluation awareness is language‑agnostic and can be induced via simple prompting.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: AI Safety, Multilingual Content Moderation, Customer Support, Healthcare, Financial Services
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: English-Only Safety Vendors, Generic Language Filtering Services
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund the development of multilingual evaluation‑awareness benchmarks within the next quarter to monitor LLM safety across languages. Buy or integrate cue‑based safety prompts into production LLMs deployed in Indic‑speaking markets by end of 2026.
papers.Tags: Evaluation Awareness, Multilingual Safety, Indic Languages, LLM Prompting, AI Governance
papers.Hook: LLMs can now be reliably prompted to refuse harmful requests equally across Indic and English languages.

papers.Title: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents
papers.Abstract: Deep search agents solve knowledge-intensive tasks through long-horizon, multi-turn interactions, where assigning credit to individual search decisions is fundamentally difficult. Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides only a single terminal reward shared across an entire trajectory. Recent process-supervision methods aim to assign credit at finer granularity, but they typically anchor credit to either surface-level trajectory states or model-internal signals, both of which become unreliable in deep search where observations are heterogeneous and retrieved contexts are long and noisy. We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, KnowGPO decomposes the information required to derive the answer into atomic knowledge conditions, and represents the state of a trajectory at each step by the subset of conditions it has satisfied. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, and the incremental knowledge gain between consecutive steps serves as an environment-grounded process reward. Experiments on Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA show KnowGPO consistently outperforms outcome-only (GRPO) and process-supervision baselines (GiGPO, IGPO) by 3.8 to 4.2 points, with our 8B model rivaling or exceeding most 32B open-source systems.
papers.Core_Innovation: KnowGPO represents each step of a search trajectory by the subset of atomic knowledge conditions satisfied for a given query, turning credit assignment into a set‑based problem. This shifts supervision from surface states or internal signals to explicit task‑relevant knowledge acquisition.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Information Retrieval, Enterprise Knowledge Management, Customer Support Automation
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Rule-Based Search Engines, Manual Knowledge Engineering
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund pilot projects that integrate KnowGPO into enterprise knowledge-base chatbots within the next 6 months. Kill investments in pure outcome-only RL for long-horizon search agents after Q4 2025.
papers.Tags: Reinforcement Learning, Knowledge Grounding, Search Agents, Credit Assignment, Process Supervision
papers.Hook: Enables RL to assign credit to search steps by tracking satisfied knowledge conditions.

papers.Title: Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.Abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) offer an alternative approach to parallel language generation; however, most existing studies directly use transformer architectures from either causal large language models (LLMs) or Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for image generation, which were not optimized for CDLMs. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on Transformer architectures for CDLMs and introduce Language Diffusion Transformer (LangDiT), combining feature and query-key normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing and calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning. LangDiT significantly reduces generation perplexity in matched LangFlow comparisons, establishing a new state of the art in continuous language generation across different model formulations. Using LangFlow as a representative CDLM, LangDiT as a plug-and-play backbone leads to a new state-of-the-art model with a generation perplexity (GenPPL) of 21.72 using 1024 NFEs and 44.72 GenPPL using 128 NFEs on the unconditional generation of 1024-token sequences on the OpenWebText dataset. When adapted to Plaid-style CDLM formulations, LangDiT results in a new leading GenPPL of 11.33 using 1024 denoising NFEs, and 27.51 GenPPL using 128 denoising NFEs. These gains are achieved while retaining each model's underlying representation, training objective, and inference sampler, isolating transformer architecture as a fundamental source of improvement. Our study identifies architectural design as an important source of improvement in continuous diffusion language models.
papers.Core_Innovation: LangDiT introduces feature and query-key normalization, broader noise conditioning, likelihood‑shortcut gradient routing with calibration, and confidence‑gated self‑conditioning to adapt transformer blocks for continuous diffusion language modeling.

papers.Decision_Perspective: Build a LangDiT‑based CDLM pilot for real‑time customer‑service chatbots within the next quarter. Fund integration of LangDiT with domain‑specific financial corpora to automate quarterly report generation by Q3.
papers.Tags: Diffusion Language Models, Transformer Architecture, Perplexity Reduction, Noise Conditioning
papers.Hook: Achieves state‑of‑the‑art continuous language generation with markedly lower perplexity via a tailored transformer.

papers.Title: Hierarchical Residual Policy Learning for Real-World Mobile Manipulation with Sparse Human Guidance
papers.Abstract: Mobile Manipulation (MoMa) is a cornerstone of autonomous robotic systems, yet real-world fine-tuning remains a formidable challenge because of high-dimensional action spaces and intricate coupling between heterogeneous modules. In this paper, we propose HiRe-MoMa (Hierarchical Residual Mobile Manipulation), a systematic framework for stable and sample-efficient real-world fine-tuning of complex MoMa systems. At its core, HiRe-MoMa adopts a Hierarchical Residual Architecture that fine-tunes a frozen base policy. A Policy-Agnostic Residual learns additive corrections atop the base policy, while Hierarchical Decoupling splits the residual into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning, mitigating gradient interference and aligning corrections with the platform's physical hierarchy. To improve sample efficiency in data-expensive real-world settings, we propose Expert-Guided Value Alignment, which leverages sparse human interventions with under 20% training coverage to reshape the critic's value landscape, effectively guiding autonomous exploration through expert priors. Extensive real-world experiments on the TIAGo++ platform demonstrate that HiRe-MoMa consistently enhances task performance with only around 30 minutes of online interaction, regardless of the base policy architecture. To our knowledge, this is among the first frameworks to enable efficient on-robot fine-tuning for mobile manipulation in the real world, providing a practical paradigm for deploying complex robotic systems in dynamic, human-centric environments. Further details can be found on our project website: https://hire-moma.github.io/
papers.Core_Innovation: HiRe-MoMa freezes a base policy and learns a policy-agnostic residual that is split into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads, where the arm head is conditioned on the base head's output to prevent gradient interference. It further aligns the residual value function with sparse human interventions via expert-guided value alignment, requiring <20% demonstration data.

papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Manual Teleoperation, Legacy Motion Planning, Traditional Robot Control Systems
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund pilot projects integrating HiRe-MoMa into warehouse mobile manipulators within the next 6 months to reduce training data acquisition costs. Kill investment in legacy teleoperation‑based fine‑tuning tools for mobile manipulators by Q4 2025.
papers.Tags: Hierarchical Residual Learning, Mobile Manipulation, Sparse Human Guidance
papers.Hook: Enables fine-tuning complex mobile manipulators using <20% human demonstrations via hierarchical residual learning.

papers.Title: Modeling and Understanding Neural Weights of Humanoid Policies with Diffusion
papers.Abstract: Recent advances in robot learning have driven rapid progress in humanoid control, enabling increasingly agile behaviors in the real world. However, humanoid control networks are typically obtained through conventional training procedures, while comparatively little attention has been given to directly modeling the distribution of their learned weights and generating functional networks in weight space. In this work, we investigate whether high-performing humanoid control networks can be generatively modeled directly through their weights. We adopt a latent diffusion framework that couples a linear autoencoder with a Diffusion Transformer. The autoencoder compresses actor network parameters into a compact latent space, and the Diffusion Transformer models the distribution of these latents. Trained on networks collected from reinforcement learning for the Unitree G1 robot, our approach generates deployable networks that perform various motions in the real world, including walking, dancing, and spin kick. Beyond generation, we further study the learned weight space to better understand the structure captured by these humanoid control networks. We identify a structural principle in the first-layer weights that consistently reflects the robot's kinematic prior. Notably, this kinematic prior emerges under both Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Imitation Learning (IL) training, suggesting that it is not specific to a particular optimization process but may instead reflect common knowledge associated with humanoid embodiment. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of generative modeling in humanoid network weight space, while providing initial insights into the information encoded by their learned weights. Additional results are available on our project website: https://humanoid-weight-diffusion.github.io/
papers.Core_Innovation: A linear autoencoder compresses actor network parameters into a latent space, and a Diffusion Transformer models the distribution of these latents; sampling from this decoder yields new weight sets that decode into deployable policies.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Humanoid Robotics, Industrial Automation, Entertainment Animatronics
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Manual Robot Programming, Traditional Control Engineering
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund research teams to integrate latent diffusion weight generators into humanoid robot development pipelines within the next 6 months. Buy or license the latent diffusion weight modeling toolkit from the authors to replace manual policy tuning for Unitree G1 and similar platforms.
papers.Tags: Diffusion Models, Weight Space, Humanoid Robotics, Latent Autoencoder, Policy Generation
papers.Hook: Generate functional humanoid control networks directly from weight-space diffusion models.

papers.Title: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents
papers.Abstract:
Training language agents is bottlenecked by the high cost of long-horizon rollouts, yet standard agentic reinforcement learning (RL) learns only from a terminal scalar reward, leaving the supervision in intermediate steps largely unused. Prior work exploits this supervision through value targets that estimate per-step success probabilities or observation targets that fit environment response. Both are hard to construct well: (1) value targets come from the same single scalar signal for each step in the trajectory, and (2) observation targets, such as web pages and terminal logs, are long and noisy and reach only one step ahead. We propose 
ame, which adds a third kind of multi-step action targets. On successful on-policy trajectories, 
ame trains the policy backbone to generate the action sequences that follows each history. Each action is also supervised when forecast from the preceding histories, forming a temporal ensemble that the shared backbone absorbs during training, and this enables acting and forecasting to co-evolve. The policy still acts one step at a time at inference, with no overhead. Across five benchmarks (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, $τ^2$-bench, and AppWorld), 
ame (1) achieves stronger aggregate performance than GRPO and RL baselines with predictive auxiliary targets across simulated environments, while improving overall performance on both realistic applications; (2) delivers up to $1.9	imes$ and $2.0	imes$ higher sample efficiency than ECHO and GRPO, respectively, on ScienceWorld; and (3) achieves these gains with a single policy backbone, without additional models, separate pretraining, or inference overhead. The codebase is available at https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/CoPE.
papers.Core_Innovation: The method adds multi-step action targets: on successful on-policy trajectories it trains the policy backbone to generate the action sequence that follows each history, and simultaneously supervises each action when forecast from preceding histories, forming a temporal ensemble of action signals that the shared backbone absorbs during training.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: AI-Driven Customer Service, Robotic Process Automation, Financial Trading Algorithms, Content Generation, Healthcare Virtual Assistants
papers.Decision_Perspective: Build training pipelines that incorporate multi-step action targets for language agents in enterprise AI platforms. Fund research into scaling this temporal ensemble approach to multimodal environments.
papers.Tags: Language Agents, Reinforcement Learning, Action Forecasting, Multi-Step Supervision, Temporal Ensemble
papers.Hook: Enables language agents to learn from intermediate action sequences, improving long-horizon planning.

papers.Title: Your Transformer Is Secretly Elastic
papers.Abstract: Scaling up transformers has produced models with broad capabilities, deployed across heterogeneous hardware and fluctuating workloads. Yet, model families offer only a few fixed sizes (e.g., S, B, L), forcing users to commit to a model based on hardware and latency constraints. This rigidity is often suboptimal under varying query loads. We introduce a retraining-free method that elastifies pre-trained transformers into a single model that adapts on-the-fly across a continuum of computational budgets. Our key contribution is a differentiable relaxation of the functional unit-ranking problem: unlike prior work, which optimizes a single importance weight per MLP block or attention head, we rank every individual MLP neuron and attention head jointly, on a common scale, by minimizing the model's loss under soft pruning across many sparsity targets, all at once. Across 27 vision and text transformer encoders ranging from 22M to 8B parameters, our method yields smooth degradation up to 60% sparsity and outperforms one-shot baselines under deep pruning. For example, pruning DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 to 50% sparsity removes 427M parameters while reducing ImageNet-1k linear-probing accuracy by only 0.8%, without the need for weight correction or retraining. At 60% sparsity, a pruned AugReg ViT-B/16 model achieves up to $1.80\times$ higher throughput and $1.26\times$ lower single-query latency on an A100 GPU. Elastic models are produced in minutes, with construction time scaling sub-linearly with parameter count.
papers.Core_Innovation: We propose a differentiable relaxation that jointly ranks every MLP neuron and attention head on a unified importance scale, enabling continuous soft pruning across arbitrary sparsity targets in a single forward‑pass optimization.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Cloud Computing, Edge AI, Autonomous Vehicles, Natural Language Processing, Computer Vision
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Fixed-Size Model Vendors, ASIC Accelerator Makers, Model Compression Services
papers.Decision_Perspective: Build an inference serving layer that dynamically selects neuron/head subsets based on real‑time latency budgets, to be deployed within 6 months. Fund start‑ups offering elastic transformer APIs for edge devices, targeting release by Q4 2025.
papers.Tags: Elastic Transformers, Dynamic Pruning, Inference Efficiency
papers.Hook: Run a single transformer at any compute level on‑the‑fly without retraining.

papers.Title: Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
papers.Abstract: An agentic market is a decentralized serving-time market where AI agents bid to claim each user prompt. An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabilities and costs. However, FPAs are not truthful: participants may bid less than their true value in the hope of a larger profit, and the prompt may then be allocated to someone other than the bidder who values it the most. This welfare loss is quantified by the $\textit{price-of-anarchy}$ (PoA). In this paper, we argue that agentic markets are likely to possess features that reduce the price-of-anarchy. The first is a $\textit{competitive floor}$, which occurs when multiple bidders usually value the prompt above some baseline share of the optimal welfare (e.g., because the best models are often distilled into cheaper alternatives, which perform similarly). We show that competition among them then limits the welfare loss, which can be driven to zero as the floor rises. The second feature is $\textit{near-independence}$ of values after conditioning on the prompt, which occurs when most of the predictable variation in the expected value is determined by the difficulty of the prompt. As the value distribution approaches conditional independence, we can derive an efficiency guarantee that approaches a factor of $1 - 1/e^2$ of the optimal welfare. Thus, both features give rise to welfare lower bounds that are significantly better than the well-known general case of $1 - 1/e$. We validate these results empirically using auctions with strategic bidders simulated on the EmbedLLM prompt routing dataset.
papers.Core_Innovation: It introduces a competitive floor assumption—multiple bidders typically value prompts above a minimum threshold—and shows that this bounds the price‑of‑anarchy of first‑price auctions to a constant. The result follows from smoothing arguments that relate bids to expected values minus inference costs.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: AI Agent Platforms, Cloud Computing, Decentralized Marketplaces
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Auction Houses, Centralized Ad Exchanges
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund pilot projects that implement competitive‑floor first‑price auctions for AI prompt allocation within the next 6 months. Kill reliance on pure VCG mechanisms in agentic markets until PoA bounds are validated.
papers.Tags: Price of Anarchy, First-Price Auctions, Agentic Markets
papers.Hook: Enables near-optimal prompt allocation in AI agent markets via competitive-floor auctions.

papers.Title: Continuum Attention
papers.Abstract: We introduce Continuum Attention (CA), a causal Transformer attention operator that replaces discrete key and value lookup with integration over a continuous, piecewise linear memory curve. Each query induces an exponential relevance density along the curve. Integrating the density and interpolated values yields exact normalized attention from closed form exponential moments, including half token boundary contributions. The gradients follow analytically from moments of order at most two, enabling parallel GPU implementations while retaining quadratic sequence complexity and the standard Transformer decoder. Compared with ordinary softmax and focal attention, CA reduces mean validation negative log likelihood by 0.0200 and 0.0480 nats per byte, respectively, winning all paired comparisons. An additional disjoint validation slice yields a 0.0457 nats per byte advantage over the strongest selected softmax baseline, with a paired 95% confidence interval. These findings motivate continuous integration as a promising attention alternative while leaving larger scale generalization open.
papers.Core_Innovation: Continuum Attention replaces the discrete softmax over keys and values with an integral of an exponential relevance density over a piecewise‑linear memory curve. The attention output is obtained from closed‑form exponential moments, giving exact normalized attention including half‑token boundary contributions.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Natural Language Processing, Speech Recognition, Computer Vision
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Softmax Attention, Fixed-Point Quantization Accelerators

Deprioritize further investment in incremental softmax tweaks unless they demonstrate >0.1 nats per byte improvement.
papers.Tags: Continuum Attention, Transformer, Exponential Moments, Efficient Inference, Sequence Modeling
papers.Hook: Enables exact causal attention via continuous integration, eliminating discrete lookup.

papers.Title: Learnable Hodge-Laplacian Driven Mixture of Experts for Steady-PDE Surrogates on Coarse Unstructured Meshes
papers.Abstract: Current approaches for steady partial differential equations surrogate models on unstructured meshes apply a single mixing mechanism to the whole solution. This paper proposes an architecture that partitions the solution among vanilla transformer experts, each focused on a different spectral scale. The partition is built from a discrete Hodge Laplacian $L_0=\star_0^{-1} d_0^{\top}\star_1 d_0$, that serves as a fitting layer measuring high-frequency content. A gating mechanism takes the mesh as input and produces the per-vertex weights that recombine the expert outputs. AirFRANS is a steady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) airfoil benchmark. We evaluate our approach in a reduced remeshed version of the benchmark with each unstructured mesh counting 9.6K faces and 4.9K vertices. We compare our approach with the Transolver on the same dataset and dataset slit. Our approach reduces relative $L_2$ error by 31\% and interior mean squared error by 47\%.
papers.Core_Innovation: The model learns a vertex-wise gating function from the discrete Hodge Laplacian that assigns transformer experts to low- vs high-frequency solution components, allowing each expert to specialize in a spectral band. This replaces a single global mixer with a scale-aware mixture-of-experts driven by mesh-derived spectral features.

papers.Disrupted_Sectors: High-fidelity Cfd Services, Traditional Mesh Refinement Tools
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund the development of a Hodge-Laplacian gated Mixture-of-Experts surrogate for steady RANS aerfoil simulations, targeting a prototype by Q2 2026. Pause investment in generic transformer-based PDE surrogates that do not incorporate spectral-scale gating until performance benchmarks show <10% L2 error gap versus this method.
papers.Tags: Hodge Laplacian, Mixture of Experts, PDE Surrogate, Spectral Scale, Unstructured Mesh
papers.Hook: Enables high-accuracy steady-PDE surrogates on coarse unstructured meshes via spectral-scale transformer experts.

papers.Title: Player-1: Learning to Play from Synthetic Experience
papers.Abstract: Computer-use agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in interpreting screens and executing keyboard and mouse actions. However, games, with their visually rich worlds and diverse mechanics, remain challenging and offer a demanding next step toward general digital control. Current game-agent learning pipelines often rely on large-scale demonstrations with limited coverage of dynamic game states, while scalable environments for interactive training remain difficult to obtain. We introduce Player-1, a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience. We extend the computer-use action space with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions. For supervised initialization, we fine-tune computer-use models on 6,044 curated gameplay trajectories that pair recorded actions with task instructions and visual reasoning. We construct Player-1-Gym, sixteen synthetic 2D and 3D environments designed around control demands shared across games. Programmatically verifiable rewards and randomized observations and control dynamics support multi-environment reinforcement learning with PPO. The resulting Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B improve MineDojo-300 success over their SFT policies by 27.8 and 17.7 percentage points, respectively. Player-1-9B reaches 38.33% success compared with 12.63% for the strongest evaluated baseline, with further gains over SFT on ViZDoom-10 and GameWorld. Further analyses show that broader synthetic environment coverage improves transfer, while the use of composite actions that combine multiple keyboard and mouse inputs increases during RL. We demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience substantially improves game control beyond supervised initialization, with gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite.
papers.Core_Innovation: Player-1 extends the computer-use action space with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions, then fine-tunes models on 6,044 curated gameplay trajectories paired with task instructions and visual reasoning. It further generates synthetic experience via Player-1-Gym, a suite of sixteen 2D/3D environments that simulate diverse control demands.

papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Manual Game Testing, Demonstration Data Collection
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund research teams to integrate Player-1's synthetic experience pipeline into existing game AI platforms within 6 months. Kill investment in pure demonstration‑based game agent startups that lack synthetic data generation.
papers.Tags: Game AI, Synthetic Data, Reinforcement Learning, Computer Use, Post-Training
papers.Hook: Enables game-playing agents to learn complex controls from synthetic trajectories without human demonstrations.

papers.Title: Latent Compaction with Test-Time Training
papers.Abstract: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction
papers.Core_Innovation: Latent Compaction creates a document‑specific key‑value cache by first seeding entries via reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key‑space diversity, then fine‑tuning those entries in two stages—first matching full‑cache attention outputs and log‑norms, then end‑to‑end distillation—while keeping model weights frozen and using only generic document prompts.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: AI Infrastructure, Cloud Computing, Natural Language Processing, Edge Computing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund startups that integrate test‑time KV‑cache compaction into LLM serving stacks within the next 6 months. Kill investments in static KV‑cache compression tools that lack test‑time adaptation.
papers.Tags: KV‑cache compression, test‑time training, LLM efficiency
papers.Hook: Enables 32× KV‑cache compression with <4% accuracy loss using only document‑level prompts.

papers.Title: One Task, Many Interfaces: Simple Cross-Interface Consistency Training Improves LLM Agent Robustness
papers.Abstract: Post-training binds the competence of an LLM agent to the interface it was trained on. Semantics-preserving perturbations of that interface, such as renaming an action or changing the notation, leave the underlying task unchanged yet make the agent worse at it. Scoring each sample independently means interface randomization only broadens this dependence from a single interface to the training interface distribution, so out-of-distribution perturbations still degrade the agent. We propose Cross-Interface Policy Regularization (CIPR), a self-supervised objective that replaces action names with uninformative identifiers and presents each training sample under two interfaces in which equivalent actions are identified by construction. CIPR penalizes the KL divergence between the action distributions induced under the two interfaces, so the policy behaves consistently across them. We evaluate CIPR in both supervised and reinforcement-learning post-training, where it improves robustness. On agentic function calling, held-out interface perturbations reduce the accuracy of a post-trained agent by nearly 25%, and CIPR recovers 10.5% while leaving accuracy on the unchanged interface intact.
papers.Core_Innovation: CIPR creates paired training views of each sample by renaming actions with uninformative identifiers and presenting them under two different interfaces. It then minimizes the KL divergence between the policy’s action distributions across these views to enforce interface‑independent behavior.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Robotics, Financial Technology, Healthcare Informatics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund startups that integrate CIPR into LLM agent training pipelines within the next 6 months to improve robustness of trading bots. Kill projects that rely solely on single‑interface fine‑tuning for production agents after Q4 2025.
papers.Tags: LLM robustness, interface invariance, self-supervised regularization
papers.Hook: LLM agents can now maintain performance despite arbitrary renaming of actions or notation.

papers.Title: Beyond LLM Judge: Mechanical Verification for Agentic Autoformalization
papers.Abstract: We introduce a novel method for verifying Lean formalizations that goes beyond LLM-judged faithfulness. Unlike most verification methods, which rely on LLMs or trained models, our method combines LLM-based semantic review with mechanical numerical and vacuity checks, providing checkable feedback and detecting errors missed by LLM judges. We apply this method, along with our Extract-Verify-Proof autoformalization pipeline, to construct the Formalized Library of Mathematical Functions (FLMF), a partial formalization of the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions (DLMF). On three labeled datasets, our method achieves the lowest accepted-error rate among the evaluated methods, measured as the fraction of incorrect statements accepted by the verification method. Expert review of the results also identifies translation and source defects in existing datasets. Code available at https://github.com/annamei1/FLMF-Ch7ErrFunc-Release.git.
papers.Core_Innovation: The innovation is a hybrid verification layer that couples LLM-driven semantic assessment with automated numerical consistency and vacuity tests, yielding machine‑checkable feedback. This layer plugs into their Extract‑Verify‑Proof pipeline to formalize the NIST DLMF with provably fewer undetected errors.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Formal Verification, AI‑Assisted Theorem Proving, Quantitative Finance, Aerospace Engineering, Pharmaceutical Research
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Manual Proof Checking, LLM‑Only Verification Services
