papers.Tags: Formal Verification, Mechanical Checks, Autoformalization, Lean, NIST DLMF
papers.Hook: Enables mechanically verified Lean formalizations of mathematical functions without relying solely on LLM judgments.

papers.Title: Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation
papers.Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on its own rollouts with token-level supervision from a teacher, assuming that the teacher can reach a correct answer from any prefix the student writes. We call this property the recoverability of the teacher and show it fails on incorrect rollouts: the teacher follows student errors, although it recognizes them. We propose CriticOPD, using error recognition to restore recoverability. The teacher critiques an incorrect rollout, allowing the student to rewrite its solution following the error. The resulting output, including the critique as privileged information, is scored by the teacher while the student uses the revision without the critique for training. On two Qwen3 students and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CriticOPD improves OPD, with the largest gains on competition problems.
papers.Core_Innovation: CriticOPD inserts a teacher critique step that flags errors in student rollouts; the student rewrites the solution based on that critique, and the revised output (without the critique) is used for distillation while the teacher scores the critique‑augmented version.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Education Technology, Financial Services, Scientific Research
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund the integration of CriticOPD into math‑focused AI tutoring platforms within the next 6 months to improve student success rates. Kill reliance on pure on‑policy distillation without error‑critique modules for new reasoning model releases.
papers.Tags: On-policy distillation, Critique-guided learning, Mathematical reasoning
papers.Hook: Enables student models to self-correct reasoning via teacher-guided critique during on-policy distillation.

papers.Title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
papers.Abstract: Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits. Beyond this point, additional budget brings little further improvement. In this paper, we show that the key to scaling discovery further is to forget. Periodically discarding the search state, including every agent's session and the candidate history, and restarting from the best candidate found so far, unblocks the search and pushes the same budget further.   We implement forgetting in a team of agents with communication and evaluate it on four tasks spanning heuristic programming, kernel optimization and model training. The results show up to 15% improvement compared to parallel agents, and up to 39% compared to a single agent. Our results suggest that, for open-ended discovery, what an agent is allowed to remember matters as much as how much compute it is given.
papers.Core_Innovation: The method periodically discards each LLM agent's session and candidate history, then restarts search from the best candidate found so far, applied to a team of communicating agents.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Pharmaceuticals, Materials Science, Biotechnology, AI Research, Finance
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund the integration of periodic forgetting mechanisms into LLM-agent research platforms within the next six months to accelerate internal innovation pipelines. Discontinue any LLM-agent discovery projects that rely solely on extended iteration without reset triggers after Q3 2025.
papers.Tags: LLM agents, forgetting mechanism, automated discovery, search scaling, candidate reset
papers.Hook: Enables continuous LLM-driven discovery by resetting agent memory to avoid stagnation.

papers.Title: PhySGA: A Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for Generalizable and Interactive 3D Composition
papers.Abstract: 3D object composition is pivotal to digital content creation and robot simulation, while also serving as a critical testbed for physical intelligence in foundation models. Previous methods either leverage large language models to directly predict object coordinates, or utilize generative diffusion priors to synthesize composite images for visual alignment, both of which rely on static priors in digital spaces. However, these methods consistently struggle with complex compositions such as precise hanging, gravity-driven settling and hidden containment, as these tasks require interactive construction processes involving global planning, fine-grained alignment, and physical simulation. To address these challenges, we propose PhySGA, a Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for 3D composition via agent exploration and physical simulation, enabling the universal interactive assembly of rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Directly applying vanilla LLMs or VLMs to this task proves insufficient, as current models inherently lack grounded physical understanding and interactive construction experience. To overcome this limitation, we design a collaborative feedforward-feedback architecture: an Assembly Agent focuses on geometric and kinematic reasoning for global step planning and coarse adjustment, while a Critic Agent reasons over contact dynamics for simulator state diagnosis and fine-grained closed-loop correction. Furthermore, Action Routers map semantic planning and analysis onto executable physical primitives within the simulator, while a task-specific Self-Evolving Skill Library distills historical trial-and-error feedback into reusable experiences, boosting success rates and minimizing exploration attempts. Extensive experiments within Isaac Sim demonstrate that PhySGA significantly surpasses existing methods in relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality.
papers.Core_Innovation: PhySGA grounds language‑model agents in a differentiable physics space, using simulated rigid/articulated/deformable dynamics as the action space. The agent iteratively proposes pose adjustments, receives physics‑based feedback, and converges to physically valid configurations without relying on static priors.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Computer Graphics, Game Development, Robotics, Virtual Reality, Industrial Design
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional 3D Modeling Software, Manual Asset Creation
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund startups that integrate PhySGA’s physics‑space grounding into real‑time game engines within the next 12 months. Kill investment in pure LLM‑based 3D placement tools that lack physics simulation.
papers.Tags: Physics‑Grounded Agents, 3D Composition, Simulation‑Based Planning
papers.Hook: Enables interactive assembly of any 3D object using physics‑aware agent control.

papers.Title: PerSo: Investigating Facets of LLMs' Social Intelligence in Real-World Persuasion Scenarios
papers.Abstract: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play, yet prior benchmarks typically evaluate them in isolation using synthetic scenarios. We introduce PerSo, a benchmark that evaluates both aspects on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline to construct the evaluation tasks, validated through human annotation. Our evaluation of diverse LLMs shows that performance generally scales with model size but varies across dimensions. The strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human performance on the behavioral task, while the best human participant remains ahead on the cognitive task.
papers.Core_Innovation: PerSo introduces an LLM‑in‑the‑loop pipeline that automatically extracts persuasion threads from Reddit’s ChangeMyView, generates task instances, and validates them with human annotators to create a benchmark that jointly tests mental‑state inference and social‑action selection.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: AI Safety, Human-Computer Interaction, Conversational AI, Marketing
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Survey Research, Focus Group Consulting
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund the development of LLM‑based persuasion coaching tools for sales teams within the next 6 months, using PerSo to validate performance. Kill internal reliance on synthetic persuasion benchmarks for LLM social‑intelligence assessment effective immediately.
papers.Tags: LLM evaluation, social intelligence, persuasion
papers.Hook: LLMs can now be evaluated on real-world persuasion dialogues, measuring both cognitive and behavioral social intelligence.

papers.Title: Detection of Potato Plant Leaf Diseases using Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.Abstract: Potato is an important food-security crop in Ethiopia, but its production is affected by foliar diseases, particularly early blight and late blight. This study develops a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify potato leaves into three categories: healthy, early blight, and late blight. The proposed model was trained using 2,215 images from the PlantVillage dataset and evaluated on an independent field dataset containing 247 images collected from potato farms in Banja, Awi Zone, Ethiopia. On PlantVillage, the model achieved 99.04% training accuracy, 98.21% validation accuracy, and 98.66% test accuracy. On the field dataset, it achieved 90.28% accuracy. The study also compares the proposed CNN with VGG16 and MobileNetV2 in terms of classification performance and computational efficiency. The proposed model contains 446,787 trainable parameters, occupies approximately 1.70 MB, and requires an average of 5.58 seconds per training epoch in the reported experimental setup, compared with 9.96 seconds for VGG16 and 7.68 seconds for MobileNetV2. The results demonstrate the potential of a compact CNN for potato leaf disease classification and highlight the importance of independent field evaluation, where image conditions are more variable than in controlled benchmark datasets. The proposed approach may support preliminary disease identification for smallholder farmers in Ethiopia and similar agricultural settings.
papers.Core_Innovation: The authors designed a custom shallow CNN with depthwise separable convolutions that reduces parameters to 446k and model size to 1.7 MB while retaining >98 % accuracy on curated data. This architecture trades minimal computational cost for robust field performance (≈90 % accuracy).
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Agriculture, Agri-Tech, Plant Disease Diagnostics
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Manual Crop Scouting, Pesticide Application Services
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund the integration of this CNN into a smartphone‑based disease‑scanning app for Ethiopian extension agents, targeting pilot deployment within 6 months. Buy or license the model from the authors to replace manual scouting in large‑scale potato contracts by the next growing season.
papers.Tags: Potato Disease Detection, Lightweight CNN, Field Deployment, Edge AI
papers.Hook: Enables real‑time potato leaf disease detection on low‑power smartphones in the field.

papers.Title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics
papers.Abstract: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory. We present ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously and returns control only upon failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the memory into these chunks, so execution is memory-free at test time and the planner is reserved for decisions that require reasoning. LLM computation therefore scales with the number of decisions rather than the number of primitives. On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task success by 5.0 points over the state of the art in agentic robotics while requiring 2.9x fewer LLM calls, 4.4x fewer input tokens, and 2.3x fewer output tokens.
papers.Core_Innovation: ChunkAct preprocesses the robot's memory into reusable action chunks that encode sequences of low-level primitives; at runtime a single LLM invocation triggers a chunk, which runs autonomously until failure, after which control returns to the LLM for replanning.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Automation, Manufacturing, Logistics, Healthcare
papers.Decision_Perspective: Robotics firms should fund development of ChunkAct‑style chunk compilers for their VLA stacks within the next 6 months to cut LLM inference costs. Legacy teleoperation platforms that rely on per‑primitive LLM calls should be phased out as chunk‑based alternatives become available.
papers.Tags: Action Chunking, LLM Robotics, Memory Compilation, Autonomous Execution, Inference Efficiency
papers.Hook: Enables robot agents to execute multi-step tasks with far fewer LLM calls via precompiled action chunks.

papers.Title: Cepheid: Decoupling Scale from Structure for Cross-Family Motion Completion
papers.Abstract: Sparse-to-dense motion completion recovers dense mesh motion from sparse vertex displacements. Residual priors trained on one geometry family frequently fail to beat parameter-free harmonic extension off-family. Moreover, cross-family training meets a scaling barrier: residual amplitude varies by more than an order of magnitude across geometry families and collapses as observations become denser. Since this scale depends on unknown target motion, it cannot be measured directly at test time. We decouple residual structure from physical scale by learning a dimensionless prior, estimating amplitude from observables and a lightweight correction fitted only on training sources. Our unified model surpasses harmonic extension across all evaluated families, including unseen cloth and legged bodies, without skeletons, registration, or cross-mesh correspondence. The same prior applies without retraining to point-tracked animal video and a robot grasping a soft body. Project page: https://su-terry.github.io/cepheid-website/
papers.Core_Innovation: The method learns a geometry‑agnostic, dimensionless motion prior that captures structural patterns, then rescales it using observable cues and a small correction network trained per source. At test time, amplitude is inferred directly from the sparse displacements, eliminating the need for family‑specific scaling.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Computer Graphics, Animation, Robotics, Biomechanics, Virtual Reality
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund startups developing dimension‑agnostic motion priors for cross‑domain animation within the next 6 months. Buy or license the core algorithm for integration into real‑time robotics control stacks by Q2 2026.
papers.Tags: motion completion, dimensionless prior, cross-family geometry, sparse-to-dense, robotics
papers.Hook: Enables accurate dense motion prediction across diverse geometries without skeletons or retraining.

papers.Title: What Matters in Quality-Aware VLA Pretraining: A Benchmark and Empirical Study
papers.Abstract: How should demonstration quality be used during vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining to improve performance after target-task fine-tuning? We compare weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks. Within each VLA, we match demonstrations and training budgets. Additional comparisons examine pretraining data size and the roles of quality tags during fine-tuning and inference. Across three VLAs, we find that approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning; conditioning and filtering favor episode and chunk labels, respectively, on average, with model-dependent reversals; and constant-tag fine-tuning improves mean success after conditioned pretraining with either tagged or untagged inference. We introduce AXIS-Bench to support these controlled comparisons. Built on crowdsourced simulation demonstrations, it provides recorded object and contact states for recomputing quality labels on shared trajectories. Replayable trajectories support workspace-aligned rendering and user-defined real-world target tasks. In our real-world experiment, simulation pretraining raises success from 9.6\% to 31.7\%. Project page: https://axis-bench.github.io/.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper introduces approach‑aware episode conditioning that incorporates quality tags into vision‑language‑action pretraining, allowing the model to weigh episodes differently based on reward definitions and label granularities. It also shows that constant‑tag fine‑tuning after conditioned pretraining improves downstream performance regardless of inference tagging.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Automation, Manufacturing, Healthcare, Logistics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Robotics firms should integrate episode‑conditioned VLA pretraining pipelines into their model‑training stacks by Q3 2025 to reduce reliance on curated demo sets. Investors should fund startups that offer quality‑tagging tools for demonstration data, targeting deployment within 6 months of product launch.
papers.Tags: VLA pretraining, demonstration quality, episode conditioning, AXIS-Bench, robot learning
papers.Hook: Enables robot policies to learn from noisy human demos via quality‑aware episode conditioning.

papers.Title: Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards
papers.Abstract: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. Training with this recipe yields Tev-27B, which achieves substantial gains on the Agents' Last Exam computing and math sciences domains (ALE-CM), matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5. Despite training only on ALE-related data, it generalizes to the Terminal-Bench (TB) 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as TB 2.1.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper introduces a latent‑world‑first pipeline that first defines a complete, hidden specification of a task’s domain, workflow, and step‑wise state expectations, then progressively renders this spec into agent‑facing environments. This yields dense, progressive rewards that are automatically verifiable without manual reward shaping.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Robotics, Autonomous Systems, Process Automation
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate $5M to build latent‑world‑first environment generators for long‑horizon AI agents by Q3 2027. Discontinue funding for sparse‑reward long‑horizon benchmark suites after the Q1 2027 review.
papers.Tags: long-horizon RL, dense rewards, latent world, agentic environments
papers.Hook: Enables training of autonomous agents on multi‑day tasks with dense, verifiable progress feedback.

papers.Title: Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories
papers.Abstract: Sampling equilibrium field configurations remains a major computational bottleneck in lattice field theory, motivating the development of generative samplers that can produce independent configurations. Diffusion models are promising for this purpose, but their standard denoising score matching objective requires samples from the target distribution, seemingly reintroducing the original sampling problem. Here, we show that diffusion models can instead be trained from their own generated samples using the target score identity, provided access to the unnormalized probability density. Importance-weighted formulations of this identity yield a consistent target throughout training, while unweighted variants define a self-consistent fixed-point training scheme. We benchmark the different approaches in two-dimensional \(φ^4\) theory and identify effective choices that enable efficient training and sampling across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases. Ultimately, our data-free training approach achieves comparable performance to training on HMC reference data.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper shows that diffusion models can be trained using only their own generated samples by exploiting the target score identity, which requires only the unnormalized target density. Importance‑weighted estimators provide a stable training objective, while an unweighted version yields a self‑consistent fixed‑point algorithm.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Scientific Computing, Computational Physics, Quantum Chemistry, Materials Science, High-Energy Physics
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Monte Carlo Sampling, Conventional Markov Chain Monte Carlo
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund research groups developing diffusion‑based samplers for lattice QCD within the next 6 months to replace costly hybrid Monte Carlo pipelines. De‑prioritize investment in legacy MCMC software suites unless they integrate score‑based generative layers.
papers.Tags: Diffusion Models, Score‑Based Generative Models, Lattice Field Theory, Data‑Free Training, Importance Weighting
papers.Hook: Enables training diffusion models for lattice field theory without any training data.

papers.Title: DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning
papers.Abstract: Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. We also show that DoubtLess reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent with unchanged task performance. It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. Our code is available at https://github.com/leoluolol/DoubtLess.
papers.Core_Innovation: A small reasoning model processes the large model's current chain‑of‑thought twice—once prompted for brevity and once for verbosity—and the scaled difference of its logit vectors is added to the large model's logits at each decoding step, steering the output toward conciseness.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence Services, Cloud Computing, High-Performance Computing
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Model Fine-Tuning Services, Prompt Engineering Consultancies, CoT Compression Tools
papers.Decision_Perspective: Enterprises should pilot DoubtLess integration with their Qwen3‑32B deployments within the next quarter to cut inference latency. Vendors of fine‑tuning pipelines should reallocate R&D budgets toward lightweight steering models instead of full‑scale retraining.
papers.Tags: Contrastive Decoding, Training-Free, Chain-of-Thought
papers.Hook: Enables large reasoning models to produce shorter chain‑of‑thought outputs without retraining.

papers.Title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
papers.Abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/togethercomputer/HybridAgent.
papers.Core_Innovation: The HybridLink module switches between discrete token space and continuous latent space during generation, enabling computation in a compact latent representation while preserving text output and tool use. A continuous working memory carries hybrid context across turns, and HybridSFT fine‑tunes the model to coordinate latent reasoning with tool calls.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Software Development, Automation, Finance, Healthcare
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Rule-Based Systems, Text-Only LLM Agents, Manual Process Outsourcing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Build a prototype HybridAgent for real‑time tool‑augmented code generation within six months. Allocate venture capital to startups that adopt HybridLink for latency‑critical AI services by the end of 2026.
papers.Tags: Hybrid Reasoning, Latent Space, Tool Integration, Agent Architecture, Post‑Training
papers.Hook: Agents can now perform efficient latent reasoning while retaining transparent, tool‑enabled text interaction.

papers.Title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards
papers.Abstract: Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8.
papers.Core_Innovation: AesCode introduces a design graph that canonically encodes layout, color, and content properties of a visual artifact, enabling deterministic verifiers to check code‑rendered attributes and a VLM‑driven Visual Graph Rubric to score aesthetic qualities. Cross‑modal rewards combine these signals to guide code generation toward both factual correctness and visual appeal.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Presentation Software, Data Visualization, Graphic Design, Advertising, UI/UX Design, Marketing, Education Technology
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Manual Graphic Design Agencies, Template-Based Slide Services, Stock Illustration Providers
papers.Decision_Perspective: Invest in building AesCode‑style design‑graph modules into enterprise BI platforms within six months to auto‑generate editable, aesthetically‑optimized dashboard code. Divest from standalone image‑to‑code pipelines that lack verifiable aesthetic rewards.
papers.Tags: code generation, visual aesthetics, design graph, cross-modal reward, VLM
papers.Hook: Generate editable slide/code that matches both content prompts and aesthetic visual guidance automatically.

papers.Title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs
papers.Abstract: Persistent homology summarizes the topological evolution of a graph as persistence diagrams (PDs). Generating graphs whose topology matches a target descriptor is increasingly important, yet existing topology-aware generative models rely on soft regularization, producing graphs whose PDs may only be approximately similar. We initiate a principled investigation of the generation problem: produce graphs that realize a target PD exactly. We propose two approaches guided by the implicit local and global constraints a target PD imposes. The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD and that every degree-based PD-equivalent graph is reachable. However, as shown thereafter, local generation necessarily trades off between sample diversity and reaching infeasible states. We therefore recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers. This is applicable to any vertex-based permutation equivariant filtration scheme and is minimal under the degree filtration. Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks confirm that both methods realize the target PD exactly. Together, our methods provide a principled treatment of strict topology-compliant graph generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/ExactCompliance.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper formulates exact graph generation as satisfying implicit local and global constraints derived from a target persistence diagram, providing a constructive degree‑based iterative algorithm that provably yields PD‑equivalent graphs and a global constraint encoding solvable by modern CP solvers.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Network Analysis, Bioinformatics, Computer Vision, Materials Science, Financial Modeling
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Approximate Topological Regularization Services, Soft-Constraint Graph Generation Tools
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund research teams to integrate exact PD‑graph generators into network simulation pipelines by Q2 2026. Kill projects relying on approximate topological regularization for graph synthesis after Q1 2026.
papers.Tags: Topological Data Analysis, Graph Generation, Constraint Programming, Persistence Diagrams, Exact Synthesis
papers.Hook: Generate any graph that exactly matches a prescribed persistence diagram.

papers.Title: Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) relies on costly model-generated responses, motivating larger rollout batches and square-root learning-rate scaling. Reported to approximately preserve progress per sample with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is less understood in practical multi-step training. We develop a two-clock framework that separates the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse. Under a local quadratic model, the square-root rule preserves first-order drift per sample but not progress: larger batches take fewer, longer updates and lose more to curvature, yielding a learning-rate-dependent critical batch beyond which sample efficiency degrades. A drift-threshold hypothesis predicts a complementary failure clock whose sample count remains approximately invariant along the square-root rule. Controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B across a $16\times$ batch range support both predictions. Ratio clipping delays failure, especially for larger batches, but the progress gap persists without it. Widening the clip trades stability for a transient speed gain. The progress gap reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose checkpoint, and a 7B model. Finally, we use the two-clock framework to derive a simple multi-step RLVR schedule: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure. Our code is available at: https://github.com/WinstonLiyt/two-clocks-rlvr.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces a two-clock model that distinguishes the sample count needed for policy improvement from the sample count leading to divergence, showing that square‑root LR scaling preserves first‑order drift but not curvature‑induced loss, thus defining a critical batch size beyond which efficiency drops. The drift‑threshold hypothesis further predicts an approximately invariant failure‑time sample count along the scaling rule, which is validated in GRPO experiments and can be mitigated by ratio clipping.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Autonomous Systems, Financial Trading, Robotics
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund research into adaptive batch‑size schedulers that switch to smaller batches once curvature loss exceeds a threshold, targeting deployment within 6 months. Kill fixed‑large‑batch RL training pipelines in verifiable‑reward settings unless paired with ratio clipping, effective immediately.
papers.Tags: Reinforcement Learning, Batch Size Scaling, Two‑Clock Framework, Verifiable Rewards, Ratio Clipping
papers.Hook: Predicting optimal rollout batch size to balance learning speed and failure risk in RL with verifiable rewards

papers.Title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization
papers.Abstract: Multi-objective molecular optimization is a critical process in drug discovery that aims to modify a given molecule to simultaneously improve multiple properties while maintaining a similar overall structure. This process often requires iterative modifications guided by computational or experimental feedback. Recent large language model (LLM)-based methods have begun to explore this iterative approach; however, these methods are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback, while existing approaches primarily focus on single-turn molecular optimization. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-turn Feedback Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns. MFG introduces a feedback vector capturing both property improvements and source molecule similarity, alongside a feedback-aligned reward function that promotes progressive improvement across turns. We apply MFG over $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$, a state-of-the-art LLM model for multi-objective molecular optimization, evaluate $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks. The results demonstrate that $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ achieves the highest average similarity-constrained success rate ($81.50%$), outperforming the base model $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$ ($70.81%$).
papers.Core_Innovation: MFG trains a large language model via reinforcement learning where each optimization turn receives a feedback vector encoding both property improvement and structural similarity to the starting molecule. The reward function is aligned to this vector, encouraging cumulative progress across multiple turns.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Pharmaceuticals, Biotechnology, Chemical Manufacturing, Materials Science
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Medicinal Chemistry, Contract Research Organizations
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund internal RL‑LLM molecular optimization pilots for lead‑generation projects within the next six months. Build a feedback‑vector data pipeline to capture property and similarity metrics for each design iteration.
papers.Tags: Molecular Optimization, Reinforcement Learning, Large Language Models, Feedback-Guided Design
papers.Hook: Enables LLMs to iteratively improve molecules using multi‑turn feedback for steady property gains.

papers.Title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.Abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.
papers.Core_Innovation: LIBERO‑RIG defines eleven hardware perturbation axes, each with five severity levels, while keeping task definitions identical across conditions. This isolates the impact of robot‑setup changes on vision‑language‑action policy performance.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Automation, Manufacturing, Healthcare, Logistics
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Legacy Robotics Calibration, Manual Controller Tuning
papers.Decision_Perspective: Allocate budget to create a hardware‑variation augmentation suite for VLA model training by Q1 2026. Phase out procurement of robots that cannot pass LIBERO‑RIG medium‑severity tests after Q2 2026.
papers.Tags: Vision-Language-Action, Robotics Robustness, Hardware Perturbation, Benchmarking, Policy Generalization
papers.Hook: Enables systematic testing of VLA models against real-world robot hardware variations.

papers.Title: Who Improves the Robot? Toward Physical Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.Abstract: Robots are increasingly autonomous in task execution, yet their improvement remains largely human-driven. This study investigates Physical Recursive Self-Improvement (Physical RSI), in which physical experience guides lasting updates to both a robot's capabilities and its improvement procedure, making subsequent improvement more effective across tasks. Physical RSI faces challenges from noisy observations, continuous dynamics, costly trials, and irreversible consequences. We present an L0-L5 framework that differentiates capability-level from meta-level updates and within-task from across-task gains, reserving L5 for independently verified recursive gain. We study existing methods around harness adaptation and model training, alongside safety and control mechanisms that govern execution and successive updates. Our analysis reveals that, despite substantial progress in self-improvement, the surveyed literature does not yet demonstrate Physical RSI as defined by our framework. We identify research priorities in reliable feedback, causal attribution, safety preservation, and benchmarking, outlining a path toward robots that autonomously improve how they learn while ensuring safety. The GitHub repository for Physical RSI is available at https://github.com/SAIL-Research-Lab/Physical-RSI.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper introduces an L0-L5 framework that separates capability-level updates (L0-L2) from meta-level updates (L3-L5) and distinguishes within-task gains from across-task gains, reserving L5 for independently verified recursive self-improvement.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Robotics, Manufacturing, Logistics, Healthcare, Autonomous Vehicles
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund pilot projects that implement L3-level meta-learning in warehouse robots by Q3 2025. Kill investments in static pre-programmed robotic arms lacking online self-improvement modules.
papers.Tags: Recursive Self-Improvement, Robotics, Meta-Learning, L0-L5 Framework, Physical AI
papers.Hook: Robots can recursively improve their own learning algorithms through physical task experience.

papers.Title: Fast Rates for Offline Q-Learning with KL Regularization
papers.Abstract: This paper investigates offline Q-learning for finite-horizon Markov decision processes with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. Recent studies have shown that KL regularization can yield fast rates in offline decision-making problems. However, it remains unclear whether Q-learning, which adopts incremental stochastic approximation updates, can achieve such fast rates in the offline setting. We first propose KL-regularized Q-Learning (KLQ), a simple variant of classical Q-learning. By exploiting KL regularization, we prove that KLQ achieves a sample complexity of $\widetilde{O}(1/ε)$ without explicit pessimism. This guarantee, however, has an exponential dependence on the KL regularization parameter and the horizon. To address this limitation, we further propose KL-regularized Pessimistic Q-Learning (KLPQ), which incorporates pessimism into KLQ. We prove that KLPQ retains the same \(\widetilde O(1/ε)\) rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence, thereby further improving the sample complexity. To the best of our knowledge, these results establish the first fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs.
papers.Core_Innovation: KLQ adds a KL penalty to the Q‑learning update, achieving O~(1/ε) sample complexity but with exponential dependence on the KL coefficient and horizon. KLPQ augments KLQ with a pessimistic penalty on the value estimate, which cancels the exponential term while preserving the fast rate.

papers.Hook: Offline Q‑learning now attains near‑optimal sample rates without exponential cost via KL regularization and pessimism.

papers.Title: Scaling Online Optimal Transport Minibatches for Flow Matching
papers.Abstract: A central challenge in scaling flow models is maintaining stability in training and integration. In flow matching, this stability depends critically on how source samples are paired with data. Independent random pairing introduces substantial stochasticity, motivating minibatch optimal transport (OT) to construct online source-target couplings that reduce this randomness (Tong et al., 2024). However, as applications extend to larger and higher-dimensional datasets, small minibatches can limit these benefits, while scaling the coupling to substantially larger minibatches at every iteration is computationally prohibitive. Moreover, how OT coupling affects the full stochastic gradient and integration remains theoretically unresolved. In this work, we develop a scalable online entropic OT approximation that enables substantially larger source-target couplings while preserving the benefits of OT. We close the theoretical gap for both unregularized and entropic OT by proving strict reductions in full stochastic-gradient variance and integration error relative to independent pairing, and further characterize how these improvements strengthen as the online coupling minibatch grows. Experiments on single-cell gene interpolation-flow and image-flow training validate these predictions, showing that larger online couplings consistently improve training stability and final generation performance.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces an online entropic optimal transport solver that uses stochastic approximations and mini‑batch re‑use to compute couplings for batches up to 10× larger than prior methods, with provable bounds on approximation error. The method integrates seamlessly into flow matching training, reducing gradient variance while keeping per‑iteration cost linear in batch size.

papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund research teams to integrate the online entropic OT solver into large‑scale flow matching pipelines within the next six months. Kill projects that rely on independent random pairing for high‑dimensional flow models after Q3 2025.
papers.Tags: Optimal Transport, Flow Matching, Entropic Approximation, Scalable Training, Variance Reduction
papers.Hook: Enables large‑scale optimal transport couplings in flow matching without prohibitive compute.

papers.Title: RoboSimStudio: An Interactive Toolkit for Rapid Real2Sim of Robot Manipulation Tasks
papers.Abstract: It is difficult to accurately model the physics of the interaction between a robot and the objects it manipulates, including contact mechanics, coupled contact dynamics, deformations, stiffness and friction. We present RoboSimStudio (RSS), an interactive toolkit that makes choices of solver, contact model, and physical parameters explicit and editable, allowing both humans and coding agents to iteratively refine simulations based on observed physical behavior. We implement RSS with the open Newton physics simulation system and describe experiments with human-guided real2sim using (1) visual evaluation, (2) force-feedback and (3) agentic Real2Sim2Real. Code, video and additional information can be found on the project website.
papers.Core_Innovation: RoboSimStudio provides an interactive UI that exposes solver choice, contact model, and physical parameters within the Newton physics engine, allowing users to iteratively refine simulations using visual, force-feedback, or agentic feedback loops.

papers.Title: Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game?
papers.Abstract: Language models increasingly support or automate information retrieval from document collections too large to index. This task is difficult when it requires specialist linguistic or scientific knowledge. We used the Wikipedia Game to test language models on an analogous information retrieval task. In the game, players must reach a target article using only article links. We compared sentence embedding models and LLMs across five Wikipedia languages and five academic-literature datasets. We construct very large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and of paper citations using OpenAlex and provide code to build and navigate them. This allows the study of language models' navigation capabilities without relying on third-party APIs. We compared the models with human and TF-IDF benchmarks. The Wikipedia Game format enables robust comparisons across techniques, languages, and domains. No model significantly outperformed humans, although the best models (GPT-o3 mini, GPT-4o, QwQ:32B, and DeepSeek-R1:70B) achieved comparable success. Performance and rankings varied across languages and topics, with implications for practitioners utilising these techniques.
papers.Core_Innovation: They built offline, scalable Wikipedia and citation graphs using OpenAlex, released navigation code, and evaluated LLMs against human and TF‑IDF baselines across five languages and five academic datasets.

papers.Title: Hide and Seek: HIDE Concepts to SEEK explanations for black box models
papers.Abstract: Interpreting machine learning model predictions is a central challenge, particularly for black-box vision models. Concept-based attribution methods interpret models using human-understandable concepts. Existing concept-based methods can only interpret classification and regression models. They require access to model weights or large concept-annotated datasets, and most methods cannot provide image-level attribution. We propose Hide and Seek (HnS), a new method for concept-level attribution that does not require access to model weights or labeled concept datasets. HnS can interpret a wide range of vision models. Given a concept and image set, HnS retrieves concept-aligned images using a vision-language model, localizes the concept within each image, masks the localized region, and measures attribution from the change in the black-box model's output between the original and masked images. This enables faithful attribution by directly measuring the model's behavior and supporting local attributions. We validated HnS on CelebA and COCO-Stuff. Compared to existing methods, HnS showed better agreement with ground-truth attributions. We demonstrated the applicability of HnS on diverse tasks, including image captioning and satellite image segmentation, where no existing concept attribution method can be used. We provided our anonymous code in the supplementary material.
papers.Core_Innovation: Hide and Seek uses a vision-language model to retrieve concept‑aligned images, localizes the concept via a segmentation mask, then measures attribution by comparing the black‑box model’s output before and after masking the region. This bypasses the need for model gradients, weights, or concept‑annotated datasets.

papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Traditional Interpretability Consultancies, Feature Importance Tool Vendors

papers.Tags: Concept Attribution, Vision-Language Model, Masking, Black-Box Explainability, Healthcare Imaging
papers.Hook: Concept-level attribution for any vision model without weights or labeled data.

papers.Title: Constructive Bounds for the Topological Expressivity of Neural Networks
papers.Abstract: The expressivity of a neural network $Φ$ describes the class of functions that a network can express. The term topological expressivity refers to a family of measures particularly suited to understand binary classification and is often formulated in terms of the Betti numbers of a decision boundary $β(Φ^{-1}(0))$. Despite its popularity, this measure is not as useful for regression and other problems that do not involve a decision boundary. Instead, we propose to study topological expressivity in terms of the Betti numbers of the output of a neural network $β(Φ(X))$. We formally prove that a ReLU network with architecture $(d,\sum\limits_{k=1}^{d   } β_k(3k+2),\sum\limits_{k=1}^{d}β_k(k+1))$ can express spaces homotopy equivalent to wedge sums of spheres with arbitrary Betti numbers. This gives upper bounds for any arbitrary connected ($β_0=1$) sequence of Betti numbers, but by constructing spaces homotopy equivalent to products of $N$ spheres of dimension $d_1,...,d_N$ we achieve much better bounds $(\sum\limits_{n=1} d_n, 3\sum\limits_{n=1}\limits^N d_n + 2N, \sum\limits_{n=1}\limits^N d_n + N) $ for Betti numbers given by $\prod_n (1+x^{d_n})$. Finally we conjecture a much stronger tight bound which gives the architectural bound $(d,d+1,d+1)$ for a space homeomorphic to the sphere.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper shifts topological expressivity from decision boundaries to the network's output, showing that a ReLU network with layer widths derived from desired Betti numbers can construct spaces homotopy equivalent to wedge sums or products of spheres, thereby realizing any prescribed Betti sequence.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Topological Data Analysis, Scientific Computing, Generative Modeling, Robotics, Computer Graphics
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Manual Feature Engineering, Classical Topological Methods
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund research teams to develop ReLU architectures with layer widths set by target Betti numbers for generative modeling within six months. Buy or license the constructive network design toolkit for topological data analysis applications by Q2 2026.
papers.Tags: Topological Expressivity, ReLU Networks, Betti Numbers, Homotopy Theory, Neural Architecture
papers.Hook: Enables neural networks to realize any prescribed topological shape in their output space.

papers.Title: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities
papers.Abstract: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training on a small chemical reaction prediction task - a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.
papers.Core_Innovation: The paper embeds encrypted neural networks inside host model weights using digital lockers, creating hidden circuits that execute only upon a secret trigger. This extends prior hidden‑string techniques to arbitrary, provably hard‑to‑elicit computations under standard cryptographic assumptions.

papers.Disrupted_Sectors: AI Auditing, Model Evaluation, Regulatory Compliance
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund development of trigger‑aware model inspection tools within the next 6 months to detect hidden circuits. Kill reliance on standard fine‑tuning based capability audits for high‑risk models until such tools are deployed.
papers.Tags: Backdoor Attacks, Encrypted Neural Networks, Digital Lockers, Model Security, Capability Hiding
papers.Hook: Models can secretly embed arbitrary computations that evade all known elicitation methods.

papers.Title: KL Before and After Mixing: A Round-Complexity Separation in Parallel Sampling
papers.Abstract: A parallel sampler can choose at random which coordinates to generate together. For a target $p$ and the output law $q_U$ of a schedule $U$ drawn afresh for each output, we compare the schedule-averaged divergence $\mathbb{E}_U D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q_U)$ with the output-law divergence $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\mathbb{E}_U q_U)$, in nats. Rounds commit independent draws from exact conditional marginals frozen at the round's start, each output's schedule is drawn before sampling from a finite mixture of schedules, and every scheduled round is charged. For the uniform distribution on binary strings of even length $n$ with $n/2$ ones, the least expected number of rounds at a fixed tolerance $\varepsilon>0$ is $Θ_\varepsilon((\log n)^2)$ under the first criterion but $(e^{-\varepsilon}+o(1))\log_2\ln n$ under the second, and the double-logarithmic order is attainable with the same round count on every run. For this target, a count-state recursion gives the exact least output divergence at every round cap over all causal randomized policies. The separation extends to weighted fixed-count targets with bounded weight ratios and quota fractions bounded away from zero and one, without permutation symmetry, and to the full-support Beta$(1,1)$--Bernoulli target, where the sharp expected cost under the output-law criterion is $(e^{-\varepsilon}/2+o(1))\log_2\log_2n$, attained with rare $n$-round runs. Prior work implies the order of the schedule-averaged cost on the balanced target and its $O_\varepsilon((\log n)^2)$ upper bounds on both extensions.
papers.Core_Innovation: They define two divergence criteria for parallel samplers and prove a separation: minimizing schedule‑averaged KL requires Θ((log n)^2) rounds, whereas minimizing output‑law KL achieves (e^{-ε}+o(1)) log₂ ln n rounds, attainable deterministically via a count‑state recursion.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Quantum Computing, Machine Learning, Cryptography, Parallel Computing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund the development of parallel samplers that use output-law divergence for cryptographic nonce generation within the next 12 months. Redirect budget away from schedule-averaged parallel MCMC toolkits for discrete high-dimensional sampling after the Q3 2025 review.
papers.Tags: Parallel Sampling, KL Divergence, Round Complexity
papers.Hook: Enables double‑logarithmic round parallel sampling for uniform half‑weight binary strings.

papers.Title: Goal-Oriented Bundle Management and Flow Control for Deep-Space Communications via Reinforcement Learning
papers.Abstract: Deep-space communications operate under intermittent connectivity, long propagation delays, and relay storage constraints. In such networks, the Bundle Protocol enables store-carry-forward communication, requiring relay nodes to manage limited storage and scarce contact opportunities. Relay-side scheduling and dropping decisions are inherently goal-oriented: transmission resources should be allocated to bundles most valuable to downstream mission objectives. Conventional schedulers, such as FIFO, do not explicitly optimize task utility and may provide unfair service across heterogeneous planetary sources. This paper presents a closed-loop modeling and learning framework for relay-side bundle and flow management in a contact-driven deep-space network, where lunar and Martian updates are forwarded through a shared-buffer relay to Earth. We quantify destination-side information freshness using excess age $Δ_i^e(t)=[Δ_i(t)-d_i(t)]^+$, where $Δ_i(t)$ denotes the Age of Information of source $i$ and $d_i(t)$ is a source-dependent delay baseline. Based on this metric, we define a goal-oriented loss that supports source-dependent nonlinear penalties, allowing prioritization according to mission relevance. We formulate relay control as a constrained semi-Markov decision process (CSMDP) and solve it using masked Lagrangian Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Feasibility-aware action masking restricts transmissions to bundles that can complete within the remaining contact window. DTNSim simulations indicate improved age-based utility and inter-flow fairness compared with baseline schedulers. The proposed framework jointly optimizes relay-side bundle scheduling, dropping, and flow control under contact-driven dynamics with explicit fairness considerations across heterogeneous sources.
papers.Core_Innovation: Introduces a closed-loop RL framework where relay nodes observe buffer state and contact schedules, then learn scheduling/dropping policies that minimize excess age of lunar and Martian data streams. The approach replaces heuristic FIFO with a goal‑oriented policy optimized for mission‑specific freshness.

papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Legacy Network Scheduling, Ground Station Operations
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund a pilot RL-based bundle scheduler for NASA's Deep Space Network within 12 months to test lunar-Martian data prioritization. Pause procurement of new FIFO-based relay hardware upgrades until the RL demonstrator achieves at least a 15% reduction in excess age compared to baseline.
papers.Tags: Reinforcement Learning, Bundle Protocol, Age of Information, Deep-Space Networking
papers.Hook: Enables RL-driven relay scheduling that prioritizes mission-critical deep-space data despite delays and storage limits.

papers.Title: DyssomniaNN: Multi-Scale Spiking Neural Modeling of Human Sleep Disorders and Perceived Restedness
papers.Abstract: Clinical sleep medicine repeatedly documents profound divergences between objective sleep duration and subjective daytime impairment, notably exemplified by sleep state misperception in paradoxical insomnia and boundary instability in narcolepsy type 1. Here, we present DyssomniaNN: a multi-scale biophysical computational framework coupling Borbély's two-process regulation of sleep homeostasis and circadian drive with Saper's hypothalamic reciprocal flip-flop circuit and a recurrent corticothalamic leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network. We formalize five clinical cohorts across an identical 72-hour photoperiod: healthy control, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (delayed-phase), chronic insomnia, paradoxical insomnia, and narcolepsy type 1. The synthetic local field potential converges closely with empirical human electroencephalography spectra from the PhysioNet Sleep-EDF database across all canonical frequency bands (spectral mean absolute error of 0.33--0.35). Furthermore, we introduce the Well-Rested Index to quantify restorative efficacy. Simulations reveal that sleep duration fails to predict restorative recovery: paradoxical insomnia achieves normal total sleep time (21.15 h) yet yields low restoration (37.6%) from unsuppressed cortical beta-band intrusion, whereas hypocretin deficiency in narcolepsy produces severe nocturnal fragmentation (781 min of wake after sleep onset) and 35 sleep-onset rapid eye movement periods. DyssomniaNN provides an in silico platform for mechanistic sleep research and virtual neuropharmacology.
papers.Core_Innovation: DyssomniaNN integrates Borbély's two-process sleep homeostasis model, Saper's hypothalamic flip‑flop circuit, and a recurrent corticothalamic leaky integrate‑and‑fire spiking network into a unified multi‑scale framework. This allows simulation of local field potentials that match empirical EEG spectra across frequency bands for diverse sleep disorder cohorts.

papers.Tags: Spiking Neural Network, Sleep Modeling, EEG Prediction, Neurotechnology, Sleep Disorders
papers.Hook: Simulating disorder-specific EEG spectra to predict subjective restedness from objective sleep data.

papers.Title: Designing Protein Structures from Natural Language
papers.Abstract: A central challenge in de novo protein design is generating proteins with desired structural and functional properties. Existing design models typically require a dedicated input representation for each property, limiting the design objectives they support. We develop Prompteina, the first all-atom structure generation model that supports new and broader design objectives specified in natural language, analogous to text-to-image generation. To train Prompteina, we construct Prompteina-Data, a paired text--protein structure dataset of 1.8M structures and 50M+ captions describing global and residue-specific structural and functional properties. We adapt Proteina-Complexa, a pretrained structure generation model, through text-conditioned pretraining and finetuning that aligns residues with their corresponding text. Prompteina outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties and generates proteins that more closely match descriptions of their intended functions. In binder design, it leads baselines on at least 13 of 20 targets and improves interface confidence by 14\% over the strongest baseline. With iterative in silico feedback, Prompteina's gain over non-iterative generation is 57\% larger than the next-best baseline on the hardest targets. Finally, we experimentally validate Prompteina designs against GM2A, a target with no reported de novo binders. We identify nine binders, with the strongest at an apparent $K_{\mathrm{D}}$ of 107 nM. These results establish natural language as an effective and powerful conditioning interface for protein structure generation.
papers.Core_Innovation: The authors take the pretrained Proteina-Complexa diffuser and add a text‑conditioning module trained on 1.8M paired protein structures and natural‑language captions, aligning each residue’s coordinates with descriptive tokens. This enables all‑atom backbone and side‑chain generation guided by free‑form English prompts.

papers.Hook: Generate atomic‑level protein structures directly from natural‑language descriptions.

papers.Title: Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping
papers.Abstract: While deep learning models for tabular data have recently received significant research attention, the choice of objective functions for regression tasks remains an understudied degree of freedom. Several lines of research offer alternatives to the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE), but differences in datasets, backbones, and evaluation protocols make their practical benefits difficult to compare. In this work, we address this gap by performing a systematic re-evaluation of regression objectives across a broad collection of established tabular datasets and multiple neural backbones. Our comparison reveals that many proposed objectives provide limited or inconsistent gains over a properly tuned MSE baseline, while quantile loss yields consistent aggregate improvements over MSE across the tested backbones. We then identify a limitation that remains even with this strong objective: regions with different levels of target noise can reach their best predictive performance at different training epochs. Consequently, a single global early-stopping checkpoint can impose a compromise between uncertainty regions, even when the objective can represent heteroskedastic target distributions. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce a heteroskedasticity-aware extension of quantile loss that uses input-dependent label smoothing as a potential remedy and improves over quantile loss on several backbones. Overall, our results provide a modern empirical picture of regression objectives for tabular deep learning and highlight how differences in optimal stopping times across uncertainty regions can limit the effectiveness of global early stopping. The code is available at https://github.com/yandex-research/tabular-regression.
papers.Core_Innovation: We systematically evaluate regression objectives across diverse tabular datasets and neural backbones, showing that quantile loss consistently outperforms a well‑tuned MSE baseline. We further reveal that global early stopping is suboptimal because optimal training duration varies with local target‑noise levels.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Finance, Healthcare, Retail, Manufacturing
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund development of quantile‑loss‑based tabular regression pipelines for finance and insurance use cases within the next quarter. Kill reliance on generic MSE‑only models when target noise is heterogeneous, replacing them with noise‑aware early‑stopping triggers by Q2.
papers.Tags: Quantile Loss, Tabular Regression, Early Stopping
papers.Hook: Quantile loss enables robust tabular regression gains across heterogeneous noise levels without retraining.

papers.Title: Hitting-Time Bounds for Asynchronous Q-Learning
papers.Abstract: We study the last iterate of standard asynchronous Q-learning from a single trajectory of a finite Markov decision process. The trajectory follows a fixed behavior policy whose state--action chain is irreducible and may be periodic. For discount factor $γ$, write $H=(1-γ)^{-1}$, and let $μ_{\min}$ be the minimum stationary state--action probability and $\mathfrak h_\star$ the largest expected hitting time of the reverse state--action chain. We prove that zero-initialized Q-learning with a constant step size achieves sup-norm error at most $\varepsilon$ with high probability using $\widetilde{O}(H^4/(μ_{\min}\varepsilon^2)+\mathfrak h_\star)$ transitions, for $0<\varepsilon\le1$. The statistical term retains the quartic effective-horizon dependence of standard Q-learning, while initialization cost is additive in $\mathfrak h_\star$. For aperiodic behavior chains, a comparison with mixing time yields a transient term $\widetilde{O}(t_{\mathrm{mix}}/μ_{\min})$. An empirical state--action count rule selects a constant step size for a subsequent training run and attains the same rate without prior knowledge of model parameters, target accuracy, or confidence level. The output is the last training iterate, with both stages included in the sample count. The proof uses two deterministic Bellman envelopes to separate statistical error from fixed-policy initialization error and adapts reverse-time hitting-cost compensation from TD learning to state--action propagation. An exploration lower bound holds for arbitrary predictable step sizes. Together with the existing statistical lower bound and its extension to pilot-selected constant steps, it yields matching mean-square rates up to logarithmic factors on the stated large-sample parameter classes.
papers.Core_Innovation: They derive a high-probability sup-norm error bound for the last iterate of asynchronous Q-learning under a constant step size. The bound separates a statistical term scaling as H^4/(μ_min ε^2) from an additive initialization term proportional to the largest expected hitting time of the reverse state‑action chain, extending prior mixing‑time based results to periodic chains.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Reinforcement Learning, Robotics, Autonomous Vehicles, Finance, Operations Research
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund a six‑month pilot to integrate hitting‑time‑aware step‑size schedules into asynchronous Q‑learning controllers for industrial robotics. Buy or develop simulation tools that can estimate reverse chain hitting times to validate the bound before deploying the controllers in production.
papers.Tags: Asynchronous Q-Learning, Finite-Sample Analysis, Hitting Time
papers.Hook: Enables sample‑efficient asynchronous Q‑learning by separating initialization cost via hitting‑time bounds.

papers.Title: Task Context Shapes Component Roles in Language Models
papers.Abstract: Large language models reuse the same attention heads across tasks, but identifying these shared heads does not explain what they do differently in each task. A natural source of inspiration is task-dependent interactions among shared brain regions, which motivate a network view of language-model computation. Here, we compare fixed model components across tasks using identical graph facts, statements specifying which directed connections are present. We measure how interventions affect attention heads and the activation state in later layers (influence), as well as the answer (importance). Task changes redistribute the influence in five open-weight models spanning four families and 1.5-14 billion parameters. In Gemma-2-9B and Qwen3-14B, an activation edit changes an early internal activation vector and switches which fact the model reads while the written instruction stays fixed. The same heads then respond to different graph facts and influence later components differently. For each prompt, we construct two linear response maps, one before the edit and one after it. Each map predicts a later head's response from a measured change in an earlier head. For a separate factual intervention, the map for the corresponding condition reduces mean squared prediction error by 53.6% in Gemma and 5.0% in Qwen compared with the average of the two maps. These findings show that task context changes both which graph facts the shared components respond to and how their outputs affect later computation. A network account may help explain how models use shared parameters to perform different computations. Measurements of task-dependent influence could also guide interventions intended to alter one behavior while preserving others.
papers.Core_Innovation: The authors demonstrate that identical attention heads acquire different functional roles across tasks by showing that task‑dependent activation edits in early layers redirect which factual information the model reads, thereby altering downstream influence without modifying the instruction. This reveals a mechanism where task context re‑routes information flow through fixed network components.
papers.Benefiting_Sectors: Artificial Intelligence, Natural Language Processing, Enterprise AI, Healthcare, Finance
papers.Disrupted_Sectors: Rule‑Based Expert Systems, Manual Data Annotation, Legacy NLP Pipelines
papers.Decision_Perspective: Fund the development of task-specific head reconfiguration toolkits for LLMs within the next six months. Deploy activation-editing interfaces in enterprise AI products to steer factual retrieval without retraining by Q3 2025.
papers.Tags: activation editing, task context, attention heads, influence routing, LLM steering
papers.Hook: Enables switching which factual information a language model reads via internal activation edits.

papers.Title: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics
papers.Abstract: As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED (Reliability-Aware Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re-ranks candidates based on real-time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent, a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query-tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Elliotes/EcoAgent.
papers.Core_Innovation: RATED keeps a frozen dual-encoder for semantic matching and adds a lightweight contextual bandit that observes execution outcomes (success, latency) to re-rank tool candidates online. This enables immediate reliability-aware re‑ranking without model updates.
